articles.title: Drones and Missiles Are Rewriting the Military Balance on the Korean Peninsula
articles.body:
The two Koreas have been close observers of the wars in Ukraine and Iran – not least because aspects of the conflicts mirror how both sides think they will win a potential war on the peninsula. The ongoing exchange of long-range drones and missiles, in particular, resembles the type of war both Koreas envision for themselves: a deep strike contest. To this end, both have recently begun developing low-cost, long-range attack drones, with some systems slated to be operational in the near term.
Long-range artillery, ballistic missiles, and nuclear weapons have, so far, shaped each side’s view of the military balance and whether deterrence holds on the peninsula. Armed drones will soon enter the picture.
These drones will exacerbate the South Korean military’s existing gaps in surveilling the North. Pyongyang’s growing missile and nuclear arsenal and diversified launch platforms have made the problem acute. With cheap attack drones, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ offensive firepower will further outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy it.
This trend is at odds with the Lee administration’s ambitious timeline for gaining wartime operational control from the United States. South Korean forces will need additional capabilities to meet the qualitative conditions previously established by the two allies.
Drones on the Korean Peninsula
Long-range drones – unarmed aerial vehicles with operational range far beyond the forward edge of battle along the armistice line – have been a feature of the inter-Korean military competition for the past two decades. The first known operational use was in 2010 when a North Korean reconnaissance drone was spotted during the Yonpyeong Island shelling. Since then, periodic drone incursions have been a feature of the inter-Korean low-intensity skirmishes.
In 2014, South Korea recovered the wreckage of three North Korean drones less than 50 miles from the border. In December 2022, five North Korean drones overflew Seoul, including the presidential office, and returned North. In response, then-President Yoon Suk-yeol floated the idea of South Korean forces conducting reciprocal drone incursions into North Korea. North Korea claimed South Korean drones overflew Pyongyang in October 2024. While officially denied, public analysis of North Korean-released images visually matched developmental South Korean reconnaissance systems.
Rudimentary platforms – small, fixed-wing, turboprop, and unarmed – have featured in these largely symbolic aerial incursions so far, alongside unpowered balloons. There is no evidence that either side has employed armed drones in cross-border operations. Drones that had been operationally used on the peninsula, however, represent only a small subset of a broader inventory that includes systems with greater range and capability.
North Korea has been importing Chinese and Soviet drones and has been developing indigenous models for reconnaissance missions since the 1980s. In 2023, North Korea unveiled a high-altitude, long-endurance (HALE) reconnaissance drone and a medium-altitude, long-endurance (MALE) multi-role drone. Both are qualitatively different from its existing unmanned aircraft – the latter, for example, is capable of firing a missile – though limited numbers are in the inventory.
For South Korea, abortive development efforts in the late Cold War resumed in the 1990s with a focus on the tactical surveillance drones supporting the Army’s ground operations. Interest in long-range systems came in the late 2000s when the Agency for Defense Development (ADD) started developing a domestic MALE, KUS-FS, and the Republic of Korea Air Force procured Global Hawks from the United States. Four Global Hawks were delivered by 2020, and the KUS-FS is expected to enter service in 2027.
The wars in Ukraine and Iran have catalyzed the two Koreas’ interest in massed, cheap, and armed long-range drones while they continue to invest in large, sophisticated unmanned systems. In 2024, Kim Jong Un ordered officials to “establish a mass-production system and begin full-scale operation” of “suicide attack drones.” Thousands of North Korean laborers, and possibly engineers, have also reportedly been sent to the Yelabuga factory in Russia producing copies of Iran’s Shahed one-way attack (OWA) drone.
For South Korea, the ADD is developing the KUS-LM – dubbed the “K-LUCAS” with reported range and payload figures comparable to the American OWA drone called LUCAS – with plans to deploy it before 2030. The system has started trials on land and sea.
Theories of Victory
These investments by both Koreas in long-range unmanned systems, for both strike and surveillance, will alter the terms of the inter-Korean military competition. In the past few decades, the main domain of the inter-Korean military competition has become a deep strike-centric contest. The ability to wage a strategic air campaign – one not directly connected to the ground fight – is now central to how each side assesses the balance. Both sides appear to believe loitering munitions fit into this air power paradigm.
North Korea has pursued missile and nuclear weapons technology to hold at risk its neighbor and its ally, the United States, with long-range fires. South Korea’s Ministry of National Defense assessed that, in a contingency, North Korea plans a surprise massive firepower attack to create favorable conditions and force a rapid end to the war. Even absent an offensive intent, the threat of catastrophic damage from nuclear missiles and conventional munitions that bypass defenses creates a powerful deterrent intended to prevent attack and ensure regime survival.
Under Kim Jong Un’s rule, North Korea has expanded its missile force to deliver both conventional and nuclear warheads deep into South Korea and, increasingly, beyond the peninsula. The nuclear arsenal, too, has increased both numerically and in centrality to North Korea’s security policy. The KPA Ground Force also operates thousands of artillery pieces – with sufficient range to reach Seoul – out of hardened sites concentrated south of the Pyongyang-Wonsan line.
North Korea appears to see drones as a complementary element of its deep strike strategy, enabled by mass, concealment, and dispersal. Indeed, Kim Jong Un noted three attributes that make OWA drones a needed investment for the Korean People’s Army: low production cost, simple manufacturing process, and ease of integration into existing firepower. Drone salvos launched in conjunction with ballistic and cruise missiles could overwhelm South Korea’s air and missile defenses. Their relatively low cost also reduces the economic burden of procurement on North Korea’s constrained economy.
In response to a nuclear-armed adversary and fear of abandonment from its ally, South Korea has pursued a counterforce “Three Axis system” to serve as a non-nuclear deterrent. This idea has seen iterative conceptual updates over the past decade. Today, the approach rests on a three-pronged framework that combines preemptive strikes on North Korean nuclear and missile facilities (“Kill Chain”), multi-layered missile defense (Air Force-operated “Korea Air and Missile Defense” against ballistic missiles and the Army’s in-development “Low-Altitude Missile Defense” against artillery and short-range rockets), and overwhelming retaliatory firepower against military and leadership targets (“Korea Massive Punishment and Retaliation”).
Efforts in the past five years have sought to integrate drones into the strategy. The Yoon administration established the Drone Operations Command in September 2023 with an explicit mission to develop an offensive concept of operations – before that, South Korea’s military had only used drones for reconnaissance and surveillance. Despite initial criticism of the command as redundant, and its subsequent disestablishment for its implication in Yoon’s 2024 self-coup attempt, the South Korean defense community appears to acknowledge the need for this function. The mission continues in the Defense Drone headquarters, the recently formed successor body that focuses on force development, manning, and equipping – albeit shedding any operational role to the services.
South Korea’s Surveillance Problems
Deterrence on the peninsula holds today as both sides possess long-range strike assets that impose what, for now, are unacceptable risks and costs if the shooting starts. While ground forces remain important in both Koreas’ force structures, the main arena of the inter-Korean competition today lies in deep strike. The drone incursions in the past decade and a half introduced an additional low-intensity element to this competition. The development and eventual deployment of armed drones will create new requirements for South Korea to operationalize its Three Axis strategy and for the United States to defend its treaty ally.
South Korea’s limited intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capacity stands out as a glaring vulnerability in anticipating this future. All three “axes” of its strategy depend on a near-perfect and near-persistent intelligence picture over North Korea, to monitor leadership movements, locate concealed facilities, track mobile missile launchers and submarines, identify incoming missiles – and now, detect drone launch sites and their launches. This is a tall order. South Korea’s ISR capabilities have long been identified as a weakness, as it historically has relied on U.S. capabilities.
ISR drones and additional ISR satellites are intended to supplement existing gaps to operationalize the Three Axis strategy, but even with systems expected to come online in the next five years, mobile targets will remain difficult to find, fix, and track. South Korea’s space-based ISR layer, in development since 2023, leaves roughly 2-hour windows between observation opportunities over potential launch sites. The South Korean Army’s Low Altitude Missile Defense, expected to come online in 2029, was designed to counter artillery threats and may be constrained by insufficient interceptors and sensor networks against drone salvos.
Thus, in the near to medium term, North Korea’s ability to disperse, conceal, and employ its drones, missiles, and nuclear weapons will outpace South Korea’s capacity to destroy them. In fact, North Korea’s rapid operationalization of OWA drones may require greater dedication of U.S. ISR assets to the peninsula.
The added challenge to South Korea’s defense strategy thus poses questions about the Lee administration’s ambitious push for wartime operational control transfer by the end of his term in 2030. The proposed change to the command structure of U.S. and South Korean forces has been tied to improvements in South Korea’s capabilities to lead the Combined Forces Command, including the capacity to operate its own ISR assets to meet operational requirements. The Lee administration has insisted on “no additional conditions” being placed on the transfer requirements. Yet, the deteriorating military balance in this domain will necessitate additional capability to meet the established qualitative conditions for making major changes to the Combined Force.
The author appreciates feedback from colleagues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies – Pat Bazylczyk, Mark Cancian, Emma Gargiulo, and Andy Lim – and the 2026 cohort of the National Committee on American Foreign Policy Korea fellowship.

articles.title: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine on deadly Kyiv strikes
articles.body:
U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine of Russian strikes that killed 6, cut power to 600,000, sources say
The U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings this week of Russian strikes on Ukraine, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning from our partners" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage at Kyiv and other locations early Tuesday.
The sources said American officials told their Ukrainian counterparts the system used to detect Russian missile launches had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the topic, told CBS News they did not believe the excuse, and they accused the U.S. instead of "playing" with the system.
When Russia launched another wave of ballistic missiles around 3 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the sources said the U.S. early warning system appeared to be working again.
The sources said the U.S. had failed to provide intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches during one previous instance earlier this year, citing the need to focus more resources on the Middle East.
Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Russia launched more than 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions during the overnight attack, primarily targeting energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power.
The strikes started soon after President Trump said in a social media post that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire."
Earlier this week, the Trump administration threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine did not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, a European and a Ukrainian official told CBS News.
Ukraine relies on U.S. intelligence for both offensive and defensive military capabilities, including data from satellites and aircraft sensors used to identify launches of Russian aircraft and missiles. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News the U.S. had not ceased intelligence sharing with Ukraine overall — calling the lack of a warning about this week's attacks a specific incident.
Ukrainian officials and soldiers also told CBS News that Ukraine's military had started experiencing difficulties Tuesday night and Wednesday morning with Starlink, the satellite technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk.
In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Ukraine's former minister of defense Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink was one of Ukraine's most important technologies, as it allows Ukrainian soldiers to communicate and carry out strikes in environments saturated by electronic warfare.
"On the night of 14 October, without warning the Defence Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals ('military package') while in motion. This complicates UAV missions, particularly interceptors and middle-strike drones, and reduces capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and signal relay," sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense told CBS News. "At present, the Ministry of Defence is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners, is collecting data from all units, and backup communication channels are being tested and put into use."
The Starlink restrictions were first reported by the Kyiv Independent and the Financial Times. CBS News has reached out to SpaceX, the White House, and the Pentagon for comment.
On Wednesday, as President Zelenskyy arrived in the United Kingdom to meet with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other officials, he called for a U.S. response to the recent Russian strikes.
"The strike was absolutely deliberate and indicative in its scale — such a demonstrative disrespect from Russia toward America has never happened before. Russia does not consider the statements of the President of America to be strong," he wrote on X. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to respond, and to respond harshly."

articles.title: Russia Innovates for War, Not Prosperity
articles.body:
Russia excels at making things that destroy – at the expense of its own future.
Since Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has concentrated its technological expertise, dwindling human capital, and oil-and-gas revenues on war, rather than on its people’s well-being.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It has sharply increased production of missiles, glide bombs, and attack drones. Russian forces have improved their electronic warfare capabilities, learned to modify Iranian-designed Shahed drones, and incorporated Chinese jet engines into Banderol quasi-cruise missiles. Cheap first-person-view drones saturate the battlefield, and Russian engineers have devised increasingly sophisticated decoys to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Russia’s war machine is inflicting ever-greater death and devastation on Ukraine.
Four and a half years of war have created a war economy in which the Kremlin can concentrate money, engineers, imported components, and industrial capacity on its military priorities. That concentration of resources has imposed mounting costs that are becoming harder to conceal.
In September, the Bank of Russia kept its benchmark interest rate at 14 percent and forecast inflation of 6 to 7 percent for 2026. Russia is no longer experiencing the apparent wartime boom that followed the invasion. High interest rates make investment and modernization expensive, while military factories compete with civilian companies for engineers, machinists, capital and materials.
12 Senators Sign Bipartisan Letter Urging Trump to Rescind Russian Diesel Deal
In an article entitled “The Coming Crisis in Russia’s Political Economy,” published in May, Nigel Gould-Davies of the International Institute for Strategic Studies argues that Russia is approaching the limits of its productive capacity. Labor is an even tighter constraint. Oil-and-gas revenue can finance government spending but it cannot manufacture skilled workers or create factories, industrial equipment, and technological knowledge. As more resources are pushed into the military economy, each additional increment produces less.
Nowhere is Russia’s predicament clearer than in semiconductors. Mikron, part of the Rostec- and Sberbank-controlled Element Group, is a leading Russian chip manufacturer. It advertises production technologies ranging down to 90 nanometers; such mature semiconductors remain essential for automobiles, industrial equipment and many military systems.
By contrast, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) began volume production of its 2-nanometer technology late last year. Russia lacks the advanced chip-design capabilities, fabrication capacity, high-bandwidth memory, packaging, interconnects, cooling systems, and sophisticated software needed to manufacture processors competitive with those produced by TSMC and other leading semiconductor companies.
This matters because technological backwardness is not measured against where competitors stood five or ten years ago but where they are today. A Russian company that replaces an unavailable Western component may keep a factory operating but it has not narrowed the technological gap – it has merely reconstructed yesterday’s technology at considerable expense.
The pace outside Russia is accelerating further. On Sept. 30, 2026, OpenAI and Synopsys announced GPT-Synopsys, an artificial intelligence (AI) system being developed specifically to help design semiconductors. AI is increasingly being applied to the process of designing the next generation of technology itself.
Russian engineers, meanwhile, have a very different assignment – finding substitutes for unavailable software, maintaining aging equipment, and solving compatibility problems caused by sanctions. Russia calls this “technological sovereignty.”
One of its own most prominent businessmen has inadvertently exposed the weakness of that claim. In May, Sberbank CEO German Gref said Russia’s largest bank hoped eventually to operate its GigaChat AI system using Chinese processors. One of Russia’s showcase AI projects may depend on sophisticated chips Russia cannot competitively manufacture itself.
According to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with official assessments, more than 90 percent of Russia’s imports of sanctioned technology were coming through China by 2026. Before the war, Russian companies could participate, however imperfectly, in a diversified international technology economy. Putin has replaced much of that relationship with dependence on a single, more powerful neighbor whose interests do not necessarily align.
The deeper damage from this process is cumulative because industrial equipment and information systems require replacement parts, software updates, firmware, calibration, technical documentation and continuing support. A machine does not stop operating the morning its foreign manufacturer leaves Russia. It becomes progressively more difficult to maintain.
The results of Russia’s import-substitution campaign point in that direction. In a May 2026 study based on official documents, statistical data, and company surveys, Heli Simola of the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) found that heavy investment in priority industries had produced only limited import substitution. In many sectors, output has declined and dependence on foreign inputs has increased.
The same problem appears in information technology. Russian technology company K2Tech reported this year that 70 percent of companies it examined remained dependent on Western backup systems. Russian replacements exist, but companies have been reluctant to abandon established foreign systems for critical operations.
Industrial deterioration is rarely instantaneous, but Ukraine has found a way to accelerate that process. Its deep drone strikes against Russian refineries and industrial facilities amount to what Ukrainians have aptly called “long-range sanctions.” Destroying a piece of equipment matters more when replacing it is difficult.
The Aug. 11, 2026 strike against the Orsk refinery illustrates the point. The refinery was forced to shut after a Ukrainian drone attack, and according to Orenburg Oblast Governor Yevgeny Solntsev, repairs are expected to take as long as six months because sanctions complicated the replacement of imported equipment.
Damage to one industrial facility consequently spreads outward – to fuel availability, transportation, military logistics, export revenues, and, ultimately, prices paid by Russian consumers.
None of the above makes Russia less dangerous. Russia has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to improvise, cannibalize commercial technologies, and solve particular military problems. This, however, is precisely the distinction that matters. A country can become exceptionally good at concentrating declining resources on weapons without becoming technologically stronger as a whole.
Putin inherited a country with considerable scientific talent, engineering traditions and industrial capacity. He has squandered that inheritance. Engineers are diverted toward weapons, civilian investment is crowded out, and Russian companies spend money reproducing technologies already available elsewhere. Dependence on Western technology has increasingly become dependence on Chinese technology. With every additional year of war, Russia risks becoming less capable of designing, building, and maintaining the technologies on which its future will depend.
Steven Fisher served as CEO of Citibank Ukraine from 2010 to 2018. He and Georgetown University’s Harley Balzer coedited Failure: Russia Under Putin (Brookings Institution Press, 2025). This op-ed was prompted in part by Balzer’s unpublished manuscript, “Technocide: How Putin’s Regime Stole Russia’s Future.”
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Aramco executives' offices damaged in Houthi attack, regional officials say
articles.body:
An overnight Houthi strike damaged executive offices at Saudi oil giant Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, two regional officials told The Associated Press on Wednesday, as fresh explosions shook Riyadh and the Iran-backed rebels intensified their missile and drone campaign against Saudi Arabia.
The reported damage to one of the kingdom's most important economic institutions came amid renewed attacks on airports, military installations and oil infrastructure, raising concerns about Saudi Arabia's ability to withstand sustained strikes and the potential consequences for global energy markets.
Residents of Riyadh reported hearing additional explosions Wednesday. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defenses had intercepted cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and drones targeting the capital, as well as a ballistic missile aimed at Dhahran and a cruise missile targeting Al-Kharj.
Dhahran is home to Aramco's headquarters, while Al-Kharj houses Prince Sultan Air Base and Saudi Arabia's state-owned Military Industries Corporation.
The attacks have increased pressure on US President Donald Trump, who has said he is considering whether American forces should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Saudi officials have reported repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the past week, with strikes killing at least 18 people and injuring more than 300.
The Houthis described the latest attacks as retaliation for what they called Saudi aggression against Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-held capital, and other areas under their control.
Russia and China involved in ceasefire efforts
Despite the escalation, diplomatic efforts to halt the fighting are underway.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis' political bureau, told AP that Oman had attempted to bring the warring sides back to negotiations, while Russia and China had also pursued contacts through Iran.
"We're welcoming any mediation that leads to an end of the war and the blockade between Sanaa and Riyadh," al-Bukhaiti said.
"We're ready for a comprehensive end of the war and the blockade from both sides, not just a temporary ceasefire."
The Houthis nevertheless continued threatening Saudi airports and oil installations.
The attacks have severely disrupted air travel across the kingdom. More than 3,000 flights scheduled to depart from Saudi airports over the past week were canceled or listed as not operating, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
The campaign has also highlighted the Houthis' ability to inflict significant disruption despite Saudi Arabia's advanced Western-supplied air defenses.
Saudi air defenses under growing pressure
Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest purchasers of American weapons, has sought additional military support from allies as it confronts daily missile and drone attacks across a vast territory.
Regional officials have warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors, while military analysts say completely preventing Houthi strikes is virtually impossible.
Saudi Arabia covers an area approximately three times the size of Texas, and Houthi weapons are capable of reaching targets more than 1,600 kilometers, or 1,000 miles, away. Some missiles can also change course during flight, complicating interception efforts.
Even successful interceptions can cause casualties and damage on the ground.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles fell on residential neighborhoods in Riyadh overnight, injuring four people, including a child, and damaging 15 homes.
The escalating attacks have revived concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and transportation networks, with repeated strikes threatening facilities central to the kingdom's economy.
Saudi strikes intensify inside Yemen
Saudi Arabia has responded with its own military operations against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, supporting the country's internationally recognized government.
The latest confrontation erupted after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of attacking an airport in Sanaa, reigniting tensions over the longstanding Saudi blockade of rebel-held territory.
The Houthis subsequently announced their own blockade against Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive approximately a week and a half ago.
On Wednesday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said two people had been killed and two wounded in a Saudi airstrike Tuesday on an oil facility in the Ras Isa port area of Hodeida province.
The Saudi-led coalition also struck an oil facility in Sanaa.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the attacks on fuel storage facilities in Houthi-held areas represented a new phase in the conflict.
He warned that a prolonged war of attrition could significantly weaken the Houthis' military capabilities.
"The Houthis are betting on pressure, while the Saudis are betting on time," Nagi said.
"The Houthis are trying to strike critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia to raise the cost of continued military intervention and support for the Yemeni government."
Humanitarian crisis deepens
The renewed fighting has also threatened to plunge Yemen deeper into the civil war that devastated the country before four years of relative calm.
The International Committee of the Red Cross reported an unprecedented increase in people suffering weapons-related injuries along Yemen's front lines, particularly in Marib, Taiz and areas near the Red Sea.
Hospitals are struggling to cope with the surge in casualties, with increasingly frequent incidents involving large numbers of wounded patients.
The World Food Program also warned that it could no longer reach more than 600,000 people dependent on humanitarian assistance in the besieged city of Taiz.
With Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continuing to exchange strikes, the diplomatic efforts involving Oman, Russia and China have yet to produce a breakthrough, leaving both the kingdom's critical infrastructure and Yemen's civilian population exposed to further escalation.

articles.title: ‘Blatant Disrespect Toward America’: Zelensky Slams Russia’s Strike on Ukraine’s Energy Sector
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky urged US President Donald Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia after a massive overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure left at least 600,000 people without electricity.
In a Telegram post on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky said Russia had launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He described the ballistic strike on Ukraine’s energy sector as deliberate and said its scale demonstrated Russia’s disregard for Washington’s calls for a ceasefire.
“Russia does not view the US President’s statements as strong,” Zelensky said, calling on the US and others to respond firmly to Moscow’s actions.
He urged Trump to impose “STRONG sanctions” on Russia, referring to legislation introduced by US Senator Lindsey Graham that Zelensky said provided the necessary tools to increase pressure on Moscow. He also called for additional interceptor missiles for Ukraine’s Patriot air defense systems.
“Peace can only be achieved through strength,” Zelensky said, invoking a principle associated with former US President Ronald Reagan.
The president added that further power outages were possible as Ukrainian crews worked to repair the damage. According to him, the attack damaged facilities and equipment at 26 sites in Ukraine’s electric power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector. He also reported casualties and injuries but did not provide figures.
Russian Overnight Strikes Target Kyiv CHP Plants and Kill Civilians Across Ukraine
Air defenses intercept 119 targets
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia began the combined attack at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 13, launching 167 aerial weapons, including 39 missiles and 128 attack drones of various types.
The missiles included Iskander-M, North Korean KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx types. The drones included Shahed-type weapons, among them 77 jet-powered drones, as well as Banderol, Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force said aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups were involved in repelling the attack.
As of 9 a.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 119 targets: four missiles and 115 drones. The intercepted drones included 59 jet-powered ones.
The Air Force reported missile and drone impacts at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their intended targets.
Ukraine again reports missing missile warnings, White House offers no explanation
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building late on Tuesday, Oct. 13, killing at least three people and injuring 21, including an eight-year-old child, Ukrainian officials reported.
The attack hit the capital at around 10:40 p.m., sparking fires across several districts. In the Desnianskyi district, a fire spread across apartments on the first through eighth floors before firefighters extinguished it.
Rescuers recovered two bodies from the building and evacuated 16 residents, while other strikes caused fires and casualties in the Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi, Darnytskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
Zelensky said CHP-4 was a main target and that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners about the incoming ballistic missiles for the second consecutive night.
The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed that no warning had come through the usual channels, while presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said military and intelligence services were investigating the missing notifications.
Notably, President Donald Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine, rejecting suggestions that the US had halted cooperation.
However, his administration has yet to explain why Ukraine received no early missile warnings for two consecutive nights.
Asked by Fox News correspondent whether the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday, Oct. 13: “I’ll have to get back to you on that.”

articles.title: Allies failed to warn Ukraine of impending missile attack, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Allies failed to warn Ukraine of impending missile attack, Zelensky says
- Ukraine says allies gave no warning before a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, and Zelensky called the strike “particularly vile” as five missiles hit civilian infrastructure.
- Trump said the US is still sharing intelligence and working with Kyiv and Moscow, while Ukraine said it has stopped attacking Russian refineries since his “energy ceasefire” announcement.
- Russia hit transport and logistics instead of energy sites overnight, killing four in Kharkiv and wounding many, as Ukraine warned that US early-warning intelligence is vital to save lives.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukraine received no prior warning from its Western partners about a Russian ballistic missile attack on its capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13, as Kyiv comes under intense US pressure to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Russia hit no Ukrainian energy targets overnight for the first time since US President Donald Trump’s surprise Oct 11 announcement of an “energy ceasefire”, but hammered transport and logistics with ballistic missiles and drones.
Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes, experts and officials say.
Speaking to reporters on Oct 13, Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine and is working with both Kyiv and Moscow to bring an end to the war. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he said.
Trump was asked whether Russia had violated the ceasefire and answered: “I’ll let you know about that later.”
Asked if Russia could use proceeds from the diesel deal to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s a diesel deal, not for us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us.”
Zelensky said Ukraine had not targeted Russian refineries since Trump’s announcement on Oct 11.
He said Kyiv had not received the usual warning from allies of ballistic missile launches before a “particularly vile” attack on Kyiv overnight, in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives,” Zelensky said on X, “and this is one of the most critical issues.” He stopped short of linking the lack of warning to any US threats.
Air raid alerts sound in Kyiv only after blasts are heard
Air alerts sounded in Kyiv on the night of Oct 12 only after several explosions had already ripped through the city.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha tried to calm anxiety by saying Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, he said the delay had been due to the specifics of the weaponry that Russia had used.
As Ukraine fights a larger, richer and better-equipped enemy, Kyiv sees the strikes on Russian oil refineries as one of its few instruments to reduce Moscow’s ability to fight.
Yet Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks – which prompted Moscow to suspend diesel exports – for a sharp rise in US fuel prices in 2026, a headache for his Republican Party ahead of Congressional midterm elections in three weeks.
Most analysts, however, say Trump’s war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise.
Russia had struck six Ukrainian energy sites on Oct 12. It was unclear whether Moscow had deliberately avoided energy infrastructure overnight and on Oct 13.
A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details.
In his nightly video address posted on X, Zelensky said he had sent proposals to US officials with a view to new meetings in coming days with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ways to resolve the conflict.
He said Ukraine supported Trump’s announcement of an energy truce provided that Russia observed it. “We need to work for peace, we need to look for ways to do the proper actions. Ukraine is ready for meetings,” he said.
Earlier, Zelensky reiterated Ukraine’s position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia.
A Ukrainian delegation held talks in the United States last week and people familiar with the meeting said Witkoff and Kushner told them that a deal to allow Russian diesel exports was part of a bid to draw Russia back to negotiations.
Ukraine says it now has cards to play
Russian strikes killed four people in Ukraine’s second-largest city, Kharkiv, and dozens were wounded across the country, Ukrainian officials said.
The Ukrainian air force said it was investigating the failure to receive surveillance warnings before the attack.
Fabian Hoffmann, missile expert at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, said Ukraine’s European allies had “very limited” ability to replace US early-warning intelligence about Russian missile strikes.
“Ukraine relies on the so-called Space-Based Infrared System which the US deploys – and the US system is really second to none and only the United States can provide that.”
Sybiha said the US request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine’s position had strengthened, alluding to Trump’s comment to Zelensky in a tense Oval Office meeting in 2025 that “you don’t have the cards”.
“In less than two years, we have gone from ‘having no cards’ to ‘not playing your cards’. That is an achievement,” Sybiha said.
Zelensky reiterated Ukraine’s position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia. REUTERS

articles.title: SpaceX limits Starlink operations in Ukraine, disrupting military ops., missile defense capability
articles.body:
SpaceX has introduced a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, stopping the operation of its military-grade version above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), disrupting combat missions, presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said on Wednesday.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," he wrote on Telegram, adding: "It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation."
Ukrainian officials fear the move was made at Trump's request
Ukraine’s security services detected disruptions to Starlink terminals across the country overnight on Tuesday night, a source familiar with the matter confirmed to The Jerusalem Post. Ukrainian officials fear the move by the company, owned by Elon Musk, may have been made at the request of US President Donald Trump.
Starlink terminals are one of the key tools enabling Ukrainians to maintain internet access amid Russia’s invasion. The disruptions reportedly interfered with several critical operations.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a social media post that Ukraine had not received an alert about incoming Russian strikes. “This is already the second time this has happened,” Zelensky wrote.
“During the first wave of drone and missile strikes, no warning was received, but an alert was issued during the second wave,” a source familiar with the matter added in a statement to the Post.
Trump himself claimed on Tuesday that the United States had not halted intelligence-sharing cooperation with Ukraine. "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel," Trump told reporters. "We want the war to end, so we're working with them and Russia on getting the war to end."
Zelensky said Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones overnight on Tuesday night, targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure across Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian president, approximately 500,000 people were left without electricity following the attack.
Ukrainian negotiators traveled to the US on Friday and Saturday to urge US President Donald Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia.
Zelensky accuses US of inaction as Russian strikes kill over 70 in two days
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to over 70.
Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelensky criticized Washington's effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war.
Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said in an emotional statement.
Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow's increasingly brutal air war.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assertion earlier on Thursday that the war is at a stalemate and that the United States would keep working toward a settlement.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelensky added.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of crippling drone missions as ties with US worsen
articles.body:
Ukraine accuses SpaceX of crippling drone missions as ties with US worsen
KYIV, Oct 14 - Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russian missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelenskiy called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since US President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelenskiy.
Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
The US president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
NO WARNING BEFORE STARLINK CUTS
Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones.
"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man". SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of US business hours.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its one-time ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organisations that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
NO WARNING AHEAD OF MISSILES
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's defence ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russian attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelenskiy cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelenskiy wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelenskiy has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just 4 out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air-defences against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia, and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120 km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine renew accusations concerning overnight strikes that kill 5
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
- Moscow claims downing 902 Ukrainian drones over 19 regions, Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014
- Ukraine claims shooting down 115 out of 128 drones and 4 out of 39 missiles launched by Russia in attacks that targeted Kyiv, Kharkiv
Russia and Ukraine on Wednesday renewed accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that have killed at least four people in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv and one in the Russian region of Saratov.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement on Telegram that three people died following Russian shelling, with cleanup and response operations underway in three districts.
A fire that erupted at the site of a strike on a high-rise building in the Desnianskyi district has been extinguished, the statement said, noting that 16 residents of the building were rescued.
“Twenty-one people were injured, including one child. Emergency rescue operations are ongoing,” it also said, adding that one person was killed and another injured following a strike on a non-residential building in the Holosiivskyi district.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said separately that energy facilities in the capital and the surrounding region have been hit by a “massive” ballistic missile strike, with power outages in the city.
The Ukrainian State Emergency Service said five people were injured in the city of Derhachi in the northeastern Kharkiv region after a drone hit a garage unit at a civilian enterprise.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that its air forces shot down 115 out of 128 drones, as well as four out of 39 missiles, launched by Russia overnight during attacks targeting Kyiv and Kharkiv regions.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a statement on US social media company X.
At least 600,000 people are now without power in Ukraine due to the strikes, Zelenskyy added, noting significant damage to 26 facilities of the country’s power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector.
He also called for “strong” sanctions against Russia, asking for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed that it launched a massive strike against communication and energy infrastructure facilities in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions that have been “used to support the military-industrial complex” of Ukraine’s military. 
Strikes in Russia
It further claimed downing 902 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses downed 493 Ukrainian drones heading toward the region between 8.30 pm (1730GMT) on Tuesday and 7 am (0400GMT) on Wednesday, with 180 of them intercepted as they approached the capital.
Saratov Governor Roman Busargin said that one person was killed in the city of Balakovo after a drone strike in the region damaged several residential buildings in the city.
“All infrastructure facilities in Balakovo are operating normally. The head of the district has been tasked with setting up an operational headquarters on-site and maintaining constant communication with residents of the affected buildings,” Busargin added.
Alexander Vedyakhin, first deputy CEO of Russian banking and financial services company Sberbank, confirmed an attack on its data center in Balakovo in remarks to journalists, adding that all company systems and services are operating normally and without disruption.
Independent verification of Russia's and Ukraine’s claims is difficult due to the ongoing war.
Moscow and Kyiv have intensified strikes in recent months, targeting each other's logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities only.
On Sunday, Trump announced on his Truth Social media platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy told Axios earlier Sunday that Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, stressing that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by guarantees.
Meanwhile, Peskov said Monday that the Kremlin had no immediate comment on the proposed halt, though contacts with the US concerning the topic were ongoing.

articles.title: Ukraine live: Russia's 'targeted' strikes on energy leave 600,000 without power, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine live: EU sees 'no indication' US intel-sharing halted as Kyiv slams Starlink restrictions
The EU on Wednesday said it had no indication that Washington had halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine after Kyiv complained it had not been warned of incoming Russian strikes. An adviser to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier said that unannounced restrictions to the Starlink satellite system were “depriving” the country of its means of defence. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
UK PM Burnham looks to 'repair bridges' between Trump, Zelensky
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he will seek to "repair bridges" between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky amid strained ties between the pair.
Burnham made the comments before he was due to welcome Zelensky to his official Downing Street residence, in a show of support for Ukraine's president following new criticism by Trump.
Russia drone attack kills 6 in Ukrainian city of Lutsk, interior ministry says
A Russian jet-powered drone attack on the city of Lutsk in western Ukraine killed six people in a retail grocery warehouse, the interior ministry and local authorities said.
Debris from a Russian jet-powered drone fell on the city, triggering a fire in the warehouse. Six people were killed and 12 wounded, the Ukrainian interior ministry told AFP.
Zelensky in London to meet with Burnham
Starlink curbs to affect Ukrainian interceptor drones and middle strikes, two sources say
SpaceX's slowdown of Starlink services for Ukraine's military will affect its ability to conduct medium-range strikes and to use interceptor drones to counter incoming long-range Russian drones, a Ukrainian defence ministry source and a military source said.
Ukrainian troops have reported that the Starlink connection is being shut off when travelling at higher speeds, causing major disruption to Ukrainian drone operations, many of which depend on satellite internet to pilot the craft.
IEA says Russian oil output up 65,000 bpd in September, still down on the year
Russia's crude oil production increased by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd, but still remained some 870,000 bpd below year-ago level, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday.
The Paris-based IEA also said that the recently announced easing of Russian diesel export restrictions was unlikely to materially change the global gasoil market balance because of a lack of operational Russian refinery capacity.
The agency, which advises industrialised countries and manages their strategic oil reserves, said Russian crude exports rose 60,000 bpd last month from August to 5.3 million bpd, while estimated refinery runs remained flat for a second consecutive month as Ukrainian strikes continued to disrupt refining operations.
Crude output in Russia, the world's third-largest oil producer, has been declining amid Ukraine's strikes on the country's energy infrastructure, including oil refineries.
Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery following what the authorities say is a Ukrainian drone strike in Moscow on September, 20, 2026. © Stringer, Reuters
In photos: Kyiv apartment building damaged by a Russian missile strike
A family evacuates their burning apartment building following a Russian strike in Kyiv on October 13, 2026. © Reuters
A residential building on fire following a Russian missile strike in Kyiv overnight on Tuesday © AP
A resident smokes a cigarette after his apartment building was hit by a strike in Kyiv on October 13, 2026. © AP
Ukraine asking US, SpaceX and NATO to clarify Starlink limitations, source says
Ukraine is in contact with the US, SpaceX and NATO to seek clarification over limitations imposed on its access to the Starlink satellite internet system, a source in the country's Defence Ministry said on Wednesday.
Ukrainian troops have reported that the Starlink connection is being shut off when travelling at higher speeds, causing major disruption to Ukrainian drone operations, many of which depend on satellite internet to pilot the craft.
Wreckage found on Baltic beach was Polish drone from military exercise, minister says
An object found on a Polish beach is the remains of a Polish drone that was destroyed as part of an exercise conducted by the country's military, Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Wednesday.
"Drone tests were conducted a few weeks ago in Ustka (a town on the Baltic coast). This is a Polish drone that was destroyed by Polish anti-drone systems during the exercises," Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
A Defence Ministry spokesperson said earlier that preliminary findings indicated the fragments belonged to a test drone from a Polish military aviation technology institute.
US diesel deal 'positive signal' for Russian economy, Deputy PM Novak says
The US diesel deal will boost Russia's economy and allow it to increase production and refining volumes with supplies shipped directly to the US and global markets, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Wednesday.
"Without a doubt, this is a positive signal for our economy," he told reporters.
Bulgaria probing report that Starlink antennas set on fire
Bulgaria is investigating a report that several antennas used for communication with the Starlink satellite network were deliberately set on fire, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Wednesday.
"The investigation is extremely intensive. We are working with partner services to successfully carry out this operation," Radev said in parliament, without confirming or denying the claim.
Ukraine uses the Starlink satellite system controlled by SpaceX owner Elon Musk for battlefield communications.
A Bulgarian opposition MP on Monday said 11 telecommunications antennas linked to the Starlink network were set on fire over the weekend "at a secret facility near Sofia".
"The burned antennas serve as the main link to Musk's satellites in space, which are actively used in the war in Ukraine," Ivaylo Mirtchev, a pro-European opposition MP, said in a Facebook post.
EU seeks to raise cash for Ukraine at IMF and G7 meetings, European Commissioner says
Ukraine faces a funding gap for 2027 and the European Union is trying to raise extra cash for the country at the meetings of the International Monetary Fund and G7 finance ministers this week in Bangkok, European Economic Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said.
Ukraine's 2026 funding is already covered, with some €31 billion from the EU waiting for disbursement as soon as Kyiv votes through the agreed reforms.
But despite another €45 billion ($50 billion) already promised from the EU for 2027, Ukraine's needs will be much higher and the EU is scrambling to organise the cash from countries such as Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan or Britain.
"This is one of the topics being discussed during the IMF and G7 meetings, where we are seeking to mobilise support from other partners," Dombrovskis told Reuters on the sidelines of the IMF meetings in Bangkok.
Bulgaria expects to join NATO anti-drone initiative this month, minister says
Bulgaria expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Wednesday, a day after a drone attack sank a cargo vessel off the country's Black Sea coast for the second time in a week.
The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine war poses to commercial shipping near NATO's southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defences in the Black Sea.
"Bulgaria will be part of this project as soon as possible. Expectations are that by October 30, we will already be part of the project," local media quoted Stoyanov as telling a parliamentary hearing.
Russia's diesel deal with US opens way for more cooperation, Kremlin envoy says
The US-Russia diesel deal can pave the way for further economic cooperation between the two countries, Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said adding that Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the diesel supplies.
The example of diesel cooperation with the US "will open other opportunities as well," he told reporters.
Ukraine says it frees more territory in Donetsk region counteroffensive
Ukraine has freed 16 villages from Russian forces in the eastern Donetsk region in its latest counteroffensive, a senior commander said on Wednesday, part of what he called a major frontline pushback amid increased Russian air attacks elsewhere.
Kyiv's Third Army Corps has waged an operation, announced last month, to dislodge Russian troops north of the strategic city of Sloviansk, one of the two main bastions in Ukraine's so-called "fortress belt" anchoring its eastern defences.
Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said recent Ukrainian assaults had liberated three more villages in the area of the counteroffensive - some 30 km (19 miles) north of Sloviansk - bringing the total of freed territory to 277 square kilometres (107 square miles) and the number of settlements to 16.
Russia, whose pace of battlefield gains has slowed this year, has demanded that Ukraine cede the 20 percent of the Donetsk region it still controls before it stops fighting.
'No change' in US intel sharing policy with Ukraine, US official
Russian attack on Ukraine's western city of Lutsk on Wednesday killed three and injured at least 12, the regional governor said.
Drone debris hit a warehouse, Roman Romaniuk said on Telegram. A residential building was damaged as well, he added.
Scope of Ukraine energy ceasefire not yet determined, Kremlin says
The terms of a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump have not been established and work is ongoing to do so, the Kremlin’s spokesman has told reporters.
Dmitry Peskov made the remarks when asked if overnight Russian attacks on several Ukrainian energy targets showed that Russia did not accept the ceasefire.
"Has anything been specified in concrete terms?" he said. "No ... and that is why work in this area is continuing."
EU says 'no indications' US intel-sharing with Ukraine halted
The EU has no indication that the United States has halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine, the EU Commission spokeswoman has said after Kyiv complained it was not warned of incoming Russian strikes.
"We have no indications that intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped," Paula Pinho, chief spokeswoman for the European Commission, told journalists.
Polish FM challenges 'big man' Musk over reported Starlink cuts
Poland's foreign minister has asked Elon Musk if he is "playing politics" with Starlink in Ukraine.
Poland has said that it pays for Kyiv's Starlink subscription, which is vital for guiding longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and eastern Ukraine that have wreaked havoc on Russian logistics.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Sikorski wrote in a post on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response to the post from Musk.
The "big man" jibe referred to a very public dispute on social media between Sikorski, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in 2025, when the Tesla and Space X boss told Sikorski, "Be quiet, small man".
NATO countries 'need to do more' to boost Ukraine air defences, says Rutte
NATO chief Mark Rutte has urged alliance members to step up support for Ukraine's air defences as Russia's strikes pound the country.
"With winter coming and with Russia's aggression unrelenting, allies need to do more, especially in support of air defence," Rutte said at a press conference in Estonia.
NATO and EU officials have previously said they are asking countries to dig deeper into their stockpiles to supply Ukraine with air defences.
Yesterday's key developments:
- Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday that a Russian ballistic missile struck a Kyiv power plant without advance warning from Western allies, killing at least two people and wounding around 20. The attack came days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, raising questions over efforts to halt strikes on critical infrastructure.
(FRANCE 24 with AP, Reuters and AFP)

articles.title: Russia Maps Out War Scenarios to 2045, Six Involving Northern Europe, Ukrainian Intelligence Says
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Maps Out War Scenarios to 2045, Six Involving Northern Europe, Ukrainian Intelligence Says
Russia is considering scenarios for direct military confrontation with European countries through 2045, including potential conflicts involving Northern Europe, Poland, and the Baltic states, Ukrainian intelligence warned on October 13.
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) published the assessment on its official website, outlining Moscow's long-term military planning and ongoing hybrid operations against Europe.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the agency, Russia has not abandoned the possibility of direct armed conflict with Europe. Moscow is examining several potential military conflict scenarios through 2045, including six involving Northern Europe and others concerning Poland and the Baltic states.
The intelligence service warned that Russia could provoke a controlled regional crisis on NATO's eastern flank, forcing the Alliance to make critical decisions under severe time pressure and uncertainty.
Such a scenario would aim to expose perceived weaknesses in NATO's ability to respond collectively rather than defeat the Alliance in a direct military confrontation.
Meanwhile, Moscow continues employing hybrid warfare tactics, including sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation, drone incursions, and espionage. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that approximately 400 Russian intelligence officers are operating across Europe.
The assessment follows repeated nuclear threats from the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, who recently claimed Moscow had no intention of attacking Europe but warned that Russia could use nuclear weapons if attacked.
Ukrainian intelligence characterized Russia's activities as part of a prolonged confrontation aimed at weakening European security and undermining support for Ukraine.
Russia's covert network inside Europe has already surfaced in specific plans and arrests. Earlier in October, Russian special services were instructed to intensify hybrid operations across EU and NATO states, relying on agents recruited by the GRU and FSB.
Starlink receiving stations in Europe were identified among the likely targets. In Latvia, two citizens were detained on suspicion of gathering intelligence for the GRU on NATO activity, radar systems, and military infrastructure, with one allegedly photographing the Ādaži military base from a private aircraft.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: U.S. moves leave Ukraine less able to defend itself
articles.body:
- Ukraine received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches for two straight nights, the Ukrainian Air Force said, detecting missiles only minutes before impact.
- Starlink also stopped working above 160 km/h for Ukraine’s military, hitting tactical drones used in defense, as Russia’s strike left 600,000 without power.
Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian strikes has been limited by two U.S. moves in a single night: the country went without early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches from its partners for a second time in a row, and Starlink, the U.S. satellite service its frontline units depend on, was cut back for the Ukrainian military just as Russia launched one of its heaviest missile attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m. on Oct. 13, and that once again no information about the launches had come from Ukraine’s partners before the missiles were in the air. The Air Force said the reasons were being investigated.
“The situation is similar to yesterday’s. No information regarding launches from enemy territory had been received from our partners. The reasons are being investigated,” the Ukrainian Air Force said in an official statement.
Ukraine has relied heavily on early warning from the United States, whose satellites can spot the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, giving Ukrainian air defense crews time to prepare and giving cities time to sound air raid sirens. Without those alerts, Ukrainian forces only detected the incoming ballistic missiles once they came within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, and tried to shoot some of them down. The lost minutes shorten the reaction time for interceptor crews and hit civilians hardest, leaving people in Kyiv and other cities less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The attack that followed was massive. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight into Oct. 14 at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. He said there were dead and injured and warned that outages could spread.
Zelenskyy said the missile salvo deliberately targeted the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, which Moscow never confirmed accepting.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military began losing their connection whenever they moved faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who is widely known by his call sign “Flash” and who has tracked Russian attempts to jam Starlink along the front, said the restriction hit the military StarShield package of the SpaceX service and that units received no notice before it took effect.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov.
The restriction falls on Ukraine’s defense, not on its strikes inside Russia. SpaceX has never allowed Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Kyiv was still asking for that permission, so Ukraine’s long-range drones and cruise missiles that hit targets in Russia do not rely on the service. Starlink has also been unavailable to Russian forces since February, when SpaceX and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry introduced a whitelist that cut off unregistered Russian terminals. Inside Ukraine, Starlink is used on tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles that operate over Ukrainian and Russian-occupied territory, so a speed cap above 160 km/h cuts the links of fast tactical strike and interceptor drones fighting Russian troops and drones along the front.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko, who first reported the change, said ordinary satellite terminals kept working and suggested SpaceX may have acted at the request of the Trump administration, while British analyst Jimmy Rushton noted that the limit does nothing to protect the Russian oil refineries Trump has criticized Ukraine for striking.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of Russia’s strike packages for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of its air defense systems, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot batteries to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for more Patriot interceptors and called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed in September.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine,” said Zelenskyy.
The Ukrainian Air Force warned that further Russian attacks cannot be ruled out. Neither the White House nor SpaceX has explained why the missile launch warnings stopped or why the Starlink speed limit was introduced, or said whether either change is temporary.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis and Saudi-led coalition trade fire
articles.body:
Tit-for-tat strikes between Saudi and Houthis, with the Saudi-led coalition striking Sanaa and its surroundings, while the Houthis target Saudi Aramco facilities
Iran and Oman are "close to establishing safe commercial shipping routes" in the Strait of Hormuz after reaching an understanding for a "temporary safe passage route”, Iran’s foreign ministry said
Major Palestinian factions gather in Cairo to discuss national unity and upcoming elections
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon, and southern Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
And so we continue our live coverage...
Two security personnel killed in attacks in southeast Iran
Two members of state security forces were killed Wednesday in two separate attacks carried out by gunmen in southeast Iran, a region plagued by violence, state media reported.
"A police officer was killed in an armed attack on a police vehicle in Mehrestan County, in Sistan-Baluchistan," state television announced.
In the same area, a female commander from the Basij, a paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was killed by "members of enemy mercenary terrorist groups", the report said.
In recent weeks, clashes between security forces and gunmen have multiplied in the historically volatile region.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday claimed "terrorist groups" operating in the east were acting within a framework of "plans devised by Israel and the United States to destabilise the country's borders".
IRGC: container ship sinks in Hormuz after hitting mine
A container ship sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement shared by state media on Wednesday.
The ship carrying more than 2,500 containers had attempted to transit what the Guards described as an unauthorised and dangerous route, the statement said, warning local vessels and fishermen to take care.
With Yemen-Saudi war, Palestinians question Iran's goals
The recent round of fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia has sparked debate among Palestinians over the role of Iran and its allies in the region.
While some Palestinians supported Houthi attacks in the Red Sea during the Israeli genocidal war, others question their impact, especially as the latest round of fighting in Yemen that erupted since mid-September, and spread to Saudi airports and other civilian facilities.
The fighting has cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz—Yemen's third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting—and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World Food Programme said on Wednesday.
Some districts are now inaccessible because of fighting and road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.
"This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most," said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement.
Saudi Aramco headquarters suffered extensive damage
Oil giant Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran suffered extensive damage in an attack on Tuesday, with a fire spreading across several floors, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Operations at the complex in eastern Saudi Arabia have continued normally but some employees have been asked to work from home, according to two of the people.
A fourth person said some functions had been shifted to global offices, adding that the fire was still burning into the early hours of Wednesday.
The facility hosts an operations centre which helps the world's largest oil company oversee onshore and offshore oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometres of pipeline.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said in a statement that Tuesday night's attack, which came as fighting between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified, had caused a limited fire.
Two of the sources said a fire started on the ninth floor of the south wing of the office block, and spread between the sixth and 10th floors.
Another source added that the top three floors of building, where the office of Aramco CEO Amin Nasser is located, were severely damaged, with part of the ceiling caved in and windows and doors blown out.
Israeli settlers set fire to mosque in occupied West Bank
Israeli settlers set fire to a mosque and graffitied its outside walls on Wednesday in the occupied West Bank village of Mikhmas.
Atta Kanaan, a Palestinian resident of Mikhmas who lives 50 metres from the mosque, told AFP that he heard the sound of breaking glass shortly after midnight on Wednesday and immediately went to the building.
