"A fire was burning fiercely, and we called the fire brigade. Young men rushed to help us with fire extinguishers, and we managed to contain part of the fire before the flames engulfed the entire mosque," he said.
Israel's military told AFP that soldiers were dispatched to Mikhmas following a report of graffiti and arson at the mosque, as well as damage to a vehicle.
Iran central bank head dismisses claims of economic collapse
US claims that Iran's economy is collapsing are an illusion, the governor of Iran's central bank said on Wednesday at an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, as Tehran faces a US naval blockade aimed at driving its oil exports to zero and draining state coffers.
Washington reinstated its blockade of Iranian ports in July and launched "Operation Economic Outcast" on August 24, a campaign aimed at severing Iran’s remaining financial and commercial links with the global economy.
According to energy intelligence platform Vortexa, Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5.
In September, Washington expanded the campaign to target Iranian airlines, further isolating the country and making links to the outside world more limited and costly.
US pressure has coincided with a sharp fall in the Iranian rial. According to exchange-rate data from Iranian currency tracker Bonbast, the rial has lost nearly 35% of its value against the US dollar since July.
Hemmati said the central bank was prioritising curbing inflation, stabilising inflation expectations, preserving financial stability and maintaining banking and payment services, while securing foreign currency for medicine and essential goods. Annual inflation reached 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran.
Iran’s central bank launched a programme in late September to sell up to $2 billion through state banks to support the rial.
Iran's rial has lost nearly 35% of its value against the US dollar since July. [Getty]
Two vessels hit by 'unknown projectiles' in Hormuz: UKMTO
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency reported that two commercial vessels were hit by "unknown projectiles" in separate incidents in Hormuz on Tuesday.
In the first incident, a 50,000-tonne container ship was hit while entering the strait, suffering minor damage, no casualties, and continued its passage, according to the agency.
In the second, a 19,000-tonne container vessel was struck by an unknown projectile while exiting the waterway, with minor damage, no injuries, and continued its journey, the agency reported.
Sanaa fuel crisis erupts after Saudi-led coalition strike
A fuel crisis has hit Yemen's Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa after the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to leave a major oil storage facility before carrying out strikes.
The coalition issued an evacuation warning for the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha central station on the western outskirts of the capital.
According to Israeli media, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggested that an attack on Iran in the coming days, ahead of the Israeli elections, would not happen.
"In my opinion, that is not convenient for us," he told Army Radio.
Netanyahu also told Army Radio that Israel's National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party will not become defense minister in the next government, assuming the Netanyahu-led bloc of parties wins.
The premier’s comments on Iran come a day after Channel 12 reported that Netanyahu had urged US President Donald Trump to renew the fighting against Iran before Israel's 27 October election and the US midterm elections a week later, as the American leader said he would make a decision on Iran "very soon."
Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia and said they struck the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco, which was hit the day before.
The Iran-aligned group said it had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in the eastern city of Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, without saying when.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday that killed 13 people.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month, reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
Yemen hospitals overwhelmed by surge in war casualties
Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as intensified fighting along multiple front lines strains its already fragile health system, the Red Cross said on Wednesday.
Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast were seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the humanitarian agency.
"Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anesthesia, oxygen and medicines.
Demand for diesel fuel will remain unusually high into 2027 because of reduced supply from Gulf producers stemming from the US war against Iran, the International Energy Agency said Wednesday.
"The gasoil market balance will remain tight well into 2027 and is dependent on a recovery of product supply from the Middle East," the Paris-based agency said in its monthly energy markets report.
"The gasoil market balance will remain tight well into 2027," the IEA said. [Getty]
Saudi to let executives attend FII conference remotely
Saudi Arabia plans to make its flagship investment conference a hybrid event, giving executives the option to tune in remotely, after deadly weekend attacks on Riyadh airport prompted a rethink of travel to the kingdom, two people familiar with the matter said.
Some participants were still expected to fly in and could land at airstrips outside Riyadh, or even in neighbouring Gulf states, and then drive to the capital to attend the Future Investment Initiative scheduled for later this month, one of the people said.
The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Earlier this month, organisers said the event would go ahead despite missile and drone attacks in the kingdom, which have struck key targets.
An administrative building at the headquarters of state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked on Tuesday evening, the Energy Ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths.
Powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Wednesday, hours after a Houthi strike hit a building in the area housing energy giant Aramco's operations centre, in a fresh escalation of the war between the kingdom and the Yemeni group.
Regional powerhouse Saudi Arabia unleashed salvos against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, while the Iran-backed group fired back at sites across the kingdom, which is the world's top crude oil exporter.
Most strikes on Saudi Arabia have targeted infrastructure on the outskirts of the capital, but the barrages appear to be getting closer to the city centre.
On Wednesday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted a missile fired by the group towards Riyadh.
In the city's downtown, residents have been seen parking their cars to stop and look up at the sky, an AFP journalist said.
On Tuesday night, the white plumes of air defence missiles could be seen streaking across the sky followed by explosions.
Saudi coalition: intercepted Houthi missile fired to Riyadh
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday it had intercepted a missile fired by the group towards Riyadh, where explosions were earlier reported by AFP journalists.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki wrote on X.
Three fishermen injured in drone incident off southern Iran
Three fishermen were injured after a fishing boat was struck in an incident involving an unidentified drone near Sirik in southern Iran's Hormozgan province, the provincial governor's office said, according to Tasnim news agency on Wednesday.
Tasnim cited local sources as saying a fishing boat was hit in what they described as an attack by a US drone, although Iranian authorities have not officially confirmed the circumstances of the incident or who was responsible.
Iran executed Ali-Sina Mostafavi after being convicted of carrying out armed attacks in the southeastern city of Kerman during the war with the United States and Israel, the judiciary's news outlet Mizan said on Wednesday, accusing him of acting in support of exiled opposition figure Reza Pahlavi and Israel.
Iran to step up attacks on shipping before US vote
Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.
IMF chief says Saudi attacks could have negative spillover
International Monetary Fund head Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday that recent attacks on Saudi Arabia could impact people "everywhere", as conflict in the energy-rich region adds to wide-ranging economic concerns.
A violent battle between a Saudi-led coalition and Yemen's Houthis has erupted in recent days, with missile strikes on airports and energy facilities across the kingdom.
The latest round of fighting was triggered by Houthi strikes on Riyadh's international airport at the weekend that left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.
The escalation compounds fears about the impact of the Middle East crisis on global growth, with crude prices sent soaring since Iran effectively shut the crucial Strait of Hormuz after it was attacked by the US and Israel in February.
"The Saudi economy is important for the region and the world," IMF managing director Georgieva said at a news conference during the Annual Meetings of the Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.
"In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere," she said.

articles.title: Are US, Israel racing to deploy space-based lasers or orbital weapons first? - analysis
articles.body:
In September, two consecutive top US military officials made public for the first time that America has offensive weapons already deployed in space.
That the US, China, and Russia have anti-satellite weapons available is no secret, and has been assumed in recent years, with China unofficially demonstrating old space weapons in 2007, and Russia and China both demonstrating newer weapons since 2021.
But a public declaration by the US set off speculation about whether the deployed weapons are focused more in the area of: 1) directed-energy weapons (lasers); 2) kinetic anti-satellite weapons (missiles); or 3) platforms for disrupting or disabling satellites’ activity without actually destroying them – this is also known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs).
A fourth method could be nuclear, but it is assumed that this was not the focus of the US announcement because the terrible consequences in space would impact the attacker as much as the defender.
In April, Unit 9900 officer Lt.-Col. "S" and space war expert Tal Inbar discussed Israeli efforts to defend its assets in space from adversaries.
Also, on June 24, with the Post noting that Russia, China, and Iran have all worked on ways to attack, damage, jam, or drag satellites in space, IDF Brig.-Gen. Yael Grosman responded, "There are threats from space. We work with the Defense Ministry with a lot of power; with the broader defense establishment, we can all bring forward achievements."
Regarding the US announcement, so far those space experts who are commenting are leaning toward category 3 of RPO.
This is especially true for deploying RPOs, which can fight off other RPOs.
The reason is that RPOs have existed in one form or another since the US used multiple space vehicles to repair one another in the 1960s. In that sense, the largest jump was developing the technology and tactics for sending one space vehicle or satellite to match the orbit of another.
Once a country makes that major scientific jump, adding on a robot arm to attack or an additional system to jam is just a matter of time and energy.
Another reason RPOs may be favored would be to avoid the debris problem caused by using kinetic anti-satellite weapons, such as missiles.
The US has said it is hoping to make major advancements in stationing anti-missile physical interceptors in space that can protect satellites by 2028.
Despite all this focus on RPOs for the US, China, and Russia, Israel has made its biggest noise regarding space weapons in relation to lasers.
On June 29, Defense Minister Israel Katz told a briefing of military reporters that Israel is developing space lasers to carry out attacks above the Earth.
This was an expansion and more specific version of a statement which Katz made earlier in June, when he committed Israel to becoming the leading player with space attack capabilities.
"One of the central goals which the prime minister and I set is that we are recruiting the best minds," since "as of today, no country has the ability to mount attacks in space. We must be the leading country in the world with this capability," said Katz.
The defense minister continued, "If we achieve this, it will ensure the advantage of deterrence, of the ability to attack, destroy, and all of the other matters, versus our enemies with large resources."
But Monday was the first time that Katz specifically mentioned space lasers.
Israel is already a leading country in developing Iron Beam as a land-based space laser, and during a visit to Elbit earlier in the summer, The Jerusalem Post saw and heard about work on presumed future fighter-jet-based lasers.
Overall, it seemed clear that Katz on June 29 was referring to Iran.
This is especially true since during the 2026 war, Israel struck multiple Iranian space war-related facilities, including facilities working on developing capabilities to attack satellites in space.
It was unclear if he indirectly also wanted to deter Russia and China from assisting Iran in this and other spheres.
According to foreign reports, lasers might be able to destroy enemy satellites and also burn up any debris that an attack in space by other means might cause.
Some have already speculated that Israel could destroy enemy space satellites using the Arrow 3 missile system, given that it already strikes ballistic missiles in space.
Yet, due to the same issue that Russia and China already fell into regarding debris, many countries are working on other techniques, such as paralyzing, damaging, jamming, dragging, or using lasers against satellites in space.
While some Israeli officials have hinted at such efforts, Katz's public statements on June 29 were the clearest one to date by a senior Israeli official.
In contrast, if Iran or other enemies advanced past Israel in space, they could attack Israeli satellites and reduce its surveillance capabilities.
After all of this, why then do most experts believe that the US's first and current focus is on RPOs, and not lasers?
It is not that the US and the other countries with space programs are not working on developing space lasers. They are.
Also, Israel's success with developing the Iron Beam for actual deployments as a ground laser has spurred other countries forward in the more general laser defense area.
But lasers in space or on aircraft are still a distant solution, as they involve a series of more complex physics and engineering problems, which invariably will take longer to solve than RPOs.
RPOs then are an immediate answer to help deter enemies from attacking, since they can be used to attack enemy satellites, as well as providing defense against other countries' potential RPO attacks.
If enemies have existing and immediate weapons to attack an object, such as a satellite, the US and other countries, potentially even including Israel, are likely to focus on immediate solutions, with the focus on space lasers being a longer-term goal.
In that sense, the US statement in September was about immediately deterring China and Russia from attacking American satellites.
In contrast, Katz's June statement was less about immediate attack, defense, or deterrence.
Rather, it was more about either bragging to the Israeli public about a future distant achievement, or psychological warfare against Iran to the extent that the Islamic Republic might believe it can work with Moscow and Beijing to go after Israel's satellite advantage.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian president Yushchenko writes open letter to Trump
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian president Yushchenko writes open letter to Trump
Viktor Yushchenko, Ukraine's third president, has written an open letter to US President Donald Trump over his agreement with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on diesel fuel.
Source: Yushchenko on Facebook
Quote: "And against this reality, Ukrainians hear calls that Ukraine should stop. That Ukraine should restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia's war. That trade in Russian energy can somehow be separated from the missiles and drones Russia sends against Ukrainian families. It cannot.
Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called 'commerce' It finances an economy geared toward total war."
Details: Yushchenko also reflected on events more than three decades ago, when the Soviet Union was breaking up.
He noted that Ukraine had then possessed the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal. "In negotiations with our allies, we agreed to give it up. We did so because we believed that a world governed by agreements was safer than a world governed by nuclear weapons."
Quote: "In 1994, the United States of America, along with its partners, signed the Budapest Memorandum, providing Ukraine with official assurances of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of our borders.
They pledged not to threaten or use force against Ukraine. America assumed a moral responsibility toward Ukraine. So how can anyone today, when a treacherous enemy has attacked us, forget America's signature on this document?"
Background:
- On 9 October, Trump said he had spoken to Putin and reached an agreement with him on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's decision to unilaterally lift sanctions on Russia and allow it to export diesel fuel was unfair and dishonest.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Russian Missile Strikes Kill 3 In Kyiv, Knock Out Power As Zelenskyy Says West Gave No Warning
articles.body:
KYIV -- Moscow launched a wave of ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv and a drone attack in western Ukraine that killed at least six people, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its Western partners about the launches.
Russian forces struck several energy facilities in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported on October 14, after Ukraine accused Russia of violating a cease-fire announced by US President Donald Trump on strikes targeting energy infrastructure.
At least five districts of Kyiv were plunged into emergency power outages after a Russian overnight strike hit one of the capital's main power plants, energy company DTEK reported.
In a post on X on October 14, Zelenskyy said Russia had used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones in overnight strikes, adding at least 600,000 people were now without power. He warned the outages could become even more widespread.
Ukraine's Emergency Service said three people were killed and 21 others, including one child, were injured, as rescue operations continued in Kyiv.
"I never thought I would leave the country, but I have a teenage child, and for the sake of my daughter, my dog, and our safety, I will leave in the near future," a Kyiv resident told RFE/RL at the scene of the strike on a residential building.
In western Ukraine, at least three people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the city of Lutsk, according to regional authorities.
"Unfortunately, three people were killed when drone debris struck the Eurohurt wholesale store," Roman Romaniuk, the regional head stated in a Telegram post.
"Two people were found dead at the scene, and another died in hospital. Another 10 people were injured," he added.
As the Russian attacks unfolded, Zelenskyy warned of more to come.
"According to our intelligence, Russia is preparing additional ballistic missile strikes," he wrote on X late on October 13.
"It is important that the world does not remain silent about this," he said, adding that "it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing." Zelenskyy reaffirmed Ukraine's support for an energy cease-fire.
"Russia is attacking Ukraine's energy grid, residential buildings, and critical infrastructure, causing blackouts in Kyiv, disrupting water supplies, and, most tragically, killing more civilians," Denys Sienik, charge d'affaires at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, said following the overnight strikes.
Responding to Zelenskyy's remarks that Ukraine received no advance warning of the ballistic missile launches and detected the first wave only as it approached Kyiv, the EU's ambassador to Ukraine, Katarina Mathernova, wrote in a post on X that "missing warning means missing time. Time to wake a child. To get downstairs. To reach a shelter."
"Ukraine needs air defense, interceptors and reliable early warnings. Every minute of warning can give someone a chance to survive," she added.
The attack came days after Trump announced a deal allowing Russian diesel exports, following a conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 9.
Trump has said that, under the deal, the United States would immediately import 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel, with millions more expected to follow.
The move has sparked criticism from European allies and from Democrats and Republicans, who warned it could embolden Putin to continue his war against Ukraine.
In a letter to Trump, a bipartisan group of 12 senators urged him to withdraw from the diesel deal with Putin, calling it "a gift to our adversary" and "a betrayal of our Allies."
"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine," the senators wrote in the letter.
Meanwhile, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko addressed an open letter to Trump criticizing his deal with Putin on diesel fuel.
"When there is talk of 'concessions' or deals with Putin, the Kremlin's answer is more missiles, more drones, and more bloodshed. Ukrainian families pay the price," he wrote.
"One does not negotiate with tyrants -- one stops them," he added.

articles.title: ‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least six, damages power sites
articles.body:
‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least 9, damages power sites
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine’s partners failed to warn of Russian ballistic missiles attack on Kyiv.
Russian air attacks have killed at least nine people in Ukraine and left hundreds of thousands without power, days after United States President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” in the more-than four year war.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Wednesday that its forces had carried out a “massive” strike against communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Ukraine, the Interfax news agency reported.
In a statement, it said Russian forces hit two plants supplying power and heating in the capital Kyiv, two other plants in the wider region and an electricity substation.
Other targets included a heating and power plant in Ukraine’s second-largest city Kharkiv, along with a thermal power facility which the ministry said supplied the Ukrainian military in the southeast of the Kharkiv region.
Moscow said its forces had also hit a data centre in Kyiv which it said was used to gather intelligence on Russia’s military.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to remain in shelters.
“Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital,” he wrote on Telegram.
DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy provider, said the attack had caused emergency power cuts in several urban districts of Kyiv.
A Russian strike on a multistorey building in the capital’s Desnianskyi district killed two people, while another attack in Golosiivsky district killed one, Ukraine’s state emergency service said.
The Ukrainian military also reported that two people were killed and six wounded in Russian attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region. Another person was killed in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region.
In the Volyn region, a Russian attack on Ukraine’s western city of Lutsk killed three people and injured at least 12, governor Roman Romaniuk said on Telegram.
Further Russian missile attacks were reported in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions, while other strikes hit Sumy and Chernihiv.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said a record number of hypersonic missiles were used in the attacks on the capital.
“Over half a million people in Ukraine are without power as a result of these strikes,” she said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no warnings from its Western partners of a Russian ballistic missile attack on the capital, raising questions about intelligence sharing.
“A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners,” he wrote on Facebook. “This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”
The president said Ukraine detected the missiles only as they neared Kyiv.
He also accused Russia of violating the “energy ceasefire” Trump announced on Sunday.
“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” he wrote on X.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect towards the United States.”
A technology adviser to the Ukrainian president said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to have been restricted overnight, preventing its military-grade version from operating above 160 kilometres per hour, disrupting combat missions.
“Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion,” Sergiy Beskrestnov said, referring to Elon Musk’s company, which owns Starlink.
“Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation.”
Russia also reported Ukrainian drone strikes overnight. The governor of Russia’s Saratov region, Roman Busargin, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Busargin said all infrastructure facilities were operating as usual. Balakovo is home to a data centre of Russia’s top lender Sberbank, a nuclear power plant and a hydropower station, whose dam spans the Volga River, among other facilities.
Sberbank later said its data centre in the Saratov region had been attacked by drones, but that all systems were operating as normal.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight. Russian authorities said about 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.
Russia’s military later put the number of downed Ukrainian drones overnight at 902, of which 180 were shot down near the capital, Moscow.

articles.title: 'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
articles.body:
'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
Ukraine's Starlink access has been restricted without warning, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
"I confirm that (Starlink owner) SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night. Currently, the restriction applies to the StarShield 'military service package' and limits speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)," he said in a post on social media.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its mid-strike campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones.
This mid-strike campaign has this year allowed Ukraine to strangle Russian logistics, hampering its ability to fight on the front lines.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that speed limitations had been discovered and the cause was being investigated.
"This complicates drone missions —specifically those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones — and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay," the source added.
A soldier working on mid-strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
In a post on social media, Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said it was experiencing "throttling" of its Starlink connectivity.
"The consequences are already being felt in the field. Since the start of the day alone, a drone unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of responsibility in the Huliaipole sector has had to cancel a number of missions due to these connectivity issues," the corps said.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Beskrestnov said.
As reported by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened Ukraine with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries.
Beskrestnov did not provide evidence that the Starlink restriction was connected to U.S. pressure on Ukraine, and the White House has not commented on the issue.
Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, also reported the restriction of access, saying "SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
The development comes after Ukraine worked with SpaceX earlier this year to deactivate unauthorized Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces. Starlink has played a critical role in Ukrainian military communications throughout the full-scale war.
The threats came after a confusing 48 hours during which U.S. President Donald Trump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Volodymyr Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine has since refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries but Russia has continued its blitz on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, most recently overnight on Oct. 14 when "several" power plants in Kyiv were hit. Trump has refused to accuse Russia of breaking the ceasefire.
The reported Starlink restrictions come as questions have been raised about U.S. intelligence sharing in relation to Russian ballistic missile launches, following two straight nights of attack on Kyiv with little to no warning.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Despite the failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 13.
But later that day, around 10:30 p.m. another wave of ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, again without the usual warning.
At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a hit on a residential building in the Desnianskyi District. Three more waves of ballistic missiles struck Kyiv throughout the night.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat told Ukrainian TV that Ukraine received no warnings from its partners about the first wave, though it did for the following three.
"Ukraine did not attack Russian oil refineries, yet Trump has already begun imposing sanctions on my country. Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia have been eased," Sternenko said.

articles.title: Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
articles.body:
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine’s energy system overnight into 14 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The barrage came three days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, which the Kremlin never confirmed, saying on 12 October only that contacts were continuing.
Ukraine held off strikes on Russian energy for two days after the announcement, Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October. Russia’s barrage opened that evening with a ballistic strike on Kyiv. For the second time in two days, it came without a launch warning from partners.
How the night unfolded
The Air Force described one massive combined strike that began at 18:00 on 13 October. By 09:00 the next day, it had counted 39 missiles on ballistic trajectories and 128 drones, aimed mainly at Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv Oblast. Air defenses downed or suppressed four missiles and 115 drones, but missiles and drones hit 22 locations, the Air Force said.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
The first wave hit Kyiv late on 13 October. Its primary target was CHP-4, a key power plant in the city, and there were hits, Zelenskyy said. Ukrainian systems spotted the missiles only on approach, with no warning from partners. After a call with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Zelenskyy wrote that Ukraine had not been warned for the second time. On 13 October, Trump said the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
A Russian strike also hit a high-rise in Desnianskyi district. Rescuers saved 16 residents, the State Emergency Service reported, and three women were killed there, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office said. The prosecutor’s office counted 19 injured in the building, including a girl officials described as seven or eight, and five more hurt by shattered windows next door. Across Kyiv, the evening and morning attacks killed four people and injured 25, the prosecutor’s office said, while Suspilne counted 32 injured.
The second wave came early on 14 October and hit several of the capital’s energy facilities, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It killed one person in Holosiivskyi district, he added. Russia attacked all three of Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants and key facilities in Kyiv Oblast that power the capital, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. Energy company DTEK reported emergency outages in five Kyiv districts.
Damage and demands
Zelenskyy reported damage to facilities and equipment at 26 elements of the power system and at four oil and gas facilities. At least 600,000 people lost electricity, he said, and outages could grow. He called the strike deliberate and said Russia had never before shown such demonstrative disrespect toward America.
He asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Lindsey Graham sanctions law, which he said was recently passed and signed. He also asked for additional Patriot interceptors.
Read also
- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
- Hours after Trump declared an energy ceasefire, Russia hit Kharkiv power plant, one of 200-plus strikes on Ukraine’s grid this week, Zelenskyy says

articles.title: Overnight attacks kill six people in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian airstrikes killed six people across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, according to Ukrainian authorities reported by the news agency AFP on Wednesday morning.
In the capital city of Kyiv, two people died when an airstrike hit an apartment building in the Desnyanskyi district, Ukraine’s emergency service reported. A third person died in an attack in the Holosiivskyi district.
Ukrainian military authorities reported that airstrikes in the central region of Dnipropetrovsk killed two people and wounded six others.
One more person was killed in the Zaporizhzhia region in the southeastern part of the country.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the overnight strikes were extensive and caused power outages across the city on Wednesday morning.
“Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have been hit by an extensive attack with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on the messaging service Telegram, according to AFP. “There are power outages in the capital.”
The Ukrainian energy company DTEK also reported blackouts on Wednesday morning in Kyiv, home to roughly 3 million people. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that 600,000 people in the capital lost electricity after the strikes, according to Reuters.
The strikes on energy infrastructure took place after U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire.
Zelenskyy said Russia’s attacks on power facilities defied Trump’s statement.
“The attack was deliberate and demonstrative in its scope. Russia has never before shown such blatant disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy wrote on the social media platform X.
AFP reported that ballistic missile strikes were also reported Wednesday morning in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces hit seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities and a data center overnight into Wednesday, according to Reuters. The ministry said the targeted sites were helping the Ukrainian military.
The Russian ministry also stated Wednesday morning that it neutralized 902 drones over Russian regions during the night.
According to the governor of the Saratov region, a Ukrainian drone strike killed one person in the city of Balakovo.

articles.title: Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s power grid
articles.body:
- Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukrainian energy sites overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.
- Zelenskyy asked Trump for strong sanctions under the Graham law and more Patriot interceptors after the strike hit infrastructure covered by Trump’s ceasefire.
Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine’s energy and critical infrastructure overnight into Oct. 14, knocking out power to at least 600,000 people days after President Donald Trump announced a halt to strikes on energy facilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said that the attack targeted Kyiv, the surrounding Kyiv region and Kharkiv, and damaged equipment at 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four in the oil and gas sector. He warned that outages could spread further and said there were dead and injured, without giving numbers. Repair crews, power company staff and the State Emergency Service were working to restore supply on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy described the ballistic missile salvo as aimed specifically at the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire Trump announced on Truth Social on Oct. 11, and called the scale of the strike deliberate and demonstrative.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
Moscow never confirmed accepting Trump’s energy ceasefire, and its scope remained disputed after the announcement, with a White House official telling Axios that the proposal initially covered oil refineries, while power plants and electricity grids might follow later. Zelenskyy told Fox News on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had held off on striking Russian energy facilities after the announcement, while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian gas and power sites. Ukraine’s charge d’affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Russia had struck electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times in the week before the announcement.
“Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” said Zelenskyy.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of a Russian strike package for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of the country’s air defenses, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot systems to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for additional packages of Patriot interceptors, saying no country should be left alone against Russia.
He also called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the sanctions law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 and which gives the president authority to raise tariffs and restrict Russian energy trade, with key measures due to take effect by Oct. 18.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures,” said Zelenskyy.
The strike followed Trump’s Oct. 9 announcement of a deal to release Russian diesel onto U.S. and world markets, starting with 300,000 tons immediately and 500,000 tons in November, after the Treasury waived diesel sanctions until April 2027. Critics in Congress have said the arrangement gives Moscow additional revenue for the war. The White House had not responded publicly to the overnight strike by Wednesday morning, and Russia’s Defense Ministry had not commented on its targets.

articles.title: Air Force Tests New Sentinel Reentry Vehicle
articles.body:
The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center tested its new intercontinental ballistic missile reentry vehicle Oct. 9, launching the developmental vehicle atop a Minotaur I rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.
The Mk21A reentry vehicle, mated to the Sentinel ICBM, will eventually replace the Minuteman III as the land-based leg of the nation’s nuclear triad. Carrying the new W87-1 nuclear warhead, it will launch atop the Sentinel’s three rocket stages, blasting into space before reentering the atmosphere to strike its target.
The Oct. 9 test launch carried no warhead and was the first announced test of the new vehicle since June 2024.
“The Mk21A is crucial to modernizing our ICBMs in response to the rapidly changing global threat picture posed by our adversaries,” said Maj. Gen. William Rogers, the Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for ICBMs, in a statement. “The reentry vehicle’s development will ensure a safe, secure and effective deterrent for generations to come.”
The Mk21A is based on the Mk21 reentry vehicle used on the Minuteman III, and is being developed by Lockheed Martin. The Minotaur I launch vehicle, provided by Northrop Grumman, is based on the Peacekeeper and Minuteman rocket motors. The Space Force helped oversee the test through its Rocket Systems Launch Program, which provides commercial launch systems and excess ballistic missile assets for government payloads.
The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center awarded Lockheed a $996 million contract for the Mk21A in October 2023 and followed with an additional $453 million contract modification in November 2025.
According to an April acquisition report released by the Pentagon in September, the latest contract modification was part of a new baseline for the program intended to “decouple its schedule from external programs and continue development with an updated, more resilient plan.”
The LGM-35 Sentinel program office is still working to overcome the cost and schedule problems that triggered a mandatory Pentagon review, and while officials claim progress, the program is undergoing a restructuring before it can meet Milestone B, which would authorize it to move into engineering and manufacturing development.
The acquisition report offers scant details on the Mk21A rebaseline effort, beyond noting that it includes a new “alternate flight test strategy” and additional test assets. It does note, however, that the June 2024 test successfully flight-tested the vehicle’s heatshield, and that Lockheed was working on integrating the arming and fuzing subsystem in February 2026. Air Force budget documents released in April projected “flight test of heatshield test vehicle and W87-1 environmental flight test unit” in fiscal 2026 and 2027.
A critical design review for the entire Sentinel system is planned by March 2027. The Air Force asked for almost $540 million to fund Mk21A reentry vehicle development in the fiscal 2027 budget request, up $184 million from 2026 as Sentinel ramps up integration and test activities.

articles.title: Record Zircon Barrage Targets Kyiv as Russia Fires 39 Ballistic Missiles at Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Record Zircon Barrage Targets Kyiv as Russia Fires 39 Ballistic Missiles at Ukraine
Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at Ukraine overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, while monitoring channels reported a record barrage of roughly 25 Zircon missiles aimed at Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Russian strikes on energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv left at least 600,000 people without electricity, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 14.
The Ukrainian President described the barrage as a deliberate strike on energy infrastructure that he said was specifically covered by a ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy argued that the scale of the operation represented an unusually open challenge to Washington.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure—the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s Air Force said air defenses neutralized 115 UAVs and four ballistic missiles during the barrage. The strikes nevertheless caused extensive damage, with Zelenskyy saying 26 facilities in Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities were affected.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale—Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong,” Zelenskyy added.
Ukrainian monitoring channels also reported that Russia used a record number of Zircon missiles during the attack, with roughly 25 reportedly launched against targets in Kyiv and the Kyiv region. Ukraine’s Air Force has not yet officially confirmed the figure.
“Unfortunately, at least 600,000 people are now without power. Outages could become even more widespread. Unfortunately, there is significant damage to facilities and equipment—at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector,” Zelenskyy stated.
He thanked repair crews, energy workers, and emergency personnel responding across the affected regions, adding that the strikes had caused deaths and injuries.
In Kyiv, the number of injured rose to 25. Among them was a 7-year-old girl in the Desnianskyi district who suffered cuts and burns to her hand.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, two people were killed and six others injured, while a business in Dnipro was damaged. Two more people were wounded in the Khmelnytskyi region, where a gas station was hit and a fire broke out at an industrial facility.
That brings the confirmed toll from the locations reported so far to at least two dead and 33 injured.
Zelenskyy called for a forceful international response, arguing that Moscow had rejected an opportunity for de-escalation.
“We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond—and to respond forcefully. Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation,” he said.
The Ukrainian leader specifically appealed to Trump to impose stronger sanctions on Russia, pointing to recently enacted legislation backed by US Sen. Lindsey Graham.
“We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures. The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor,” the Ukrainian President wrote.
He also renewed Ukraine’s request for additional Patriot interceptor missiles as Russia expands its use of ballistic weapons, which are among the most difficult threats for Ukrainian air defenses to stop.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine. It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia,” Zelenskyy concluded.
Earlier, the Ukrainian President stated that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities for two consecutive days following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, while Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Zelenskyy labels latest Russian attacks as disrespect toward US
articles.body:
Ukraine accused Russia on Wednesday of violating Donald Trump’s "energy cease-fire" and wasting an opportunity for de-escalation, following a wave of deadly strikes that targeted power supplies nationwide.
Kyiv in particular faced a barrage of powerful ballistic missiles and attack drones targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure, despite the U.S. president's surprise weekend announcement.
Four people were killed in the city and power to at least 600,000 people was cut after significant damage was reported to power facilities and equipment.
Power plants also came under ballistic missile attack in the eastern Kharkiv region, hitting electricity and heating infrastructure, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted the latest attack as "entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," adding: "Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," he wrote on X.
Trump blindsided both Kyiv and Moscow Sunday by unilaterally announcing an "energy cease-fire," two days after enraging Ukraine's Western allies with news of a deal with heavily sanctioned Russia to supply diesel fuel.
The U.S. leader has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy – and even said he should be replaced as president – for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
A senior Ukrainian official confirmed to AFP reports in recent days that Washington threatened to pull intelligence-sharing with Kyiv that it relies on to detect incoming attacks.
The renewed signs of strain with Trump have cast doubt on those arrangements, as air raid sirens warning of approaching drones or missiles failed to sound on Monday night and Tuesday night before explosions were heard.
That has occurred only rarely in the past. Ukrainian officials attributed the issue to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues.
But Zelenskyy on Tuesday evening said Ukraine had received "no early warning from our partners" about ballistic missile launches, calling it "absolutely unjust."
An aide to Zelenskyy meanwhile said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals also appeared to have been restricted overnight, disrupting "a number of missions" by Ukrainian defense forces.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," said Sergiy Beskrestnov.
A senior Ukrainian official told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that Starlink speeds had been "throttled," suggesting that it was done to Russia's advantage.
"What is important is that this has been ongoing since last night. Some restrictions were already being reported yesterday evening, so, in effect, it is happening in sync with this morning's Russian ballistic attack," they added.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to hold off from striking Russian energy infrastructure, but accused the Kremlin of having "squandered the opportunity for de-escalation" in the nearly five-year conflict.
Russia has previously targeted Ukraine's power stations and heating infrastructure, crippling supplies before winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20 degrees Celsius.
Ukraine has been pushing its allies for more military support as Kyiv increasingly comes under attack, particularly the supply of advanced interceptor systems to shoot down missiles and fast, jet-powered drones.
Russian ballistic missile attacks were also reported in the eastern region of Kharkiv and Zhytomyr in the northwest, and other strikes hit Sumy in the northeast and Chernigiv in the north.
Two people were killed in the central Dnipropetrovsk region and a further person in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast, the authorities said.
The governor of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, citing preliminary estimates, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defense forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying toward the Russian capital overnight.
Russian authorities said around 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.

articles.title: 'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
articles.body:
'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
Russia demonstrated its disregard for U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire by launching drones and missiles against Ukraine's power grid overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 14.
Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said, calling it "ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
At least three people were killed, and another 22 were injured as a result of the Russian strike that hit a residential building in the Desnianskyi district and power plants elsewhere in the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia has ramped up aerial strikes against Ukrainian energy sites as winter nears, despite Trump's unexpected and unilateral announcement on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
Even as Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since Trump's ceasefire announcement, Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked by a reporter on Oct. 13.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," Zelensky noted, adding that at least 600,000 people are without power and reporting damage to 26 power facilities, as well as four oil and gas sites.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," the Ukrainian leader added.
The comments come as Washington piles on pressure on Kyiv to halt its aerial campaign against Russian refineries, which he linked to rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts.
The Kyiv Independent has previously learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials with cutting intelligence sharing and arms sales unless it stopped attacking Russian refineries.
While Ukrainian and U.S. sources told the Kyiv Independent earlier this week that Washington has not yet stopped intelligence support, questions about the early warning provided by partners are mounting as strikes now hit Kyiv even before the alarm sounds.
Presidential Advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov and Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, claimed on Oct. 14 that Elon Musk's SpaceX has limited the speed of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, causing disruption to "a number of critical missions."
"The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor," Zelensky noted, urging Washington to impose sanctions on Russia under late Senator Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill and calling for additional supplies of Patriot interceptors.

articles.title: Russia launches 39 missiles, 128 UAVs at Ukraine; 4 missiles, 115 drones downed or suppressed – Air Force
articles.body:
Russian forces on Wednesday overnight deployed 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types against Ukraine, of which air defense forces shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 UAVs, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"On the night of October 14 (from 18:00 on October 13), the enemy launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine using strike UAVs and 39 missiles of various types approaching targets on a ballistic trajectory," the Air Force said in a message on Telegram.
In total, the radio-technical troops of the Air Force recorded 167 air attack weapons – 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types.
According to preliminary data as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 enemy UAVs, including 59 jet-powered drones. According to the Air Force, this accounts for 90% of the total number of strike UAVs.
Russian forces used Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles, as well as Shahed strike drones, including jet-powered ones, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The main directions of the strike were Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv region. According to the Air Force, a key feature of the attack was the simultaneous deployment of various air attack weapons from multiple directions, along with a large number of ballistic missiles targeting energy infrastructure facilities.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary information as of 09:00, impacts of missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 22 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As of the time of publication, the attack was ongoing, with Russian strike drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Ukrainian soldiers in combat have access to Starlink satellite internet restricted
articles.body:
Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.
SpaceX did not confirm any changes to Starlink’s functionality and it was not immediately clear why the restrictions had been put in place. Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign, where it uses the satellite internet system to navigate drones to hit targets behind the front in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine. But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals have been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk, an ally of Trump, had previously cut off Starlink service to Ukrainian soldiers during an offensive that took a small amount of Russian territory.
Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.
Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.
Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit several power plants and key substations that carry electricity to the capital, including from a major power plant.
“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” he said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”
At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.

articles.title: Kyiv Mayor Faces Questioning as Russian Attack Triggers Fresh Water Cuts
articles.body:
Kyiv is experiencing water supply issues once more on Wednesday after another Russian attack on Ukraine’s energy grid.
The attack, comprising ballistic missiles, hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building, killing at least three and injuring 26.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Kyiv City State Administration reported reduced water pressure in multiple districts as a result of the attack, with reduced voltage preventing the pumps from operating normally.
“Due to the power outage of some water supply facilities in the capital, the pumping equipment was stopped in an emergency,” it wrote in a statement, adding that restoration work is ongoing.
According to the agency, the upper half of the Pecherskyi district has no water, while the lower part has reduced pressure. The Solomyansky and Shevchenkivskyi districts also suffer from reduced pressure.
State media Ukrinform noted that Kyivvodfond, a municipal water-management firm, has developed an online map of available manual water pumps around Kyiv.
In October, the capital reported multiple water outages caused by Russian attacks, two months ahead of the cold spell. Most Ukrainians interviewed by Kyiv Post on Tuesday named water disruptions as their top concern for the upcoming winter, as signs of an energy truce touted by Washington remain elusive, with Ukraine’s energy grid not included.
Kyiv also said it was not warned by its allies for the first wave of ballistic missile strikes amid rumors of a US intelligence cutoff.
Ukraine’s Business Leaders to Tackle War Risks and Economic Resilience at 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum on Oct. 26
Kyiv authorities urged locals to stock up on food and water on Sunday, Oct. 11, after a Russian attack left over half of Kyiv’s households without running water.
Kyiv mayor summoned
On Wednesday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko was summoned to the Verkhovna Rada to answer questions about the city’s readiness for Russian attacks on power facilities.
The session is ongoing at the time of publication, and it was preceded by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s criticism of Kyiv’s response to the impending energy crisis, arguing that the capital trails behind other regions in preparedness.
However, Klitschko has defended the city’s preparedness, noting that progress is being made through backup systems despite limited funding, as facilities can’t be fully shielded without adequate air defense.
The standoff is also part of a longstanding animosity between the two that predates Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Iraq faces a potential six-month gap in its air defences following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces, with new systems not expected to arrive until early next year.
The coalition completed its military withdrawal at the end of September, removing air defence systems that had helped protect parts of the country, including the Kurdistan Region.
Baghdad says agreements have been reached to purchase new equipment, but the first systems could take up to six months to arrive.
The transition has taken on added urgency after two drones targeted a camp for Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of Iraq's armed forces, said Baghdad had made "tangible progress" in acquiring new air defence systems.
He said the first batch would arrive within six months and be deployed across the country.
The package would include advanced radar systems, interceptor weapons and aircraft, he said, as part of a wider plan to strengthen Iraq's control over its airspace.
Numan said the country's security situation remained relatively stable and that Iraqi forces were maintaining a high level of readiness.
However, the announcement leaves questions over Iraq's ability to detect and intercept aerial threats before the new systems become operational.
Iraq has long struggled with limited and ageing air defence capabilities, while drones and missiles have become an increasingly prominent security threat.
A Defence Ministry official nevertheless played down the prospect of an immediate security vacuum.
"The available Iraqi air capabilities are not at a high level, and there is no denying that, but the security situation in the country is relatively calm," the official told The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The official said Iraq retained "reasonably good capabilities" and that there were currently no expectations of major security breaches.
Concerns are particularly acute in the Kurdistan Region.
Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said on Monday that both federal Iraq and the autonomous region required effective air defence coverage.
"Let us be realistic. The Kurdistan Region and Iraq as a whole need an air defence system," he told the MERI Forum in Erbil.
Barzani said an earlier agreement negotiated under former prime minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani with the United States had included plans to provide air defence capabilities covering Kurdistan.
"Air defence is not only a need for the Iraqi state. The Kurdistan Region also needs it," he said.
He also stressed that weapons should remain under state control.
Military expert Aqil al-Shammari warned that the process could take longer than the six months announced by the government.
He said another three months could be required to integrate the equipment, establish command-and-control systems, train personnel, arrange maintenance and complete deployment.
"Owning the system does not mean providing complete air coverage," the former brigadier general told The New Arab.
Shammari said the transition period would be a major test of Baghdad's ability to protect Iraqi airspace.
Kurdish officials had warned before the coalition withdrawal that removing foreign forces and their air defence systems without an immediate replacement could leave the region vulnerable.
The withdrawal forms part of a wider transition towards a new security relationship between Baghdad and Washington focused on training, technology and military co-operation without a direct US combat presence.
They have argued that protecting Kurdistan's airspace is ultimately the responsibility of the federal government because it forms part of Iraq's national airspace.
Those concerns intensified after two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
No casualties were reported, but the attack renewed fears that gaps in Iraq's air defences could leave the Kurdistan Region vulnerable to further drone strikes.
The withdrawal has also raised wider questions over whether Baghdad can manage its security without the coalition's military presence.

articles.title: Ukrainian military says SpaceX restricted Starlink terminals without warning
articles.body:
Ukrainian military says SpaceX restricted Starlink terminals without warning
SpaceX has restricted the Starlink satellite communication terminals used by Ukrainian troops at the front, slowing the drones that rely on them, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, and Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the Ukrainian defense minister and a volunteer.
The news outlet Ukrainska Pravda, citing the military, reported that the restrictions targeted Starshield, the faster military version of Starlink used by drone operators. One commander sent the outlet a video showing two Ukrainian drones climbing into the sky with their connection “dropping out,” leaving them unable to continue their mission.
A source in the Ukrainian Armed Forces told Ukrainska Pravda that standard Starlink terminals installed on drones work at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 mph), but that speed is not enough for some missions, which is why drone operators use Starshield, the military version of Starlink.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about these restrictions, and it led to the failure of a number of missions. It’s obvious that this action can’t be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Volodymyr Zelensky said over the past two days that Western partners did not warn Ukraine about missile strikes on Kyiv. The United States told Ukraine it had not shared intelligence because of poor weather conditions, according to Politico.
The United States threatened last week to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block arms deliveries unless Kyiv agreed to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to reporting from the Financial Times.
