- US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack
- Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel

articles.title: Ex-President Yushchenko calls on Trump to abandon trade with Russia, concessions to Putin
articles.body:
Third President of Ukraine Viktor Yushchenko addressed an open letter to President of the U.S Donald Trump, criticizing the authorization of trade in Russian diesel fuel and calling for the fulfillment of security commitments under the Budapest Memorandum, the politician published the appeal on Facebook on Wednesday.
"It looks wild and painful when calls are heard for Ukraine to 'stop,' instructions on whom we should elect and how to live, or when a green light is given to trade in Russian diesel. Every dollar from this diesel is a purchased missile that will strike our homes tomorrow," Yushchenko stressed in his appeal.
According to the former president, trading with an aggressor country during wartime directly finances its war machine, while talks by the U.S about the possibility of concessions or agreements with Vladimir Putin immediately provoke the Kremlin into new strikes with ballistic missiles and guided aerial bombs against residential neighborhoods in Kyiv, Zaporizhia, Odesa, Dnipro, and Kharkiv region.
Yushchenko reminded the head of the White House that following the collapse of the USSR, Ukraine voluntarily surrendered the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal in exchange for official guarantees of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of borders, sealed by the U.S signature on the Budapest Memorandum in 1994.
In addition, the former Ukrainian head of state drew a historical parallel with Washington's policy in the 1930s, when the U.S supplied oil to Imperial Japan for the sake of preserving stability, which ultimately led to the Japanese air attack on Pearl Harbor using American fuel. At the same time, the politician pointed to the joint struggle of Ukrainians and Americans in World War II, mentioning Ukrainian-born Sergeant Michael Strank, who raised the US flag over Iwo Jima, and Ukrainian Alexander Silvashko during the historic meeting of allies on the Elbe on April 25, 1945.
Concluding the appeal, Yushchenko emphasized that the Ukrainian people will never yield their territory and will not succumb to Russian missile blackmail, summarizing that "one does not negotiate with tyrants – one stops them."

articles.title: Poland urges Europe to switch to 'war-mode' defense production
articles.body:
Jo Harper
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Poland’s Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on Tuesday urged Europe to put weapons and ammunition production on a wartime footing to counter Russia's military build-up, Polish state news agency PAP reported.
He also urged the EU to allow urgent defense purchases from NATO allies outside the bloc.
Speaking in Warsaw following talks with European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius on strengthening European military capabilities, accelerating arms production and securing defense supply chains, Kosiniak-Kamysz said, "I personally favor switching to wartime mode in the production of weapons and ammunition throughout Europe.”
He argued that Russia was already operating in that way, without waiting for others, while Europe could no longer afford to remain complacent.
Kosiniak-Kamysz identified three priority areas for European defense investment: affordable long-range precision-strike capabilities, drones and counter-drone systems, and artificial intelligence.
He urged greater flexibility in European defense procurement, arguing that urgent purchases should be opened to NATO allies outside the EU when European manufacturers could not supply the necessary equipment quickly enough.
"We also propose that, in the case of critical purchases requiring rapid delivery, when it is not possible to obtain this equipment in the European Union, we should open up to our NATO allies who will be able to help us," he said.
The proposal highlights tension in European defense policy between efforts to strengthen the EU's domestic arms industry and the immediate need to acquire military capabilities in response to Russia's war against Ukraine.
It could also have implications for defense manufacturers in non-EU NATO countries, including Türkiye, Britain and the US, although the Polish minister did not identify specific countries or suppliers in his remarks.

articles.title: Mephedrone dealer with seven convictions kills six Russian drone recon troops during Kupiansk offensive, including a secret FSB operative
articles.body:
A court in Russian-occupied Donetsk is currently hearing a criminal case against Russian serviceman Alexei Korolev, who is charged with murdering two or more people, along with large-scale extortion. The Insider found that Korolev is a repeat offender who went to the front from prison, where he was serving an 11-year sentence in a case involving large quantities of mephedrone, a synthetic stimulant drug. The Ukrainian state project I Want to Live previously identified Korolev as the gunman who killed six fellow soldiers in the Kharkiv Region one year ago. The Insider confirmed that all six victims died on the same day — Oct. 25, 2025.
I Want to Live said the men served in a reconnaissance company, but The Insider was able to uncover an additional detail: Rodion Kravets, one of those killed by the former prisoner Korolev, had served in the highly secretive 16th Center of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), which conducts signals intelligence and organizes cyberattacks.
In February 2026, the Ukrainian project I Want to Live, citing a source in the Russian army’s 68th Motor Rifle Division, reported that a former prisoner sent to the front had shot and killed six service members from the reconnaissance company of the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade. At the time, there was no independent confirmation of the incident. Another hearing in Korolev’s case was scheduled for Oct. 13 in Donetsk. According to the official file, the case reached the court on March 24, 2026, five months after the six soldiers died. Korolev’s lawyer, Yekaterina Kulik, confirmed to The Insider that the case involves a serviceman. “This is a case against a serviceman. All hearings are being held behind closed doors,” she said. Kulik declined to provide further details, citing attorney-client confidentiality, but she did not deny that the case involved the killing of Russian soldiers.
A shooting during the offensive on Kupiansk
According to I Want to Live, a conflict between soldiers of Russia’s 121st Motor Rifle Regiment of the 68th Division and reconnaissance troops from the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade broke out Oct. 24-25, 2025 near the village of Lyman Pershyi in the Kupiansk District of Ukraine’s Kharkiv Region. The project said the dispute began after a Russian FPV drone mistakenly attacked an all-terrain vehicle carrying soldiers from the 121st Regiment.
On the evening of Oct. 24, several assault troops went to the reconnaissance company’s command post to confront the drone operators. According to the I Want to Live source, soldiers from the 121st Regiment were intoxicated, beat the reconnaissance troops who were there, took drone-control equipment, and left.
On the morning of Oct. 25, reconnaissance company commander Yuri Davydov assembled a group of soldiers in order to recover the equipment taken by the 121st Regiment. The dispute flared again at the unit’s position. According to the Ukrainian project, Sgt. Vadim Petukhov reminded grenade launcher operator Alexei Korolev of his prison past and threatened him with sexual violence. Korolev then grabbed a weapon and opened fire. Six soldiers were killed and two others were wounded.
The incident took place during Russia’s offensive on Kupiansk. In its Oct. 24, 2025, assessment, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) cited pro-war Russian bloggers while describing offensive operations in and around the city, referring to units of the 68th Motor Rifle Division and drone operators from the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade.
Six killed on the same day
The Insider checked the list of alleged victims against a database of Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine that is maintained by the independent exiled Russian publication Mediazona and the BBC. All six service members named by I Want to Live appeared in the database with the same date of death — Oct. 25, 2025:
- Vadim Petukhov, 28, a sergeant from Cherepovets in the Vologda Region;
- Dmitry Galatov, 32, a sergeant from the Tambov Region;
- Rodion Kravets, 22, a corporal from the Krasnodar Region;
- Sergei Nizovtsev, 24, a junior sergeant from Kopeisk in the Chelyabinsk Region;
- Pavel Serov, 37, a junior sergeant from the Yaroslavl Region;
- Vyacheslav Kuznetsov, 24, a corporal from the Krasnodar Region.
According to I Want to Live, reconnaissance company commander Yuri Davydov and driver Alexander Velikanov were wounded.
Elite drone operator and specialist from the FSB’s 16th Center
According to I Want to Live, Vadim Petukhov headed an FPV crew in a UAV platoon at the Rubikon Advanced Unmanned Technologies Testing Center. The Insider was unable to independently confirm that detail, but it did find photos and videos on Petukhov’s social media that appear to show him among troops wearing expensive tactical gear. Petukhov concealed his face and personal details while alive, and photos showing his face were posted on VKontakte only after his death.
The most unusual pieces of information The Insider found concerned 22-year-old Rodion Kravets. Bank application records reviewed by the outlet list military unit 71330 as his workplace and his position as “specialist.” The forms also say he began working there in June 2023. Military unit 71330 is the FSB’s Center for Radio-Electronic Intelligence on Communications, known as the 16th Center, one of the security service’s most secretive units.
According to a British government report, the FSB’s 16th Center intercepts, decrypts, and processes electronic communications, conducts technical intrusions into foreign networks, and carries out cyber intelligence operations. The European Union has also attributed cyberattacks to the 16th Center.
Kravets was later listed as a private in military unit 61899, the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, which took part in the offensive on Kupiansk. It is unclear whether he had left the FSB’s 16th Center or was serving at the front on temporary assignment. During the same period, Kravets became a defendant in a petty theft case, suggesting the prosecution may have been suspended or closed because of his military service in the combat zone.
What else is known about those killed
Another one of those killed, 32-year-old Dmitry Galatov, commanded a reconnaissance squad in the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, according to I Want to Live. In other people’s contact lists, his number was saved under names including “Dima Tambov Commander” and “Dima Tambov Unit Commander.” The only two images on his VK profile showed him in military gear holding an anti-tank guided missile system, and a picture of a character dressed as an NKVD officer. Like Petukhov, Galatov concealed his face and personal information on social media.
37-year-old Pavel Serov served as a junior sergeant in military unit 61899, the 27th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, according to records reviewed by The Insider. He was also facing a criminal case for “intentionally destroying or damaging military property during an armed conflict or combat operations.” The investigation was suspended due to the fact that Serov was serving in the military.
Vyacheslav Kuznetsov, from the Krasnodar Region, served as a reconnaissance combat engineer, according to I Want to Live. The Insider found his page on the social network VK under the name “Vyacheslav Aliyev,” where he posted photographs of armed troops in tactical gear. His final post was dated Oct. 21, 2025 — four days before Mediazona’s listed date of death. In November, a user named Sergei Ryabokon wrote on the page: “Rest in peace, brother.”
Seven convictions and six dead
Alexei Korolev, who is accused of killing the six reconnaissance and drone troops, began his criminal career in the early 2000s. An Aug. 14, 2024, appellate ruling by the Belgorod Regional Court lists six earlier convictions handed down by courts in Vladimir in 2003, 2007, and 2011. He had been convicted of robbery, armed robbery, theft, fraud and hooliganism.
Korolev was released from prison on June 17, 2016, after serving another sentence and, according to a 2023 judgment, later joined a group involved in trafficking large quantities of drugs. Fifteen other people were charged with him. Prosecutors said the group distributed drugs through online stores and dead drops. Investigative records referred to synthetic drugs including mephedrone and substances containing alpha-PVP.
Investigators said Korolev worked as a bulk drug courier, receiving the coordinates of hidden caches from handlers and transporting narcotics between regions. In October 2020, he picked up a shipment from a cache in the Tula Region for delivery to the Moscow Region. Police stopped the car he and his wife were traveling in and found 10 packages of drugs. Korolev later admitted in court that he had helped transport the narcotics.
On Nov. 16, 2023, he was sentenced to 11 years in a special-regime penal colony for attempted large-scale drug distribution by an organized group. On Aug. 14, 2024, the Belgorod Regional Court upheld Korolev’s sentence and rejected his request for a reduction. Yet a year later, he was out of prison and carrying a weapon.
Alexei Korolev is now back in pretrial detention awaiting a verdict on murder and extortion charges.

articles.title: Russian strike on Kyiv kills three, injures over 20; parts of city lose power
articles.body:
Russian strike on Kyiv kills three, injures over 20; parts of city lose power
Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring 21, according to data from Ukraine’s State Emergency Service.
A strike hit a multistory apartment building in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district late on October 13, sparking a fire. The bodies of two people killed in the blaze were found. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said an 8-year-old child was among those injured. Sixteen people were hospitalized, four of them in serious condition.
In Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district, a strike on a non-residential building killed one person and injured another, the State Emergency Service said.
Klitschko also said a massive ballistic missile strike had hit energy facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, triggering power outages in the capital.
Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine’s Western partners again failed to warn it that Russia would launch another ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 13. He said the main target was the city’s energy infrastructure, specifically the CHPP-4 power plant, one of Kyiv’s main energy facilities.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said on the morning of October 14 that the Russian Armed Forces had carried out a massive strike on communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and the Kharkiv region, which it said served the military-industrial complex and the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
Donald Trump announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in the energy sector. Volodymyr Zelensky said the Ukrainian Armed Forces had “received all the relevant orders” in connection with this. The Kremlin said on October 13 that contacts on the energy ceasefire were continuing, but there had been no changes so far.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 91 across Ukraine over past day as ballistic missiles strike Kyiv for second straight night
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 91 across Ukraine over past day as ballistic missiles strike Kyiv for second straight night
At least 10 people were killed and 91 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles and 128 Shahed-type drones, regional authorities said on Oct. 14.
In Kyiv, at least four people were killed and 25 others injured in overnight missile strikes on the capital, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said. At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a Russian strike on a nine-story residential building in the city's Desnianskyi District. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that at least one additional victim from Kyiv's Darnytskyi District was hospitalized, and another person killed in the city's Holosiivskyi District.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media, adding 600,000 people were without power.
In total, Zelensky said Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles including Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles from Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions in Russia, as well as with 128 Shahed-type UAVs, including 77 jet-powered ones.
Ukraine's Air Force said it neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 Russian drones overnight.
In Kyiv Oblast, one person was injured over the past day by Russian strikes, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said. Civilian facilities, energy infrastructure, homes, warehouses and production facilities, and commercial establishments were hit in Russia's attacks on the oblast.
In Rivne Oblast, a Russian drone strike on a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people over the past day, Rivne's National Police branch said. Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, injuring nine people, including a child, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russia targeted the region with eight ballistic missiles, as well as multiple drones, Syniehubov said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed and 17 injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast, one person was injured by Russian mortar shelling, the Sumy military administration said. Russian forces attacked with a wide arsenal of artillery, mortars, glide bombs, and UAVs. In total, air alert in the oblast lasted 18 hours and 36 minutes during the day.
In southern Kherson Oblast, two people were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, said regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin. Russia attacked multiple settlements in the oblast with air, drone, and artillery fire, damaging critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential areas.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was killed and three injured over the past day, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov. In total, during the day, Russia launched 1,030 strikes on 56 settlements of Zaporizhia region using artillery, UAVs, and rocket launchers, he said.
In western Lviv Oblast, Russian drone attacks injured three people over the past day, said regional governor Maksym Kozytskyi.
Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured five others, including a child, over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Chernihiv Oblast suffered several Russian strikes on a school and administrative building, but no casualties were reported over the past day, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

articles.title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
- Published
A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners".
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people had been killed and 21 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. He said "several energy facilities" in Kyiv had been hit without giving more detail.
Kyiv has reported multiple Russian strikes since US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine two days ago.
In the early hours of Wednesday, Klitschko said the "massive missile attacks" had knocked out power to parts of Kyiv.
Kyiv officials have urged residents to stay in shelters after declaring a red alert due to a "missile threat".
Following the strikes on Tuesday, Zelensky said: "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
"It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."
It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats.
Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case.
"We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said.
"We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end."
Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."
But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there".
It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.
CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war.
It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down.
That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russian attack on energy grid leaves 600,000 without power, damages 30 facilities
articles.body:
A massive overnight Russian strike on critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv damaged 26 electric power elements and four oil and gas facilities, leaving at least 600,000 consumers without electricity supply, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on Wednesday.
"A targeted Russian ballistic strike specifically against energy infrastructure, regarding which the President of America defined a ceasefire. The strike was absolutely deliberate and demonstrative in scale – there has never been such a show of disrespect from Russia toward America," the head of state wrote on his Telegram channel.
According to the president, overnight Wednesday Russian forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure. The attack resulted in dead and wounded, and the scale of power outages may increase. Energy repair crews and units of the State Emergency Service are working at the impact sites.
Zelenskyy emphasized that with this attack Russia rejected the possibility of de-escalation and demonstrated contempt for U.S statements regarding an energy truce. In this regard, the Ukrainian head of state called on U.S President Donald Trump to introduce tough sanctions against the Russian Federation provided for in the recently passed and signed law by Senator Lindsey Graham, as well as to provide Ukraine with additional missile packages for Patriot air defense systems.

articles.title: Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army
articles.body:
Ukraine and NATO have unveiled two artificial intelligence (AI) tools in Vilnius, Lithuania, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on 13 October. One forecasts Russian drone attacks near the front and is ready to join the Armed Forces’ situational awareness systems. The other helps plan artillery fire and is still in testing.
A forecast of where, when, and which drones will fly targets the main source of losses near the front. In March, Ukraine’s military put the share of front-line casualties caused by FPV drones at up to 80%. In May, Ukraine’s drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said Russia was copying Ukraine’s model to grow its drone forces. A month earlier, Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov wrote that adding more drones no longer fundamentally changes the battlefield. The next stage, he said, is full integration of AI.
Forecasting Russian drone attacks
The NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC) presented both at a three-day seminar in the Lithuanian capital. NATO’s Allied Command Transformation and Ukraine’s Armed Forces built the tools with JATEC’s support.
“The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems,” the ministry said.
Model No. 13 works from past data, weather, and the current battlefield situation. The ministry said it can identify the intensity of attacks, the areas, the time windows, and the types of drones with a high probability.
Ranking artillery options
Model No. 32 is a decision-support module. It tests whether artillery plans can be generated automatically. It weighs the mission’s requirements and current operational data, including available weapons, ammunition, firing positions, and constraints.
Ukraine’s new military AI does more than watch the battlefield—it helps commanders plan what comes next
First, it applies logistics, ballistics, and impact-zone parameters to throw out unworkable options. Then it scores and ranks the rest. That means less hand-based comparison, faster decisions, and a more efficient fire loop, the ministry said. The prototype is now with the Ukrainian military for trials. If the trials succeed and it is validated, it could be expanded to other units that strike Russian forces.

articles.title: Russia strikes military-linked energy facilities across Ukraine (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Russia strikes military-linked energy facilities across Ukraine (VIDEOS)
Russian forces launched an overnight barrage against energy and communications infrastructure across Ukraine, targeting facilities that support the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said.
In a statement on Wednesday, the ministry said high-precision ground-based weapons and long-range attack drones were used to attack facilities in Kiev, its suburbs, and Kharkov Region.
In Kiev, the ministry said the strikes hit the Darnytskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-4) and Kiev CHP-5, which it said were supplying power to Ukrainian military installations and defense manufacturers. It also reported that it hit the ATM Ukrsibbank data center, which was used for collecting intelligence about Russian forces.
In the region of Kiev, the targets included Kiev CHP-6, the Trypilska thermal power plant, and the Kievskaya electricity substation. According to the ministry, the facilities supplied power to military logistics hubs, weapons storage sites, and defense enterprises.
In Kharkov and the surrounding region, Russian forces struck Kharkov CHP-5 and the Zmievskaya thermal power plant, which supplied electricity to military-industrial enterprises and Ukrainian defense installations.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky confirmed the attacks, saying Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight. “At least 600,000 people are currently, unfortunately, without electricity,” he said, warning that further outages are possible. He added that significant damage was done to 26 elements of Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, amid reports of critically low stocks of US-made Patriot interceptors.
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko claimed that three people were killed and at least 22 were injured in the barrage, adding that the attacks caused extensive electricity outages.
The head of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, Aleksandr Pertsovsky, also reported strikes on infrastructure in five regions – Kharkov, Kiev, Vinnitsa, Khmelnitsky, and Ternopol – with locomotive and carriage depots, maintenance facilities, railway stations, and rolling stock coming under attack. He described the material damage as substantial, adding that railway personnel did not suffer any casualties.
The attacks come amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington over intelligence sharing. US President Donald Trump recently said “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” as Zelensky’s term expired more than two years ago. He also urged the Ukrainian leader to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Zelensky replied that he is ready to do so if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy facilities.
Following the strikes, Zelensky said Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches for the second time that week. He also claimed that the US threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian refineries.
However, he stressed that cooperation has not been halted, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
The latest barrage came after the Russian Defense Ministry vowed earlier this month to intensify strikes on military-related facilities in Ukraine in response to Zelensky’s threat to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Air Force: partners warned of later missile waves
articles.body:
- Ukraine received no partner warning before the first Russian ballistic missile wave overnight into Oct. 14, but did for the next three, Col. Yurii Ihnat said.
- The first wave hit Kyiv at about 22:40 after a similar gap in warnings the previous night, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukraine’s partners warned it about three of the four waves of Russian ballistic missiles launched overnight into Oct. 14, but sent no alert before the first wave hit Kyiv, Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Col. Yurii Ihnat said on national television.
Ihnat said he wanted to clarify the issue because many people had asked whether Ukraine was still receiving launch warnings from its partners. The Air Force had said late on Oct. 13 that, for a second night in a row, no information about ballistic missile launches from Russian territory had come from partners before an attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m., and that the reasons were being investigated.
“Indeed, we first issued a notice at around 22:40 that there had been no notification from partners about ballistic missiles, but in the next three waves of attacks, notifications from partners about the use of ballistic missiles did come through,” said Col. Yurii Ihnat.
The early warnings come from partner satellites and monitoring systems that can detect the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, and Ukraine has relied heavily on data from the United States for this. With a warning, air defense crews have time to prepare and cities can sound air raid sirens earlier. Without one, Ukrainian forces only spot the incoming ballistic missiles once they come within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, which leaves interceptor crews less time to react and civilians less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The first wave struck Kyiv without that warning, and the attack grew through the night. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. Zelenskyy said the strike hit energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, and asked Washington for more Patriot interceptors, the main U.S.-made system Ukraine uses to shoot down ballistic missiles.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military stopped working at speeds above 160 km/h (100 mph), disrupting combat missions, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who has tracked Russian efforts to jam Starlink along the front. Starlink is not used for Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia, where SpaceX already blocks the service, so the restriction falls on tactical strike and interceptor drones operating over Ukrainian and occupied territory.
Ihnat did not say why the warning for the first wave did not come, or why no alert arrived before the previous night’s attack. The Air Force said earlier that it was looking into the reasons, and neither the White House nor the U.S. Department of War has commented on the missed warnings.

articles.title: Russian missile attack on Kyiv kills one
articles.body:
Russian missile attack on Kyiv kills two, Zelenskiy says no warning received
Oct 13 - Russian forces struck the Ukrainian capital with ballistic missiles on Tuesday, killing two people in a high-rise apartment and hitting a thermal power plant in the second attack in 24 hours without warning from Kyiv's Western allies.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said the main target was energy infrastructure. He said it was unfair that Kyiv was enduring attacks without warnings from partners and said intelligence showed that more strikes were likely.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strike on the nine-storey building had killed two people and injured 21. Sixteen were being treated in hospital and four were in a serious condition.
Emergency crews were battling fires in apartments throughout the building and residents were being evacuated. Reuters pictures and TV footage showed firefighters training hoses on the building's shattered facade.
"Once again, no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically thermal plant No. 4," Zelenskiy said on Telegram.
"According to our intelligence, the Russians are preparing further ballistic missile launches."
"The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound to abide by what the president of the United States said," he added, referring to US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire at the weekend.
"And it is certainly unfair that they are destroying our energy infrastructure while Ukraine is not even receiving warnings about ballistic missile launches."
Zelenskiy had earlier said that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a previous overnight attack on the capital.
Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence even as he pressured Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes, experts and officials say. REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine downs four ballistic missiles, 115 drones in massive Russian overnight attack
articles.body:
Ukraine downs four ballistic missiles, 115 drones in massive Russian overnight attack
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, October 13, Russia launched a massive combined attack on Ukraine using attack drones and 39 missiles of various types following ballistic trajectories toward their targets.
The main targets were Kyiv, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region.
The attack was notable for the simultaneous use of different types of aerial weapons launched from multiple directions, as well as the large number of ballistic missiles aimed at energy facilities.
In total, the Air Force’s radio-technical troops detected 167 aerial attack assets: 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types:
39 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh and Rostov regions;
128 attack drones, including Shahed drones (77 of them jet-powered), Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and Italmas drones, as well as Parodiya decoy drones. They were launched from the directions of Millerovo, Oryol, temporarily occupied Donetsk, Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Wednesday, October 14, air defense had shot down or suppressed 119 targets:
Four Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks ballistic missiles;
115 drones of various types, including 59 jet-powered drones, accounting for 90% of all attack drones deployed.
Preliminary reports indicate that missile and attack drone strikes were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations as of 9:00. Some of the Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As Ukrinform reported, four people were killed in a combined Russian attack on Kyiv.

articles.title: Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
articles.body:
Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
"There will also be an important meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham," Zelensky said upon his arrival.
"We are preparing decisions that will strengthen us."
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid." The Ukrainian president is set to hold talks with Burnham at 10 Downing Street and will meet King Charles III as part of the visit.
The British government also announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
Burnham has also instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia, according to the press release.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.

articles.title: Russian Overnight Strikes Target Kyiv CHP Plants and Kill Civilians Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian forces targeted all three of Kyiv’s municipal combined heat and power (CHP) plants in an overnight attack on Oct. 13-14, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi reported on Wednesday. Strikes across Ukraine killed civilians and damaged civilian infrastructure.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Kharkiv and surrounding regions, Koretskyi said on Telegram. In the Kyiv region, Russian forces also struck critical infrastructure supplying electricity to the capital and central regions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Energy workers and emergency responders began working at the affected sites early in the morning, conducting firefighting and debris-clearing operations. Specialists have also started priority restoration work at the targeted facilities, according to the prime minister.
The attacks followed an evening strike on a high-rise residential building in Kyiv that killed two people and injured 25. Another person was killed and one injured in a separate morning attack on the capital, Koretskyi said.
Railway infrastructure was also targeted in five regions. No casualties were reported at the railway facilities, as timely evacuations helped protect workers and others at the sites. Restoration work is ongoing.
Industrial fires and residential damage reported across Ukraine
In the Khmelnytskyi region, Russian drone attacks sparked fires at industrial sites in the Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported on Telegram.
‘Blatant Disrespect Toward America’: Zelensky Slams Russia’s Strike on Ukraine’s Energy Sector
Falling drone debris also caused a fire at a gas station in Khmelnytskyi district, injuring two people. In the city of Khmelnytskyi, drone debris ignited fires at two private homes in a residential neighborhood. No casualties were reported there.
Emergency crews were repeatedly forced to leave their work sites because of renewed Russian attacks. Eighty rescuers and 22 pieces of equipment were deployed to extinguish a fire at one of the industrial facilities in Khmelnytskyi District.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian attacks killed two people and injured six others, including a child, according to the DSNS. In Pavlohrad, a strike on an open area killed one person and injured four others, including a child. In Nikopol district, attacks on the district center and the Myrivka community killed another person.
Russian forces also struck an enterprise in Dnipro overnight, injuring a man and triggering a large-scale fire. In Synelnykove district, attacks on the Yavornytske and Mykolaivka communities injured a woman and damaged a private house. Emergency responders extinguished all fires caused by the attacks, the DSNS said.
Strikes hit Sloviansk, Ternopil and railway infrastructure
In the Donetsk region, a Russian airstrike on a residential area in Sloviansk wounded seven people and damaged five apartment buildings. A fire broke out in a non-residential building and was later extinguished.
A car also caught fire following a Russian attack in Bylbasivka. Firefighters had to suspend their work because of the continuing threat posed by Russian drones.
In Ternopil, a Russian drone strike damaged an administrative building and sparked a fire on the second floor. Rescuers extinguished the blaze, and no casualties were reported.
Russian forces also attacked a railway infrastructure facility in the Vinnytsia region, causing a large fire. Emergency crews had to interrupt their work because of the threat of follow-up attacks involving drones and ballistic missiles. Responders eventually extinguished all remaining hotspots, and explosives experts inspected the site for unexploded ordnance. No fatalities or injuries were reported.
In the Kharkiv region, five people were injured in a Russian attack on the city of Derhachi, as per DSNS. A first person-view (FPV) drone struck a garage at a civilian enterprise, sparking a fire that spread across 200 square meters and engulfed trucks inside the building. Emergency crews extinguished the blaze.
Koretskyi thanked rescuers, police officers, medics, energy workers and others involved in responding to the attacks and helping affected residents.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: Canada’s Dominion Dynamics, Ukraine’s TENCORE Sign Deal to Build TerMIT Ground Vehicles in Canada
articles.body:
Canadian defense technology company Dominion Dynamics and Ukraine’s TENCORE signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to manufacture TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) in Canada, with initial production targeted for 2027, according to the press release.
TENCORE is a leading Ukrainian developer and serial manufacturer of UGVs for military and dual-use applications. Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the company has delivered over 4,000 robotic platforms to Ukraine’s Armed Forces (AFU), actively deployed across more than 50 combat brigades.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The biggest lesson from Ukraine is speed. Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback, and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale. Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers, and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles,” the press release quoted TENCORE co-founder Roman Tkachenko.
The MOU, signed at the Canadian Pavilion during the AUSA 2026 defense conference in Washington, also provides for integrating AuraNet, Dominion’s autonomy stack for pan-domain command and control, as the onboard intelligence layer for TerMIT. Nadia Theodore, Canada’s deputy ambassador to the US, attended the signing ceremony.
“Canada has the workforce and the suppliers to build at scale. This agreement is how two companies start turning that commitment into vehicles, and we intend to move fast,” the press release quoted Eliot Pence, founder and CEO of Dominion Dynamics.
Shakhtar Dream of Champions League Return to Ukraine as London Keeps War in Spotlight
The deal follows a joint declaration on defense cooperation that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Volodymyr Zelensky signed in September. Both countries committed to manufacturing thousands of battle-tested drones and unmanned systems in the next two years, with one-third earmarked for Ukraine’s defense, the companies wrote.
The partnership will support the deployment and continued development of AuraNet for Ukraine’s front lines, according to the press release. It will also create high-skilled jobs in Canada and strengthen the country’s sovereign defense technology base.
Dominion plans to manufacture TerMIT in Canadian facilities. A TENCORE team will lead the initial technology transfer and train technicians in Canada to build the UGV, the companies wrote. Since 2024, TENCORE has delivered more than 5,000 UGVs to Ukrainian military units, the press release says.
Dominion also aims to develop an Arctic-hardened TerMIT for Canadian operations and for export to NATO allies. The companies will continue to work toward definitive agreements.
Dominion Dynamics was founded in 2025 and builds autonomy, sensing, and command-and-control systems. According to them, it has deployed its technology with the Canadian Armed Forces across the High North.

articles.title: America’s broken promises, Iran’s resolve, and the dangerous game over the Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
The latest diplomatic deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz exposes the central problem in the US–Iran confrontation: Washington wants concessions from Iran, but Tehran is demanding clear commitments, credible guarantees, and an end to what it sees as a pattern of pressure, shifting demands, and broken trust.
On 11th October 11, 2026, Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, described the US response to Iran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz as insufficient. Tehran says Washington has accepted some conditions while leaving others unclear. The two sides also disagree over the sequence of implementation, particularly whether Iran’s nuclear programme should be addressed at the outset or whether the immediate priority should be restoring maritime security and resolving the conflict. Qatar has served as an intermediary in the negotiations. These are not minor technical disagreements; they go to the heart of whether either side believes the other will honour an agreement.
This is precisely why Washington’s assurances are no longer enough for Tehran.
From Iran’s perspective, what is the value of another diplomatic promise if the terms remain ambiguous, the demands keep changing, or military pressure continues while negotiations are supposedly underway? A country cannot be expected to make consequential strategic concessions merely because a powerful adversary says that an agreement is possible.
Credibility must be demonstrated through specific commitments, verifiable implementation, and guarantees that cannot be casually discarded when political circumstances change.
The core issue is not simply whether the Strait will reopen. It is whether the United States expects Iran to negotiate as an equal party with legitimate security concerns or to negotiate under pressure until it accepts Washington’s preferred terms.
For years, Washington has relied on sanctions, military deployments, diplomatic leverage, and the threat of escalation to influence Iran’s decisions. The United States may regard these measures as instruments of national security. Tehran, however, sees them as evidence that negotiations can become another arena of coercion. That perception cannot be dismissed if Washington genuinely wants a durable settlement.
You cannot demand trust while refusing to address the reasons that trust has collapsed. You cannot preach diplomacy while making the other side fear that concessions today may become vulnerabilities tomorrow.
Iran’s refusal to accept an inadequate response is therefore a declaration that negotiations must have substance.
Tehran is signalling that it will not automatically exchange strategic leverage for vague assurances. Whether one agrees with Iran’s policies or not, the underlying principle is straightforward: an agreement must contain obligations for both parties, not concessions for one side and discretion for the other.
Iran is also demonstrating strategic confidence. It has not accepted the proposition that American military and economic power automatically entitle Washington to dictate the outcome. Its position is that its security, sovereignty, and national interests must be addressed before a settlement can be considered credible. That confidence does not guarantee Iran will prevail in every confrontation, nor does it remove the considerable economic and military risks it faces. But it does show that pressure alone has not produced the diplomatic outcome Washington seeks.
READ: Iran’s IRGC Navy threatens to sink US warships approaching Strait of Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz: where the real leverage lies
The Strait of Hormuz is not an ordinary shipping lane. Before the current conflict, approximately one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flows passed through this strategic chokepoint. Prolonged disruption can affect crude prices, shipping insurance, transport costs, inflation, and the economies of countries far removed from the battlefield. Reuters coverage of the Hormuz negotiations
That reality gives this confrontation consequences well beyond Washington and Tehran. Energy-importing nations, particularly those already vulnerable to higher fuel prices, have every reason to demand a serious diplomatic solution.
But there is an important distinction: leverage is not the same as victory. Restrictions on maritime traffic can impose costs on the United States and its partners, but they can also hurt Iran, neighbouring countries, commercial shipping, and ordinary people worldwide. The strongest diplomatic outcome would be one that converts this dangerous leverage into enforceable security arrangements rather than allowing the global economy to remain hostage to an escalating confrontation.
Washington must therefore decide whether its objective is a sustainable agreement or the appearance of having forced Iran to submit. Those are two very different outcomes.
Israel’s role: Strategic pressure or child’s play?
Israel cannot be separated from this crisis. The war began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran on 28th February 2026, according to Reuters reporting. The resulting confrontation has made the question of security guarantees central to Tehran’s calculations.
From Tehran’s standpoint, there is little reason to trust a diplomatic process if military escalation remains a possibility while negotiations continue. Iran can reasonably ask whether any agreement reached with Washington would survive a change in strategy, renewed attacks, or pressure from regional allies.
And this is where Israel’s approach deserves sharp scrutiny.
If Israeli leaders believe that repeated military strikes, threats, and pressure can permanently resolve a strategic conflict with a major regional adversary, that assumption risks becoming a dangerous political fantasy. Tactical military operations are not the same as a durable political settlement. Destroying infrastructure does not automatically eliminate political resistance, and demonstrating military capability does not guarantee that an opponent will accept the victor’s preferred terms.
Calling such a strategy “child’s play” is a forceful political criticism of an approach that mistakes coercion for resolution. Serious statecraft requires more than threats, military posturing, and the expectation that an adversary will eventually surrender its interests.
Israel has its own security concerns, including Iran’s nuclear programme and regional military capabilities. Those concerns cannot simply be wished away. But neither can they justify an endless cycle in which military escalation creates new grievances, new threats, and new obstacles to diplomacy.
If Washington and Israel want a more secure Middle East, they must recognise that security cannot be built indefinitely on the assumption that Iran will eventually break under pressure.
READ: Iranian attacks target 6 ships near Strait of Hormuz in 1 day, highest since war with US began
The United States must confront the crisis of credibility
The deeper problem is credibility. Critics of US foreign policy point to past disputes over international agreements, sanctions, and the use of military force as reasons to question whether American commitments will endure. Such criticisms must be examined case by case, rather than treating every allegation of betrayal as automatically proven. Nevertheless, the present deadlock demonstrates that assurances alone are insufficient when the parties disagree over obligations, sequencing, and the risk of renewed conflict.
Washington cannot expect Iran to accept an agreement whose key provisions remain unclear. Nor can it expect Tehran to treat negotiations as insulated from military threats when the conflict itself has repeatedly undermined diplomatic progress.
If the United States genuinely wants to demonstrate that its word carries weight, it should put forward explicit commitments, establish a verifiable timetable, clarify the reciprocal obligations of both parties, and identify mechanisms for resolving alleged violations. These measures would not require Washington to abandon its security interests. They would require it to show that diplomacy is more than a temporary instrument for extracting concessions.
The same standard must apply to Iran. Tehran must also make its obligations clear, address legitimate maritime-security concerns, and recognise that a durable settlement requires protections for commercial navigation and regional stability. An agreement cannot endure if either side treats compliance as optional.
The final message
Iran is telling Washington that the age of expecting automatic concessions in exchange for ambiguous promises is over. Whether Tehran can sustain its position under continued economic and military pressure is a separate question. But the current impasse makes one fact clear: neither power has yet established the trust necessary for a lasting settlement.
The United States has enormous military, financial, and diplomatic resources. But power has limits. Sanctions cannot manufacture trust. Threats cannot guarantee political submission. Military superiority cannot, by itself, produce a legitimate and lasting peace.
Iran, for its part, must understand that national strength is measured not only by resistance but also by the ability to turn bargaining power into concrete, sustainable gains. Its confidence will matter most if it can secure enforceable commitments while avoiding a wider war that damages its own people and the wider region.
Israel, too, must confront the limits of a strategy built primarily around military pressure. No country can bomb its way to permanent regional stability while ignoring the political conditions that sustain conflict.
The world does not need another round of declarations, threats, and theatrical diplomacy. It needs commitments that can be verified, obligations that apply to everyone, and a settlement that cannot be discarded the moment political calculations change.
If Washington wants Iran to trust its word, it must prove that word is worth trusting. If Israel wants lasting security, it must recognise that perpetual escalation is not a substitute for political resolution. And if Iran wants its strategic strength to translate into lasting success, it must use its leverage to pursue a settlement that protects its sovereignty without sacrificing regional stability.
The Strait of Hormuz is the immediate flashpoint. Trust is the underlying crisis. Until that crisis is addressed honestly, every new proposal risks becoming another exchange of demands, another missed opportunity, and another warning that the costs of failed diplomacy will be paid by millions of people who never chose this confrontation.
