articles.title: Ukrainian foreign minister: Putin is not simply attacking Ukraine, he is openly defying the US
articles.body:
Ukrainian foreign minister: Putin is not simply attacking Ukraine, he is openly defying the US
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, commenting on overnight Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, has said Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin has rejected the US-proposed "energy ceasefire".
Source: Sybiha on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Sybiha noted that Putin responded to peace efforts by launching 39 missiles and more than 120 drones. Ukraine's energy facilities were the main targets of the attack.
Quote: "Putin is not simply attacking Ukraine. He is openly defying the United States and treating every attempt to stop this war with contempt.
There can be no economic rewards for aggression. No sanctions relief. No concessions that allow Russia to finance its next wave of terror. Every dollar that reaches Moscow's war budget is another resource for attacks on Ukrainian civilians and threats to transatlantic security."
Details: Sybiha called on Ukraine's partners to tighten sanctions, enforce them more rigorously and provide additional air defence support to Ukraine immediately.
"Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not incentives to continue the war," he concluded.
Background:
- US President Donald Trump claimed that the "energy ceasefire" he had announced between Ukraine and Russia is in effect and said reports of violations needed to be checked.
- On 11 October, Trump claimed on his social media platform Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire.
- The Kremlin said it had nothing to say about the energy ceasefire announced by Trump.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Ukraine says Starlink restricted operations overnight, disrupting military missions
articles.body:
Ukraine says Starlink restricted operations overnight, disrupting military missions
Elon Musk's Starlink imposed restrictions on the operation of internet terminals in Ukraine overnight, disrupting military missions, an adviser to the Ukrainian president said on Wednesday. The official said Ukraine was given no prior warning about the restrictions to the satellite system it relies on for battlefield operations.
The operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to be restricted overnight, a technology adviser to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Wednesday, disrupting Ukrainian military missions as Russia launched targeted strikes on the country's energy infrastructure.
Ukraine uses the satellite system controlled by SpaceX owner Elon Musk for its battlefield communications, but the tech titan has shifted his stance on Ukraine several times since Russia's invasion in 2022.
"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said the adviser, Sergiy Beskrestnov.
"Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added. "Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.
US President Donald Trump called for a pause in attacks on energy infrastructure while moving to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Read moreTrump, Zelensky clash over diesel deal as Russian strikes on Ukraine kill at least 21
A senior Ukrainian official told AFP that the disruption "severely restricts logistics, first and foremost".
Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, added that units had been forced to cancel some missions.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," it said in a statement to Reuters.
Ukraine has been using Starlink terminals to provide satellite internet connections as an alternative to radio control for its drones.
"Some restrictions were already being reported yesterday evening. So, in effect, it is happening in sync with this morning's Russian ballistic attack," the official added.
Trump wrote in a social media post Sunday that "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
But there is no sign either side is ready for such a ceasefire, with Ukraine reporting that a Russian missile struck a power plant in Kyiv on Tuesday evening.
Zelensky said in August that Kyiv was seeking to develop an alternative to Starlink in partnership "with a European country" that he did not identify.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis use Chinese parts to build Iranian ballistic missile, boost attack range - report
articles.body:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis are developing their own version of Iran's Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile using parts imported from Chinese companies, according to a Tuesday Wall Street Journal report citing new data from UK-based independent monitor Conflict Armament Research.
The missile would have a maximum range of approximately 1,200 miles, according to the WSJ. This would put all of Saudi Arabia and Israel in range.
The Houthis, a US-designated terrorist organization under a United Nations arms embargo that controls large parts of Yemen, have been fighting the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in a civil war since 2014.
The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28. Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.
The Conflict Armament Research report was based on information from Yemeni authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments in 2025, which included the missile equipment hidden among a range of other goods, according to the WSJ.
“When you have imports like that, there is a possibility that they are already manufacturing or that they are trying and it doesn’t really work out,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament, told the Wall Street Journal, adding that because the Houthis weapons facilities are well camouflaged, it is unclear how far along missile production has proceeded.
China says it is respecting arms sales ban
China claims to be adhering to the UN arms embargo on the Houthis, per the WSJ. However, the report noted that while some of the Houthi-imported materials could have civilian uses, some were parts specifically designed for missile production.
The imported parts include custom-made metal missile components, including parts of the motor and of the airframe, the missile’s basic structure, the Wall Street Journal noted, adding that Yemeni authorities also found fins which stabilize the missile in flight and parts of a solid-propellant rocket motor of a Kheibar Shekan-series missile.
Yemeni authorities also seized tools, testing equipment, and raw materials, including the ablative material which protects sections of the missile from the intense heat produced by a ballistic missile, the WSJ added.
Why are Iranian Kheibar Shekan missiles particularly advantageous?
Iran has been using Kheibar Shekan missiles, cheap, mobile, and accurate missiles, which have a range of at least 1,400 kilometers in their strikes against US assets across the Middle East, the Wall Street Journal cited US officials as saying in July.
The solid-fuel, medium-range Kheibar Shekan missiles differ from older Iranian missiles that require prelaunch fueling, a lengthy process which the Kheibar Shekan can bypass by being kept fueled and are capable of being loaded quickly into trucks or other vehicles for launching, making it easier to evade US and Israeli warplanes seeking to knock out Iranian missile launch sites, military experts told WSJ at the time.
Danya Saperstein and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Allies warned Ukraine of three ballistic waves, but not the first – Air Force
articles.body:
Allies warned Ukraine of three ballistic waves, but not the first – Air Force
Colonel Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, has said that during Russia's attack on the night of 13-14 October, Ukraine's partners did not warn it about the first wave of ballistic missiles but did give advance notice of the three subsequent waves.
Source: Ihnat during the national joint 24/7 newscast
Details: Ihnat clarified whether Ukraine had received warnings from its partners, as the issue has prompted many questions.
Quote: "At around 22:40, we initially said we had received no warning from our partners about ballistic missiles. However, our partners did alert us to the ballistic threat ahead of the next three waves of attacks."
Background:
- On the night of 13-14 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with 39 ballistic missiles and 128 drones, mainly targeting Kyiv and Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts. Ukrainian air defence forces shot down or jammed four missiles and 115 drones.
- Reports of a missile threat reached users immediately before or as the explosions occurred.
- The president's office said Kyiv had received no warning from its partners about the strike and that the military and relevant services were investigating the circumstances.
- A similar situation occurred at 22:10 on 12 October, when Russia launched five ballistic missiles on Kyiv. Ukraine's Air Force said it had received no information about missile launches from Russian territory, leaving insufficient time to issue an air-raid warning.
- Commenting on the strike, Ihnat noted that this was not the first time intelligence had arrived too late. He said he hoped Ukrainian intelligence would work with Kyiv's international partners to determine the cause of the delay.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Kyiv continues to receive intelligence from the US.
	
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Striking where it hurts: Ukrainian drones are having a tangible effect on the Russian economy
articles.body:
Russia’s losses from Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries have already reached 1% of GDP — and that's if Vladimir Putin is to be believed. Putin, of course, is hard to believe, but even 1% of GDP is an enormous sum — roughly half of the federal government's current budget deficit. And on top of that, mounting strikes mean the figure is likely only to rise — especially if the three recent attacks on Yandex data centers signal a new trend. According to The Insider’s estimates, each successful strike on an oil refinery costs Russia an average of around 23 billion rubles ($274 million), while a strike on an online marketplace warehouse costs 450,000 rubles ($5,350) per square meter. In the long run, these losses will weigh on the budget and drive down consumer demand — two key drivers of the Russian economy.
Average cost per unit
Unlike the production of crude oil, refining generates relatively little revenue for the Russian budget. When a refinery shuts down, the costs are borne by businesses: the refinery’s owner, fuel consumers, and intermediaries. Repair costs can be roughly estimated from equipment prices or the total cost of modernizing a refinery (since exact prices for individual units are rarely disclosed). For Russia’s large refineries, of which there are 37, several examples are available.
The Ministry of Energy estimated that 95 secondary-processing units were rebuilt and commissioned in Russia between 2011 and 2018, at a total investment of 1.6 trillion rubles. That works out to just under 17 billion rubles per unit, by a very rough estimate. Between 2019 and 2026, another 27 units were commissioned, against a target of 40, with investments totaling 512 billion rubles. That amounts to nearly 19 billion rubles per unit on average. The figures broadly corroborate each other and reflect rising costs, partly due to sanctions.
Bringing a single secondary-processing unit online costs 19 billion rubles – the average over the past seven years
Replacing imported oil-refining equipment with domestic alternatives has been a particular challenge. Foreign technologies dominated the original modernization projects, and after sanctions were imposed, the Ministry of Industry and Trade sought to promote import substitution. However, the industry continues to rely heavily on Asian suppliers.
There are also figures for individual companies. In 2023, Gazprom Neft ceremonially launched a new primary oil-processing complex in Omsk, costing more than 66 billion rubles. It replaced six older units built to previous environmental standards. In other words, replacing each old unit cost about 11 billion rubles.
Matthew Sagers, an expert at S&P Global Commodity Insights, estimated that damage from a single Ukrainian drone attack in 2024 could have cost anywhere from several million to tens of millions of dollars. Around the same time, Sergey Vakulenko wrote that refinery repairs could run into tens of millions of dollars.
If the energy truce proposed by Trump is agreed to, it would give Russian refineries time to carry out repairs. But if the deal Ukraine is willing to accept — but which Russia is not — falls through again and the Ukrainian Armed Forces step up their attacks on refineries, major overhauls may soon be necessary, according to one industry source. Such an overhaul takes at least six months, as the unit must be designed by an engineering institute, approved, manufactured, and installed.
Repairs involving imported equipment could take even longer, as the necessary components may simply be unavailable. Recovery from a fire can take longer still, requiring an assessment of the site, the dismantling of damaged structures, and the removal of debris.
What would it cost to repair the Moscow refinery?
On the night of Sept. 20, a drone attack damaged the Euro+ complex at the Moscow refinery. The complex, which includes an ELOU-AVT-6 primary oil-processing unit, was commissioned in 2020 at a cost of 98 billion rubles.
ELOU-AVT is an integrated processing unit in which crude oil undergoes atmospheric and vacuum distillation after desalting. A typical configuration includes an electrical desalting unit, an atmospheric distillation unit, and a vacuum distillation unit, often along with gasoline stabilization and fractionation units. Most of these components are available from Chinese suppliers, albeit in smaller capacities than the original equipment. A search for “atmospheric distillation column,” for example, returns numerous offers. An atmospheric distillation unit can also be ordered separately from China, although available prices are only rough estimates.
“The Russia factor for Chinese equipment is four,” one industry source told The Insider, explaining why equipment repairs are becoming more expensive. In other words, Chinese equipment delivered to Russia costs four times the price quoted on a website or in a catalog. Meanwhile, European equipment routed through China is prohibitively expensive and economically viable only for specialized items that cannot be sourced elsewhere.
The cost of Chinese equipment comparable to that used at the Moscow refinery can be estimated from several international projects involving Chinese contractors. In 2016–2017, China Petroleum Engineering & Construction Corporation (CPECC) modernized an atmospheric distillation unit at an Algerian refinery under a contract worth $408 million (approximately 23 billion rubles). The engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract covered the refurbishment of the atmospheric distillation unit, installation of a naphtha hydrotreating unit, and construction of a new control room.
At the Moscow refinery in Kapotnya, similar processes are part of the Euro+ complex: atmospheric and vacuum distillation in an ELOU-AVT-6 unit with an annual capacity of 6.6 million tons, as well as diesel fuel and naphtha hydrotreating. The Kapotnya refinery also has a unit for recovering sulfur from hydrogen sulfide, which was not included in the Algerian project.
A larger example is Kuwait’s Al-Zour refinery, which far exceeds the Moscow refinery in capacity. Its main processing units, including the atmospheric and vacuum distillation facilities, were built by China’s Sinopec Engineering in a consortium with Spain’s Técnicas Reunidas and South Korea’s Hanwha. The lump-sum turnkey (LSTK) contract ran from 2015 to 2019 and was worth $4.1 billion (equivalent to 265 billion rubles at the Central Bank’s average annual exchange rate). In addition to atmospheric and vacuum distillation and hydrotreating, the Kuwaiti project includes vacuum gas oil hydrocracking and a large elemental sulfur recovery unit. Similar facilities are also part of the Moscow refinery.
Another benchmark is China’s Zhongke refinery, with an annual capacity of 10 million tons. Built between 2017 and 2020, its first phase cost approximately $5.6 billion (around 360 billion rubles). Alongside atmospheric and vacuum distillation, it includes fluid catalytic cracking, hydrocracking, and an aromatics complex, as does the Moscow refinery.
However, an ELOU-AVT-6 unit cannot simply be bought off the shelf. Such facilities are not sold as finished products on the open market; they must be designed and built or reconstructed for a specific refinery. Publicly available figures offer only rough estimates for comparable units. In 2012, construction of a new ELOU-AVT-6 unit was estimated at 8.3 billion rubles. In Azerbaijan, dismantling and installing an operating ELOU-AVT unit with one-third the capacity cost $75–80 million in 2018, (equivalent to approximately 6–7 billion rubles at the time). In Russia, contracts for building new ELOU-AVT units comparable in capacity to the Azerbaijani facility were estimated at 14 billion rubles in 2017.
An ELOU-AVT-6 unit cannot simply be bought off the shelf: each must be built for a specific refinery. The price includes design, manufacturing and installation, and now runs to hundreds of billions of rubles
In other words, Chinese equipment for facilities comparable to those at the Moscow refinery can cost anywhere from several hundred million dollars to several billion dollars for an entire integrated refinery, depending on its scale and the range of secondary processing units.
The total cost of delivering equipment from China to Russia is three to four times the Chinese price, once logistics, customs duties, adaptation to Russian standards, and intermediaries’ margins are included. Repairs will therefore cost at least 25 billion rubles, with the upper end potentially reaching half a trillion rubles after markups.
The cost of the fuel shortage
Unfortunately, the full impact on the fuel market is difficult to assess. Rosstat has not published gasoline and diesel production data since May 29, 2024, leaving experts to guess. The most impressionistic approach is to look at gas stations — the length of queues and the level of tension among those waiting. But this is no basis for a serious assessment.
In early July, Ukraine’s General Staff put the share of affected refining capacity at 42.74%. The Financial Times estimated that by the end of July, 45% of capacity was nominally offline, with more than 30% actually idle. Refining output had fallen to 25–30% below normal levels. Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, estimated the losses at 25–30%.
Experts broadly agree that Russian oil refining has fallen to 3.8–4.2 million barrels per day, down from 5.3–5.5 million barrels per day in 2024–2025 — a drop of 20–25%. The International Energy Agency forecasts a similar level of 4 million barrels per day. In September, it lowered its baseline forecast for the next 18 months.
Even an accurate estimate of lost refining output, however, does not tell us how much consumption has changed. That is crucial to assessing the indirect damage caused by the attacks. Short-term shortages can be partly offset by drawing on reserves, importing fuel, rerouting supplies, or increasing output at other refineries. The economic impact must therefore also be assessed from another angle: transport activity.
Sergei Vakulenko, an expert at the Berlin-based Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, proposed using traffic accident statistics to gauge the severity of the fuel crisis, reasoning that they reflect the intensity of road traffic. His model showed that the number of accidents in July 2026 was 7.9% below the expected level, while the preliminary figure for August was 12.4% lower. The decline was particularly pronounced in more rural areas. Allowing for subsequent revisions to the data, Vakulenko estimated that gasoline consumption fell by 7.5–10% in August.
Payments by heavy trucks offer another indirect indicator. The Platon system charges vehicles weighing more than 12 metric tons a per-kilometer fee on federal highways, excluding toll roads. Monthly payments can be reconstructed from the operator’s reports by comparing the cumulative toll collections over time. (However, one adjustment is necessary, as the rate was 3.34 rubles per kilometer in 2025 but rose to 5.19 rubles in 2026.)
Using this method, The Insider calculated that between Aug. 15 and Sept. 15, 2026, truckers paid for 1.93 billion notional kilometers of travel, down from 2.4 billion a year earlier — a decline of about 20%.
Platon toll collections from August 15 to September 15 indicate that truck mileage fell by 20% year on year
A drop recorded over a single month is not enough to draw sweeping conclusions. But even if only one in ten trucks was taken off the road (rather than one in five), or all trucks kept running but traveled 20% fewer kilometers, the figures still point to a negative economic impact. After all, road freight is critical to the Russian economy.
As Putin himself said on Oct. 1: “Ukrainian forces began striking refineries and openly declared their goal: to damage our economy. Did they achieve it? Partly. By our estimates, we lost about 1% of GDP.” Notably, Putin did not specify the period covered by his estimate, but if he meant annual GDP, then the figure would be 232 trillion rubles, according to Finance Ministry projections. If true, that would put the losses from all the attacks at 2.32 trillion rubles — slightly more than a third of the projected 2026 budget deficit of 7.3 trillion rubles, and more than half the remaining liquid assets of Russia’s National Wealth Fund, which stood at 4 trillion rubles on Sept. 1.
Putin acknowledged that strikes on oil refineries had cost the Russian economy roughly 1% of GDP, but did not specify that this amounted to more than 2 trillion rubles
The estimate presumably includes destroyed property, repair costs, and losses caused by refinery disruptions — such as downtime, higher supply costs, and losses at businesses affected by fuel shortages. If Putin was referring to the current year, about 50 successful attacks on refineries were recorded in the first half of 2026, according to The Insider, followed by roughly the same number in July–September. That would put the average cost of each of the 100 successful strikes at 23 billion rubles (though this remains a very rough estimate based on an interpretation of figures released by the Kremlin).
Marketplaces: Goods burn, obligations remain
Russia’s retail sales totaled 61 trillion rubles in 2025. Though not a core economic sector, retail is just as vital to everyday life as the availability of fuel at filling stations. Alexander Maslennikov, deputy secretary of Russia’s Security Council, described the economic impact of strikes on warehouses belonging to the Wildberries online marketplace as “very limited” and “symbolic.” He acknowledged, however, that the attacks cause localized economic losses and affect small businesses.
The direct damage to the retail sector from strikes on Wildberries warehouses consists of the value of destroyed goods and damage to the warehouse infrastructure itself. Wildberries operates warehouses of varying sizes, and the Pareto principle applies to e-commerce too: 20% of products generate 80% of profits. In other words, 20% of the goods destroyed could account for 80% of the losses. Even so, some rough estimates of the damage are already available.
Following attacks on warehouses in Elektrostal (250,000 square meters) and Kotovsk (108,000 square meters), Kommersant reported that the cost of rebuilding the logistics complexes would range from just over 20 billion to 35.8 billion rubles. The variation reflects differing estimates of construction costs from industry sources, ranging from 60,000 to 100,000 rubles per square meter. The midpoint is 80,000 rubles per square meter, a useful benchmark for estimating damage from future attacks.
Estimating the value of goods destroyed by fire is even more speculative. Although products vary widely in price, we can assume that warehouses contain a roughly equal mix of cheap and expensive goods. On that basis, we can estimate the average value of goods destroyed per square meter. Ideally, we would use cubic meters, but warehouse capacity is not reported in those terms. Reports on fires also measure the affected buildings by floor area, not volume.
The value of goods destroyed in the fires in Elektrostal and Kotovsk was estimated at 150–170 billion rubles across a combined area of 360,000 square meters. That works out to an average of 444,000 rubles per square meter. In the attacks on warehouses in Krasnodar (150,000 square meters) and Nevinnomyssk (100,000 square meters), the value of destroyed goods was estimated at 100–120 billion rubles. That likewise comes to around 440,000 rubles’ worth of goods per square meter.
The average value of goods destroyed in fires at Wildberries warehouses is around 440,000 rubles per square meter, based on media reports
Other losses must also be considered. Every day that a distribution center remains out of operation costs tens of thousands of sellers when it comes to lost revenue, and it can take weeks for goods to be unblocked after an attack. Meanwhile, entrepreneurs’ working capital remains tied up and loan interest continues to accrue. Many lack financial reserves and are forced either to operate in the informal economy or shut down. Losing inventory depletes sellers’ working capital, as they must buy new stock to resume trading.
Even when insurance covers part of the losses, the wait for compensation itself represents a direct cost. Disputes between sellers and marketplaces are consequently increasing. According to SPARK, between July 15 and Sept. 15, Wildberries was named as the defendant in 599 new lawsuits, up 53.6% from the same period in 2025. Competitor Ozon’s main legal entity faced 236 new cases, more than twice as many as a year earlier.
For the government, this is a direct blow to the tax base, as the Finance Ministry loses VAT and corporate income tax revenue from an entire sector. If sellers’ lost revenue amounts to 445–508 billion rubles, the resulting tax losses can be estimated at 10–30 billion rubles. For sellers under the general tax regime, corporate income tax is calculated on profit margins of 15–25%, implying losses of 13–25 billion rubles.
Under the simplified tax regime, sellers pay 6% of their total revenue, which would mean tax losses of 26.7–30.5 billion rubles. A realistic estimate of the government’s one-off revenue losses is therefore 13–30 billion rubles. The lower end represents corporate income tax on a 15% margin applied to 445 billion rubles, while the upper end is the 6% simplified tax on 508 billion rubles. The actual mix of tax regimes could shift the estimate, but it provides a useful benchmark.
An alternative estimate, based on data from The Moscow Times, suggests even greater losses. According to the publication, Wildberries’ turnover has already fallen by a quarter due to sellers leaving the platform. With annual turnover of 6.1 trillion rubles, that implies 1.5 trillion rubles in lost revenue. VAT alone on that amount, at 20%, would total 300 billion rubles, excluding corporate income tax and taxes paid by sellers.
Moreover, a report by the Center for Tax Policy and the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Economic Forecasting estimates that the government could lose 440–690 billion rubles in marketplace-related tax revenue in 2026 because of the way these platforms operate. The attacks are only exacerbating this trend.
These are one-off losses, however. The long-term impact is more serious: depleted working capital will force some sellers out of business. Our calculations suggest that the loss of just 10% of active sellers would reduce annual tax revenue by 35–50 billion rubles and social insurance contributions by another 7–10 billion rubles. We assume that 10% of sellers account for roughly 10% of turnover — about 610 billion rubles out of 6.1 trillion. At a 6% simplified tax rate, that would mean 36.6 billion rubles in lost tax revenue. Social insurance contributions, normally around 30% of payroll, would add another 7–10 billion rubles, (although the exact amount is difficult to estimate).
The actual range could be wider depending on the mix of tax regimes, but we use this as a working estimate. In reality, the loss of working capital might force out 5% or 20% of sellers rather than 10%, significantly changing the outcome.
In any event, attacks on warehouses, like those on oil refineries, have also begun to fuel inflation. Prices on marketplaces rose by 10–30% within days of the attacks, and gasoline prices increased by 16.5% between January and August 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to Rosstat data. The year-on-year increase in August was 25%. Insurance payouts to businesses rose by a third in the first half of 2026, according to RBC. Higher insurance premiums will also feed through into prices over time.
Insurers are lowering their liability limits, and some risks are no longer covered at all. The loss ratio in terrorism insurance has exceeded 100%. Market rates for terrorism and sabotage insurance have risen tenfold over the past four years, according to Energogarant. Businesses are also rethinking their investment plans: why build a new production facility if a single attack could put it out of operation?
“Yandex”: The Ukrainian Armed Forces will find everything
Three of Yandex’s key data centers came under attack between Oct. 8 and 11. All three of the company’s supercomputers were housed at these facilities, with a combined computing power of 50.36 petaflops. Two of them — Lyapunov and Chervonenkis (the most powerful) — were located at the data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Region. “We cannot yet confirm that the equipment at the Sasovo data center can be restored,” Yandex said, warning that some services might become unavailable to users. Damage to the supercomputers would also affect the development of YandexGPT, the company’s neural network, which uses them for training.
The third supercomputer, Galushkin, was housed at the Vladimir data center, which shut down completely following a drone attack on the night of Oct. 11. Yandex also described its remaining resources as unstable and warned customers that its cloud platform was operating in emergency mode.
All of Yandex’s supercomputers may have been damaged. There is no reliable confirmation, but neither is there evidence to the contrary
Restoration could take up to six months. Sanctions restricting supplies of high-tech equipment will make repairs more difficult and expensive. The supercomputers ran on chips made by the U.S. company Nvidia, and the scale of the damage has yet to be officially assessed. Yandex spent 6 billion rubles building the Sasovo data center in 2011 and invested another 700 million rubles in its renovation ten years later, according to TASS. Investment in the Vladimir data center was expected to total around 9 billion rubles, according to Vladimirskie Vedomosti.
Many businesses, in Russia and abroad, rely on Yandex services hosted primarily at these three data centers. Cascading internet outages following the latest attack on Oct. 11 affected at least six countries, The Insider found. In Russia, two federal information systems — VetIS and Saturn, responsible for veterinary oversight and pesticide traceability — were switched to emergency mode. Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance attributed the disruption to a power outage in Vladimir Region.
Sources in the logistics industry reported that electronic waybills had stopped working for many companies. Their use had only just become mandatory. “A couple more strikes like this, and we’ll be back to paper,” one source said. T-Bank, ticketing services, online stores and cinemas, Russian Railways, and educational platforms also experienced problems.
The Russian economy rests on two main pillars: raw-material exports, which have funded the state budget, and domestic consumption, which generates demand and jobs. Drone strikes have hit both at once. The Ukrainian Armed Forces are targeting government revenue and consumer demand simultaneously, straining an economic model accustomed to offsetting structural problems through high oil prices, fast-turnover retail, or IT businesses whose services keep the system running efficiently and flexibly.

articles.title: Allies Warn Ukraine of Delayed Missile Waves, Air Force Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s partners warned it about three waves of Russian ballistic missile attacks overnight, although no warning arrived before the first wave, Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Speaking during the national telethon, Ihnat clarified the sequence after earlier military statements and comments by President Volodymyr Zelensky raised questions about missing launch notifications.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We gave our first report at around 10:40 p.m. that there had been no warnings from our partners about ballistics,” Ihnat said, according to RBC-Ukraine.
Warnings about the use of ballistic missiles did arrive during the following three waves, he added. Ihnat did not identify which partners provided them or explain why the initial warning was missing.
Zelensky says missiles were detected seconds before impact
The clarification follows two consecutive evenings when Ukraine reported receiving no advance warning before Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv.
Discussing the Monday, Oct. 12 attack in his Tuesday evening address, Zelensky said five missiles had been detected only seconds before impact.
“Normally, we receive advance warning from our partners, which are crucial for our defense,” he said.
After another strike on Tuesday evening, Zelensky again said there had been no advance warning. That attack hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a residential building.
Ihnat’s Wednesday account confirms the absence of an initial alert while establishing that warnings were received later in the overnight attack.
US-Russia Diesel Deal: What’s The Big Idea?
Sybiha cites weapon type, Trump denies intelligence cutoff
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha offered a different explanation for the delayed alert during Monday’s attack, attributing it to the type of weapon Russia used.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, he confirmed that Ukraine continued receiving US intelligence. He did not disclose whether the scope of that cooperation had changed.
Trump also denied that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence.
“No, we haven’t,” he said when asked on Tuesday, adding: “We are helping them.” Neither statement explained why the missile-launch warnings had been missing.
Refinery dispute fuels questions over US support
Concerns intensified after reports that US envoys threatened to restrict intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
Axios cited a Ukrainian official who said Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner conveyed that warning during talks in Miami. A US official disputed that an explicit threat had been made.
Zelensky subsequently told NPR that Washington had warned about a possible suspension of intelligence cooperation over refinery strikes, according to RBC-Ukraine’s account of the interview. The White House referred NPR to Trump’s remarks that intelligence sharing continued.
Officials have not publicly established a connection between those warnings and the missing missile alerts. Ihnat’s latest statement confirms that partners supplied information during the subsequent waves, but leaves the failure before the first strike unexplained.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine leave 600,000 without power as Zelenskyy says Moscow ‘disrespecting’ US – Europe live
articles.body:
No indication intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped, EU says
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine, but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
Burnham pledges to try to 'repair bridges' between Zelenskyy and Trump
UK prime minister Andy Burnham said he will seek to “repair bridges” between US president Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy amid strained ties between the pair, AFP reported.
Burnham made the comments before he was due to welcome Zelensky to his official Downing Street residence, in a show of support for Ukraine’s president after new criticism by Trump.
“What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back,” Burnham told the British parliament.
“Therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together. That is the role I intend to play.”
The pair is expected to meet this afternoon, and the Ukrainian president is also expected to meet King Charles III.
Interestingly, Zelenskyy departed for London from the Polish city in Rzeszów reverting to flying from Poland after months of flying from Moldova’s Chișinău during a period of strained relations with Poland over history.
Merz calls for 'creative efforts' to tame the rise of extremism
In pretty pointed remarks against the surging far-right Alternative fur Deutschland, Merz also recalls the opening line from the 1950 Schuman declaration, which said:
“World peace cannot be safeguarded without the making of creative efforts proportionate to the dangers which threaten it.”
Adapting it to today’s Germany and Europe, Merz urges parties to recommit to that “creative effort” and not “a scornful desire for disintegration, a delight in division, or exclusion or fear of others.”
“We must summon that effort and we will - not least in the face of the extremism that has always been a part of our society and is now surging with full force into this parliament, into state parliaments, and into the everyday life of our country.”
He acknowledges that “this extremism … has roots in legitimate dissatisfaction and legitimate feelings of injustices,” but insists it would not resolve any of the people’s problems.
Merz warns of 'time of upheaval' as he doubles down on support for Ukraine and proposes new trade measures to protect EU industries
Over in Berlin, Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Bundestag, talking about his government’s plan of reforms, his plans for this week’s EU summit in Brussels and Ukraine.
He warns lawmakers that Germany faces “a time of upheaval, with crises and wars, some of which lie beyond our control.”
Merz repeats his key lines on the much-needed investment in Germany’s defence capabilities, and doubles down on his support for Ukraine.
He dismisses any suggestion that Germany’s support for Ukraine comes at an expense of social and welfare spending.
“This is simply not a case. Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our own country. Not a single euro,” he said.
Merz warns that “the danger is very real and concrete,” as Russia continues to show “willigness to escalate: against Ukraine, against our eastern European neighbours, and indeed against our own country.”
“Against this backdrop … it is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue to play down the situation,” he said.
He says some comments were almost “deliberately driving the division … and disinformation” to “derivse partisan, political advantages from it.”
Turning to this week’s EU summit, Merz says the discussions will focus on the next EU budget with “negotiations now entering a decisive phase.”
He stresses Germany’s priorities of security and competitiveness, with a call to “further cut back EU bureaucracy and accelerate approval processes to boost and enable investment across Europe,” particularly in decarbonisation, AI and defence.
He also talks about the importance of a new legal regime for pan-European startups, advancing the EU’s capital markets union, and on developing new trade relationships with global partners while reducing “one-sided dependencies” with existing partners.
“We will no longer stand idly by while other states harm our economy through heavy subsidies, artificially devalued currencies, overcapacity, and aggressive pricing. We will not stand idly by any longer.”
(Yep, he probably means China.)
His comments come ahead of his planned trips to Japan, South Korea and Singapore.
He says the European Council will discuss creating “a new trade defence instrument” to respond “swiftly and forcefully to targeted attacks on our industries and supply chains.”
“These decisions would, among other things, provide the European Commission with a tool to react rapidly without needing to consult the European Council first. The European Council, for its part, would then have the power to reverse such a move by a qualified majority. This makes us faster and more effective, and gives the Commission a powerful tool.”
Nord Stream suspect's lawyers argue Nord Stream may have not been a crime, ask for case to be dismissed
Over in Germany, we have an update on the Nord Stream trial which began in Hamburg earlier today (10:43).
Defence lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Serhii Kuznetsov’s lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany’s imports of natural gas before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target, Reuters reported.
“Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor’s infrastructure without harming any human beings?”
Kuznietsov’s lawyers also argued that he was still an active duty solider an as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak about anything during his service for reasons of secrecy linked to national security, AP reported.
Protesters gathered outside the Hamburg court in support of the defendant, with a sign that read: “What are war crimes?”
“Russia is the only war criminal that belongs in the dock,” said one of the dozens of protesters.
Bulgaria says Russia likely behind Black Sea drone strikes but 'we cannot prove it'
In the Bulgarian parliament, prime minister Rumen Radev has said that Russia was most likely behind drone attacks in the Black Sea that sank two ships, but that “we cannot prove it”.
AP quotes Radev saying “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
The Russian ambassador to Bulgaria was summoned yesterday over the issue, and Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova has called for an immediate halt to hostilities in the Black Sea and a moratorium on drone attacks against commercial and civilian infrastructure.
Bulgaria investigating report that Starlink antennas set on fire near Sofia
Bulgaria is investigating a report that several antennas used for communication with the Starlink satellite network were deliberately set on fire, prime minister Rumen Radev has said.
“The investigation is extremely intensive. We are working with partner services to successfully carry out this operation,” AFP reports Radev said in parliament, without confirming or denying the claim.
A Bulgarian opposition MP has claimed 11 telecommunications antennas linked to the Starlink network were set on fire over the weekend “at a secret facility near Sofia”.
A spokesperson for the Sofia prosecutor’s office confirmed to AFP that an investigation was under way but said no one has been charged.
A fire broke out at a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in September, with the country’s digital affairs minister calling the blaze an act of “sabotage” and prime minister Donald Tusk describing it as an “act of hybrid warfare”.
Germany’s foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, has said his country has not observed a substantial reduction in US support for Ukraine, and does not expect to. The statement comes amid the US and Russia having secured a diesel supply deal, and reports that Elon Musk’s Starlink service has been reduced for Ukrainian forces.
Moscow has said that the US-Russia deal over diesel “will open other opportunities as well”.
Reuters reports Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Moscow would overcome any sanctions-related difficulties to ensure the diesel supplies were delivered, and that the deal could pave the way for further economic cooperation between the two nations.
Reuters, citing local media, reports that Bulgaria expects to join a Nato anti-drone initiative by the end of October. The news comes a day after a drone attack sank a cargo vessel off the country’s Black Sea coast for the second time in a week.
Defence minister Dimitar Stoyanov said “Bulgaria will be part of this project as soon as possible. Expectations are that by 30 October, we will already be part of the project.”
Eutelsat shares jump as Ukraine flags curbs on Starlink military-grade service
And Reuters is reporting that shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat rose sharply on Wednesday after Ukraine said SpaceX’s Starlink had introduced restrictions on its military-grade service, fuelling investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.
Eutelsat shares were up 11.6% by late morning, while Luxembourg-based rival SES, which also provides satellite connectivity services, gained 2.7%.
No indication intelligence sharing with Ukraine has stopped, EU says
The European Commission declined to comment on reported disruption to Starlink’s services in Ukraine, but said there are “no indication that [US] intelligence sharing has stopped.”
Repeatedly asked about the issue, the commission spokespeople said they were “aware of the report” on Starlink, but declined to comment “until we have more information.”
“[It is] important also to say that we have no indications that, intelligence sharing has stopped,” the chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said.
EU 'headed for a very, very difficult winter,' commission warns as energy markets remain 'very volatile'
The European Commission has warned that the EU is “headed for a very, very difficult winter” with high energy prices expected to cause an affordability crisis and “a very volatile” in the energy markets.
The warning was delivered by the EU’s energy spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen when answering questions about proposed changes adding flexibility to rules on methane imports to help save costs.
She stressed the EU was “not facing a security supply issue for the time being,” but it faced a “very unpredictable” situation in the coming months.
“We do not have visibility, for example, what and when something will happen in the Strait of Hormuz, where 20% of gas and oil is being blocked since many, many months,” she said.
The commission’s chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, added that the changes are needed as “we could not anticipate that we would have a crisis in the Strait of Hormuz,” which continues to affect prices and supply of energy.
Why is the far right on the rise in Europe? - Reddit AMA
Lucy O’Brien
This summer in Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt.Meanwhile, support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe.
There are now radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year. How might these elections shape the political future of the continent?
Jon Henley and Ashifa Kassam, our European correspondents, will be answering your questions live on Reddit r/geopolitics from 4pm CEST.

articles.title: Raytheon wins $8B deal for nuclear command terminals
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon an $8 billion ceiling contract to modernize and restart production of strategic communications terminals for nuclear command and control.
- The sole-source contract runs through October 2036, with $800,000 obligated at award, and work in Marlborough, Massachusetts, and Largo, Florida.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Raytheon a contract worth up to $8 billion to modernize and restart production of the satellite communications terminals that link the president and military commanders to U.S. nuclear forces, the U.S. Department of War announced on Oct. 13.
The indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract covers development work to modernize the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center’s strategic communications terminals, services to restart their production, and technical studies. Raytheon received the contract without competition and will do the work in Marlborough, Massachusetts, and Largo, Florida, through Oct. 12, 2036. The U.S. Air Force put only $800,000 of fiscal 2026 research and development money on the contract at award, with the rest to be ordered over the next decade as needed. The announcement did not say which terminals will be built or how many.
The terminals are part of the U.S. nuclear command, control and communications network, known as NC3, which lets national leaders pass orders to bombers, missile crews and command posts under any conditions, including during a nuclear conflict. The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center’s Strategic Communications Division at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts, which awarded the contract, buys and sustains that equipment.
Raytheon’s main work for the division is the Family of Advanced Beyond Line-of-Sight Terminals, or FAB-T, which connects ground command posts and aircraft to the military’s most protected communications satellites, the Advanced Extremely High Frequency constellation and the older Milstar. FAB-T is built to keep working through jamming and nuclear effects, and it carries presidential voice conferences, warnings of incoming attacks and emergency action messages, the coded orders used to launch nuclear weapons. Raytheon took over the program from Boeing in 2014, and the original plan called for 61 ground and 23 airborne terminals.
The company has steadily added to that work. In 2023 the U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon $625 million for Force Element Terminals, the FAB-T version fitted to B-52 bombers and other aircraft, and in March the service raised the ceiling on a separate Raytheon contract for Advanced Extremely High Frequency terminals by $2 billion, to nearly $3 billion. The new $8 billion ceiling is the largest award yet for the company’s strategic communications terminals, and the reference to restarting production suggests the U.S. Air Force expects to buy more terminals after earlier production runs ended.
The U.S. Air Force is modernizing most parts of the nuclear triad at the same time, including the B-21 Raider bomber, the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile and the Long Range Standoff cruise missile, all of which will need communications links that can survive an attack.

articles.title: Russia launches massive ballistic missile strike on energy grid: air defence brings down 4 out of 39 missiles and 115 drones
articles.body:
Russia launches massive ballistic missile strike on energy grid: air defence brings down 4 out of 39 missiles and 115 drones
Russia attacked Ukraine with 39 ballistic missiles and 128 drones on the night of 13-14 October, mainly targeting Kyiv and Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts. Ukrainian air defence forces shot down or jammed four missiles and 115 drones.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force; President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote from the Air Force: "The key factor was simultaneous use of offensive aerial weapons of various types from different directions and a large number of ballistic strikes against energy facilities."
Details: The Air Force noted that since 18:00 on 13 October, the Russians have launched 39 missiles and 128 drones on Ukraine. Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles were launched from Russia's Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh and Rostov oblasts.
The Russians also used Shahed, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and Italmas drones and Parodiya decoy drones. Of the UAVs launched, 77 were jet-powered.
The drones were launched from the areas of Russia's Millerovo and Oryol and temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea and from the waters of the Sea of Azov.
Early reports indicate that as of 09:00, air defence forces had brought down or jammed four missiles and 115 drones, including 59 jet-powered ones.
Hits by some of the missiles and drones have been recorded at 22 locations. Intercepted aerial assets and debris crashed at eight locations. Some of the Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack. As of 09:00, several strike drones were still in the sky over Ukraine.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv. A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American president."
Details: Zelenskyy said that the Russian attack has left at least 600,000 people without electricity, and blackouts could affect even more consumers.
The president added that the Russians have significantly damaged facilities and equipment at 26 energy sites and four oil and gas facilities. He emphasised that some people are reported to have been killed and injured, although he did not specify their numbers.
Zelenskyy called the strike deliberate and demonstrative, stating that Russia has squandered an opportunity to de-escalate the hostilities.
He called on the US and Kyiv's other partners to respond decisively to the attack, urging Donald Trump to introduce tough sanctions against Russia. He also asked partners to supply Ukraine with additional interceptor missiles for Patriot systems.
Background: On the night of 13-14 October, three people were killed in a Russian attack on the city of Kyiv. First responders are continuing to deal with the aftermath in three districts in the capital.
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Zelensky reveals what US threatened Ukraine with
articles.body:
Zelensky reveals what US threatened Ukraine with
Ukrinform reports this, citing an interview Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky gave to NPR.
"The Trump administration warned it could cut off intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces stop long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia," NPR reported, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky added that his generals had informed him that the warning had been communicated at the military level.
He told NPR that Ukraine was striking Russian energy and logistics facilities to weaken the Kremlin's ability to wage war.
He said that Ukraine wanted to end the war but would continue the strikes until Russia stopped attacking Ukrainian energy facilities.
Zelensky stated that Trump's decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel would not affect prices in the United States because the available volumes were insufficient.
Zelensky also revealed that he learned about Trump's proposed "energy truce" through social media.
He also rejected President Trump's claim, made over the weekend, that Ukraine was responsible for rising diesel prices. Zelensky emphasized that the increase was caused by the war involving Iran.
"Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Russia, with US approval, will immediately supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the global market and significantly increase its export volumes going forward.

articles.title: Kiev mayor demands answers about ‘missing billions’ for capital’s defense
articles.body:
Kiev mayor demands answers about ‘missing billions’ for capital’s defense
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko has accused Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s government of withholding funds needed to protect the capital from Russian strikes, while blaming his administration for the city’s problems.
The longstanding feud between Klitschko, one of the leaders of the 2014 coup that ousted then-President Viktor Yanukovich, and Zelensky has intensified as the two sides trade accusations over deteriorating living conditions in Kiev.
The capital has suffered regular blackouts as Russian forces target power infrastructure supplying Ukrainian industry, including facilities producing long-range kamikaze drones used to attack Russian oil refineries. Speaking in parliament on Wednesday, Klitschko accused the central government of using state-funded propaganda outlets to smear him.
“Talk is cheap, and one could pin World War III on Klitschko just as well,” he said. “But I am not alone to question: Where is air defense for the capital? Where is the reinforcement of Ukrenergo [energy system] sites? Where are the billions allocated for that?”
The former heavyweight boxing champion, who leads the UDAR party, said Kiev has continued to function despite the “slap in the face” its administration received from the central government.
A day earlier, Zelensky claimed that Kiev is less prepared for Russian strikes than even frontline settlements under Ukrainian control, and announced “rational changes” to the capital’s governance. Klitschko previously claimed that Zelensky was considering removing him from office and putting a political appointee in charge of Kiev.
Several Ukrainian corruption investigations have involved the alleged embezzlement of funds intended for defense projects. Last week, the State Bureau of Investigation accused four suspects of taking kickbacks through inflated contracts for fortifications in Sumy Region. The alleged $840,000 scheme involved funds allocated by the central government to the Lviv regional administration.
In another case reported by the National Police in June, a former deputy mayor of Kharkov was accused of involvement in a scheme that resulted in $340,000 in losses through inflated prices for construction materials used in fortifications.
Zelensky’s government has faced a series of corruption scandals involving people close to him since last November. A recent opinion poll suggests that Ukrainians rank government corruption as a greater concern than Russian missile and drone strikes.
The Ukrainian leader is facing additional pressure after President Donald Trump accused him of harming US interests by attacking Russian oil refineries amid the global fuel crunch. Trump suggested that Ukraine should replace Zelensky with someone willing to compromise.
Zelensky has since complained that the US has stopped providing early warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes. There have also been reports of restrictions on Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite internet system aimed at preventing its use on fast-moving platforms. Starlink is owned by Trump ally Elon Musk, who has backed the US president’s call to replace Zelensky.

articles.title: MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
articles.body:
MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
LONDON, Oct 13 - MI5 spy chief Ken McCallum delivered his annual speech on Tuesday outlining his view of the threats to Britain, from hostile states such as Iran and Russia to the development of artificial intelligence.
Here is a summary of the main threats and issues he detailed in his speech and subsequent questions from media:
RUSSIA
McCallum called Russia, which denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain and other Western countries, "aggressor number one". He said it was escalating "hybrid" warfare, staying below the threshold that would trigger a direct NATO response.
He said Russia's capabilities had been reduced by the expulsion of 1,000 officials from embassies since the invasion of Ukraine, which meant it had to rely on native volunteers and criminal proxies.
IRAN
Tehran is also using criminal proxies - to target opponents, Iranian media organisations and Israeli interests in Britain - and has expanded its hybrid campaign in the last year, McCallum said.
He said operations connected to Iran had yielded more than 50 arrests in the UK, and that many had been aimed at Jewish communities.
The other shift had been "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites", he said.
Tehran also rejects accusations of malign activity in Britain.
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
McCallum said AI was "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders", producing tailored propaganda and material for individuals.
MI5 has caught potential attackers using it to try to improve reconnaissance and attack methodologies. AI-enabled drones added a new challenge, he said.
McCallum said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists developing bioweapons or even creating new pathogens.
AI also presented a risk in itself.
"Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are, is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel and deserves the serious attention it is getting."
TERRORISM
Britain in April raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe", meaning an attack within the next six months is highly likely.
McCallum said Al Qaeda and Islamic State continued to inspire plots, and MI5 was still having to respond to attempts to carry out mass-casualty attacks.
He said the most marked trend of the last year had been the increase in cases where extreme anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievances were tipping over into terrorist intent.
An investigation into one 13-year-old who had been radicalised by extreme right-wing ideology had led to an unnamed foreign partner thwarting a lethal attack on its soil, he said.
BREXIT
On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia had interfered in Britain's 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union, something Moscow has denied.
Asked about such interference, McCallum said it was public knowledge that Russian media such as Russia Today "came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum", and there had been a certain amount of activity from trolls and bots.
But he said Russian online trolling had been comparatively unimpressive. REUTERS

articles.title: Romania scrambles fighter jets after drones spotted near Ukrainian border
articles.body:
Romania scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and deployed a military helicopter after three drones were detected near the country’s border with Ukraine, the Defence Ministry said on Wednesday.
The drones were identified near the Ukrainian city of Vylkove, close to the Romanian border and the Danube Delta.
Romanian authorities issued an RO-Alert warning to residents in the northern part of Tulcea County over the possibility that objects could fall from the air.
Two Romanian Air Force F-16 fighter jets took off to monitor the situation, while a military helicopter was also deployed to conduct surveillance in the border area.
The ministry said radar data showed that the drones remained in Ukrainian airspace and did not cross into Romania.
The public warning was subsequently lifted after authorities determined that there was no immediate threat to Romanian territory.
Romania, a NATO and EU member, shares a border with Ukraine along the Danube and has repeatedly scrambled military aircraft in response to drone activity near its territory.
Drone fragments have previously been discovered in Romanian border areas following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and infrastructure along the Danube.
Bucharest has strengthened air surveillance and defensive measures in the region amid concerns that the conflict could spill across NATO borders.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis vow more attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities after Aramco HQ hit
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia and said they struck the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco, which was hit the day before.
The Iran-aligned group said it had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in the eastern city of Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, without saying when.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday that killed 13 people.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month, reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
In a broad threat, the Houthis urged "international shipping companies," civilians and workers to evacuate airports and oil facilities, which they declared legitimate military targets.
Saudi-led forces say they intercept missile
The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.
The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
Saudi Aramco headquarters suffered extensive damage in Houthi attack, sources say
Oil giant Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran suffered extensive damage in an attack on Tuesday, with a fire spreading across several floors, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Operations at the complex in eastern Saudi Arabia have continued normally but some employees have been asked to work from home, according to two of the people.
A fourth person said some functions had been shifted to global offices, adding that the fire was still burning into the early hours of Wednesday.
The facility hosts an operations center which helps the world's largest oil company oversee onshore and offshore oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometers of pipeline.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said in a statement that Tuesday night's attack, which came as fighting between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified, had caused a limited fire.
Two of the sources said a fire started on the ninth floor of the south wing of the office block, and spread between the sixth and 10th floors.
Another source added that the top three floors of building, where the office of Aramco CEO Amin Nasser is located, were severely damaged, with part of the ceiling caved in and windows and doors blown out.
Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
Saudi Arabia to let executives attend 'Davos in the Desert' remotely after attacks
Saudi Arabia plans to make its flagship investment conference a hybrid event, giving executives the option to tune in remotely, after deadly weekend attacks on Riyadh airport prompted a rethink of travel to the kingdom, two people familiar with the matter said.
Some participants were still expected to fly in and could land at airstrips outside Riyadh, or even in neighboring Gulf states, and then drive to the capital to attend the Future Investment Initiative scheduled for later this month, one of the people said.
Earlier this month, organizers said the event would go ahead despite missile and drone attacks in the kingdom, which have struck key targets.
Asked for comment, an FII media representative pointed Reuters to a joint statement from the CEO and the chairman of the FII Institute sent before Saturday's attacks.
"As we prepare to welcome thousands of delegates to Riyadh for the exceptional 10th edition of the Future Investment Initiative, their safety and well-being remain our highest priority," CEO Maha Al Saud and Richard Attias, chairman of the executive committee, said.
On Monday, major oil bosses dropped out of an international conference in Riyadh which continued in person as planned at a convention center 10 km (6 miles) from Riyadh airport.
The move to a hybrid model for FII shows how Saudi Arabia is trying to maintain its push to attract global investment despite an escalating war with the Houthis that has challenged its efforts to turn Riyadh into a hub for global events. The kingdom has used the FII to showcase its plans to diversify its economy from oil and attract foreign investments.
The typical attendance of a large number of world leaders, corporate chieftains and financiers has led the event to be nicknamed "Davos in the desert," in a nod to the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Switzerland.

articles.title: Kremlin says Trump did not specify scope of energy ceasefire
articles.body:
Kremlin says Trump did not specify scope of energy ceasefire
                                        
                        —
                14 October, 13:34
                                        Dmitry Peskov. Photo: Russian media
                                    
The Kremlin has said that US President Donald Trump did not specify exactly what the energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia is supposed to cover.
Source: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, as reported by Russian media outlets
Details: Peskov was asked whether Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities mean that Moscow is dissatisfied with Trump's statement about an energy ceasefire. He replied that the statement had not been specific.
Advertisement:
"Work on this matter is continuing," he said.
