articles.title: Peacekeeping and dividing: The US intervention in Sudan takes a familiar path
articles.body:
Peacekeeping and dividing: The US intervention in Sudan takes a familiar path
At the end of September, the US refused to issue a visa to Sudanese Armed Forces leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, just days before his scheduled speech at the UN General Assembly in New York City. According to Sudanese sources, the refusal stemmed from al-Burhan’s unwillingness to sign a 90-day ceasefire agreement proposed by Massad Boulos, the senior adviser to the US president on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs.
When civil war broke out in Sudan on April 15, 2023, the US refused to support either side of the conflict. Washington officially maintained a neutral stance toward both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and pushed for a transfer of power to a civilian-led government.
However, US policy has recently become tougher with regard to the SAF and al-Burhan, who also heads the Transitional Sovereignty Council recognized by most countries. Besides denying al-Burhan a visa, Washington is also pushing the UN to expand the existing arms embargo (which currently targets only the Darfur region, largely controlled by the RSF) to encompass all of Sudan.
Visa scandal
The US decision to deny al-Burhan a visa drew sharp criticism from the UN and various international observers. A spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Stephane Dujarric, said Guterres is “deeply concerned that a visa has reportedly not yet been issued to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of Sudan.”
A few days before the planned trip, Sudan’s permanent representative to the UN, al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Muhammad, sent a letter requesting UN intervention to allow al-Burhan to attend the meeting.
The US State Department, however, declined to comment on the visa controversy. Spokesperson Tommy Pigott stated that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the RSF and their leaders represent the legitimate, constitutional government of Sudan.
“The United States and President Trump stand ready to work with anyone who is a serious partner for peace in Sudan,” Pigott added.
In accordance with the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the US is committed to facilitating visa issuance for representatives of UN member states, including political opponents. However, the US has frequently deviated from these obligations in practice. Notably, the Obama administration denied entry to former Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir in 2013, preventing him from attending the UN General Assembly.
Al-Burhan, who was scheduled to speak at the General Assembly on September 24, ultimately canceled his trip to New York City. Instead, the Sudanese delegation was led by the foreign minister.
The Boulos plan
Massad Boulos’ proposal, initially presented in February, consists of five key elements: establishing an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, ensuring access for humanitarian organizations and protecting civilians, establishing a permanent ceasefire, transitioning to a civilian government, and post-war reconstruction.
As part of the American initiative, a nationwide 90-day humanitarian ceasefire is meant to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and safeguard civilian populations; a coordinating committee will also be created to oversee the implementation of the ceasefire. The plan also calls for establishing a UN mechanism involving the African Union and the League of Arab States in order to monitor a limited withdrawal of troops and deploy international observers.
In July, the Sudanese government expressed doubts regarding the political aspects of this plan but generally supported the humanitarian initiatives. The RSF, on the other hand, agreed to a three-month humanitarian ceasefire but rejected the demand for troop withdrawals from captured territories.
In September, Boulos confirmed that the US continues to collaborate with partners – including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and European nations – to achieve a humanitarian ceasefire in Sudan. Nevertheless, both sides remain skeptical: The army fears that a pause would allow the RSF to regroup, while the Rapid Support Forces are reluctant to lose ground in Darfur and Kordofan.
US sanctions and allegations of the use of chemical weapons
In Washington, many view al-Burhan as the more favorable partner compared to his rival, RSF commander Muhammad Hamdan Daglo. However, despite the numerous war crimes committed by the RSF – especially following their takeover of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur State – Washington has officially maintained an equidistant stance toward both sides and positioned itself as a mediator.
The US has repeatedly imposed sanctions on both the armed forces and the RSF, but the primary focus has been on Sudan’s Armed Forces and General al-Burhan. The first round of sanctions was announced on June 26-27, 2025. At the time, the US State Department declared that the armed forces used chemical or biological weapons (reportedly chlorine) against their own population during clashes with the RSF in 2024. Washington called this a violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention and international law.
The Sudanese government adamantly rejected the accusations, calling them baseless and politically motivated, asserting that Sudan neither produces, stores, nor uses chemical weapons, and expressed willingness to cooperate with the US in a technical investigation of the claims.
The sanctions severely restricted the export of sensitive American goods and technologies to Sudan, and imposed an outright ban on Sudan’s access to loans, guarantees, and any form of financial assistance from the US government.
A second package of sanctions was implemented in June-July 2026, further restricting the government’s access to international financing, banning the export of certain American goods to Sudan, and preventing Sudanese airlines from using US airspace. According to the US State Department spokesperson, these sanctions will remain in effect until Sudan eliminates “all chemical weapons and production facilities under international verification.”
In regard to the RSF, the US has applied individual measures. In April, at Washington’s initiative, the UN Security Council imposed sanctions on four RSF leaders, including Muhammad Hamdan Daglo’s brother, citing war crimes and crimes against humanity in El Fasher. Nevertheless, the main economic pressure points are directed against Sudan’s Armed Forces.
Critics argue that while the aim of these sanctions is to penalize violators of international law, they could exacerbate the humanitarian crisis by limiting supplies not only of arms but also of essential goods, as all resources will be diverted toward military operations, leading to the worsening of living conditions.
Does US policy legitimize the divide?
Following the fall of El Fasher – the last stronghold of the army in Darfur – the RSF solidified control over the entire region. In July 2025, they announced the formation of a parallel government in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur State. The presidential council, made up of 15 members, was headed by RSF commander Muhammad Hamdan Daglo himself.
The US has not officially recognized the structure, but is effectively engaging with it as a legitimate political actor, even in the wake of UN sanctions against its members. Washington continues to view the RSF as a potential participant in peace talks; however, this stance inadvertently legitimizes Sudan’s fragmentation by acknowledging the RSF as a parallel political entity with its own administration and agenda. The proposals risk leading to a de facto division of the country, with the Sudanese Army controlling the north, east, and center of the country, and the RSF controlling Darfur and parts of the south.
Russia’s veto
On September 11, 2026, the UN Security Council unanimously voted to extend the existing arms embargo on the Darfur region for another month, a measure initially implemented in 2004 amid the brutal ethnic War in Darfur. However, US efforts to broaden these restrictions to encompass all of Sudan have met with strong opposition from Russia and China. Russian Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN Anna Evstigneeva questioned why the council was being asked to expand the embargo at this particular moment, pointing out that similar concerns were not raised in 2023 when the Rapid Support Forces posed a threat to Khartoum and other major cities.
“The Sudanese government and its armed forces now have an undisputed advantage on the ground and serve as guarantors of state institutions, national unity, and civilian protection,” she said, noting that all available resources are necessary for achieving these goals.
The US argues that the current sanctions framework is outdated and no longer reflects the realities of the ongoing conflict. Russia’s potential veto has effectively blocked a US resolution aimed at extending the embargo to all of Sudan and increasing sanctions pressure on both sides of the conflict.
However, the US is not backing down. On October 8, the UN Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region for another two months, until December 11, unanimously adopting a draft resolution tabled by the US. Once again, the renewal period is as short as possible – essentially a technical rollover. Over the course of these two months, member states will continue negotiations on broader amendments to the sanctions regime. China, Russia, as well as the DR Congo, Somalia, Liberia, and Pakistan, oppose the US initiative, favoring instead a sanctions regime strictly limited to Darfur without expanding its scope.
Campaign in the US media
Just days before the Security Council vote, the US media again started talking about the Sudanese Army’s alleged use of chemical weapons – a key factor influencing the US initiative to broaden the embargo. In early September, The New York Times and Washington Post published findings from a joint investigation based on a supposedly leaked confidential dossier, which included videos, photographs, blueprints, and intercepted communications – totaling around 150 files.
Massad Boulos, while presenting his initiative to the UN Security Council, explicitly cited the use of chemical weapons as one of the justifications for the need to extend the embargo.
Russia and China oppose this proposal, even though there was no formal vote on the US resolution. According to Evstigneeva, Moscow “will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions.” China’s representative to the UN, Sun Lei, stated that expanding the embargo could worsen the humanitarian situation and lead to the further fragmentation of Sudan.
The Boulos initiative comes amid an apparent shift in the dynamics of the war in Sudan. The Rapid Support Forces have been affected by a new wave of desertions; meanwhile, the Sudanese Army is ramping up operations in Darfur and the Blue Nile region. It has also achieved significant gains in North Kordofan by capturing several strategic locations in recent months. This offensive ensured the safety of the National Export Highway linking Khartoum (via Omdurman) to El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and intensified pressure on RSF supply lines.
The risks of US intervention
Despite its stated peacekeeping intentions, US involvement in Sudanese affairs risks complicating an already challenging situation. Firstly, tying visa issuance to specific ceasefire conditions sets a dangerous precedent for using access to international institutions as leverage.
Secondly, US initiatives effectively reinforce Sudan’s division by recognizing the RSF as a legitimate power alongside the official army. This could drive both sides toward a permanent split rather than fostering compromise within a unified state.
Lastly, expanding sanctions and embargoes without considering local realities may trigger an even greater humanitarian disaster, limiting supplies of not just weapons but also essential goods. History shows that unilateral pressure seldom leads to peace; more often, it prolongs conflict and fuels radicalization. The US policy toward Sudan risks deepening the country’s divisions and extending the conflict, potentially turning Sudan into yet another ‘frozen’ hotspot on the African map.

articles.title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on espionage charges (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Russia arrests Japanese journalist on espionage charges (VIDEO)
Russian security officers have detained a Japanese journalist accused of collecting defense-related information for one of Tokyo’s intelligence services, the Federal Security Service (FSB) has announced.
The suspect, identified by Russia’s Foreign Ministry as Yuki Imai, worked for the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun’s bureau in the Far Eastern Russian city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk and held ministry accreditation. He was detained in Sakhalin Region ahead of a planned departure from Russia and transferred to Moscow, the FSB said.
According to the agency, the correspondent gathered and stored restricted information about the number of Kuril Islands residents mobilized or volunteering to serve in the Ukraine conflict, intending to pass it to Japanese intelligence.
An FSB officer said the journalist repeatedly tasked local residents with obtaining the data despite knowing it was restricted and could not be published. The agency also said he had privately admitted to having contacts with Japanese intelligence.
The FSB released footage of the detention and documents found in the journalist’s hotel room bearing the label “For official use only.” The remaining text on the pages was blurred.
The journalist is currently being held in custody while the investigation continues.
Commenting on the arrest, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Tokyo of using accredited journalists to gather information aimed at undermining Russian security, saying this was not an isolated incident.
She warned that the case would further damage bilateral relations, lamenting Japan’s “anti-Russian course” and its refusal to address Moscow’s concerns about Japanese “remilitarization.” Zakharova urged Tokyo to abandon hostile actions against Russia.
Tokyo said on Wednesday that it had requested more information about the arrest and has demanded “fair and impartial treatment” for the journalist. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it was still confirming the details, stating that ensuring the journalist’s safety was its top priority.
Relations between Moscow and Tokyo have deteriorated since Japan joined Western sanctions over the Ukraine conflict in 2022, prompting Russia to suspend peace treaty negotiations. Last month, Russia also demanded the removal of US Typhon missile systems deployed in Japan, describing them as a threat to regional security.
The countries have never signed a post-World War II peace treaty, although a 1956 declaration ended the state of war and restored diplomatic ties. A longstanding obstacle remains Japan’s claim to the four southernmost Kuril island groups, which came under Soviet control in 1945. Tokyo calls them the Northern Territories, while Moscow regards them as an integral part of Russia.

articles.title: Americans urged to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia over Iranian, Houthi attack threats
articles.body:
The US Mission in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday urged Americans to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing risks from Iranian and Houthi missile and drone attacks, armed conflict and terrorism, Anadolu reports.
In a post on US social media company X, the mission shared a travel advisory maintaining Saudi Arabia at Level 3, or reconsider travel, while designating the area along the Yemen border Level 4, or do not travel.
The US travel advisory system has two lower levels: Level 1, which calls for normal precautions and Level 2 for increased caution.
Under the advisory, US government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use any airport in the country and are prohibited from traveling within 20 miles (32 kilometers) of the Yemeni border. They also require special authorization to travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir and Najran, as well as the cities of Qatif, Taif and Yanbu.
The mission advised Americans in Saudi Arabia to take similar precautions.
The advisory said that since the outbreak of hostilities between the US and Iran on Feb. 28, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran. It said commercial flights remain operational from Saudi Arabia but have at times faced significant disruptions.
It said Iran and the Iran-backed Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks into Saudi Arabia, targeting cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic sites and energy facilities.
The advisory said falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk and warned US citizens against photographing, filming or sharing information about interceptions or affected sites.
READ: Saudi-led coalition launches airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s Sanaa
It cited terrorism, exit bans and the enforcement of Saudi laws governing social media activity among the risks facing travelers.
The advisory follows security alerts issued by the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia in recent days amid attacks and threats targeting the kingdom.
The embassy renewed its security alert on Monday for a third consecutive day following attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an attack targeting King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The embassy warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions and urged US citizens to exercise caution at major airports.
Saudi authorities have reported missile and drone attacks targeting airports and other sites in the kingdom in recent days, while the Houthis have threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.
A Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has intensified military operations against Houthi positions in Yemen, including airstrikes in the capital, Sanaa.
READ: Haaretz: Saudi crown prince opposes Israeli involvement in war against Houthis

articles.title: Sanaa oil facility hit after Saudi Arabia, Houthis issue threats
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the latest developments across the Middle East
Here's the latest:
Houthi media reported that Saudi Arabia struck an oil facility near the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday, after the Saudi-led coalition ordered civilians to evacuate the site
The Iran-backed rebels also warned employees and civilians to distance themselves from Aramco sites in Saudi Arabia as they planned to target the company's sites
Deadlock in the Strait of Hormuz continues as Iran's Revolutionary Guards target tankers going via an "illegal route", with US President Donald Trump vowing a harsh response if war resumes
Israeli attacks continue in southern Lebanon, the Gaza Strip and the Occupied West Bank
Houthis trying to drive up oil prices ahead of Nov 3: Trump
President Donald Trump on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi militants of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and warned that he would "never forget" their attacks on Saudi Arabia, amid a widening regional conflict fueled by the US war with Iran.
"The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, accusing the group of resuming attacks at Iran's behest after a period of relative quiet following US strikes in Yemen last year.
Trump also made clear that his warning would extend beyond the November 3 midterm elections, saying, "I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!"
Two killed in oil company strike: Houthi-run health ministry
Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry said two people were killed when an oil company in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah was attacked, blaming Saudi Arabia for the strike.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
Israeli army wounds two Palestinians in Ramallah raid
Israeli army fire wounded two Palestinians on Tuesday during a raid in the city of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian health ministry.
A hospital in the city received "a young man with a serious gunshot wound to the lower back and a 14-year-old with a live bullet wound to the upper thigh, in addition to numerous cases of suffocation, as a result of the (Israeli army) assault on Ramallah", the ministry said.
The army raided the former headquarters of the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, seizing documents and furniture, according to AFP journalists who witnessed and filmed the scene.
Israeli forces were deployed in the neighbourhood for nearly four hours, fired tear gas and stun grenades toward a group of reporters, and wounded four of them, according to AFP journalists and eyewitnesses.
In a separate incident on Tuesday, four Palestinians from the same family were injured after settlers stormed their home in the village of Talfit, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, according to a medical source and a family member.
Trump says Yemen's Houthis are 'behaving very badly'
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said Houthi militants who control vast swaths of Yemen were "behaving very badly" as consequences of the US-Iran war spill into the broader Middle East.
Trump told reporters that he "might" ask Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to intervene and support Saudi interests.
"President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask," Trump said.
Saudi will not allow threats to security, Red Sea navigation
The Saudi cabinet vowed on Tuesday, in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, that it would not allow threats to the kingdom's security or Red Sea shipping.
The cabinet said in a statement carried by the official SPA press agency that the kingdom "will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait to be threatened".
It added that the Iran-backed Houthis "will face the consequences of their crimes and repeated attacks" on Saudi airports, holy cities and economic facilities, following several deadly strikes on the kingdom.
Houthis issue warnings for Riyadh airport, two Aramco sites
Yemen's Houthi movement has issued an evacuation warning for Riyadh's airport and two Aramco facilities in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, shortly after a massive strike targeted a Yemeni oil facility near Sanaa.
It said it will target the Aramco oil facilities in Dhahran, east of the kingdom, and the capital Riyadh, as well as the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The airport has been hit several times already, killing more than a dozen people.
🔴🇮🇷🇸🇦The Houthis have urged all Saudi citizens to evacuate immediately and stay away from the facilities that will be targeted today: - Two Saudi Aramco facilities in Dharahn and Riyadh. - King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. https://t.co/9CWNMUezYU
Iraq faces a potential six-month gap in its air defences following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces, with new systems not expected to arrive until early next year.
An alleged Hezbollah weapons shipment seized by Lebanese authorities last week has raised questions over the type of explosives the group is using to develop its arsenal, amid reports that it is preparing for another round of war with Israel.
Qatar's revenues fell 42 percent in the first half of 2026, its emir said on Tuesday, as gas infrastructure and exports took a severe hit during the Middle East war.
Qatar, the world's second-largest exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG) after the US, lost a "significant proportion" of its exports, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani told the annual session of the Shura Council advisory body in Doha.
"The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, together with the direct damage inflicted on some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, disrupted a significant portion of the country's exports," the emir said.
"It is only natural that the crisis would have a negative impact on public finances, as the total revenues declined by 42 percent during the first half of the year," he added.
However, a major expansion of North Field, the world's biggest gas field, is going ahead, the emir said.
Attack on Yemen oil facility in Sanaa: Houthi-run TV
Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV reported on Tuesday an attack on the Yemen Oil Company in Sanaa.
The reported attack came shortly after the Saudi-led coalition ordered the evacuation of the facility ahead of a military operation.
Footage shows large plumes of smoke rising from the Yemen Petroleum Company’s Al-Sabaha Central Station in Sanaa following a Saudi airstrike. https://t.co/0wE4WhpqkD

articles.title: Thales quadruples Belfast missile output for Ukraine
articles.body:
Thales is now building Lightweight Multirole Missiles at its Belfast site at four times the rate it managed in 2022, and has committed £100 million to expanding that capacity further, the company told the UK Defence Journal after the Prime Minister announced accelerated deliveries of the weapon to Ukraine.
Phil Siveter, chief executive of Thales in the UK, said: “We are proud that the Prime Minister continues to see Thales in the UK as a trusted partner of the UK Government. Our Lightweight Multirole Missiles are designed and built at our site in Belfast, which has been supplying complex weapons to the UK for more than 70 years. With the support from Government, we have been able to quadruple our production to meet the global demand, and we are committed to investing £100m to expand this capacity further.
“The work carried out in Northern Ireland helps to sustain 1,100 direct jobs and supports around 700 more across our UK supply chain, giving the UK a sovereign capability it can rely on when it matters.”
Andy Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, pledging faster deliveries of air defence missiles alongside further military aid and tighter sanctions on Russia, with Britain pressing international partners to restrict Russian liquefied natural gas exports and to lean harder on Moscow over its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Prime Minister said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.”
All of that rests on a single production line in Belfast, a site that has built complex weapons for Britain for more than seventy years, through Shorts and then Thales, and it is the home of the Starstreak family from which LMM descends. Starstreak and LMM share the launcher and much of the surrounding equipment, which is part of why the line has been able to grow quickly.
LMM is a laser beam riding missile weighing around thirteen kilograms, with a range of about six kilometres. It is fired from shoulder launchers, from lightweight multiple launchers on vehicles, and from the Royal Navy’s Wildcat helicopters, where it carries the name Martlet. Against drones it is substantially cheaper than the surface to air missiles that would otherwise be expended on them, which is the characteristic that has driven demand since 2022.
The Belfast expansion is the kind of industrial response the Strategic Defence Review and the Defence Investment Plan have both called for, with onshore capacity that can be surged when a war consumes stock faster than peacetime contracts replace it.

articles.title: EU disburses $3.2B to Ukraine for drones, missiles, air defense systems
articles.body:
Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission on Wednesday disbursed €2.86 billion ($3.2 billion) to Ukraine to fund drones, air defense systems, missiles, and other urgent military needs amid continued attacks.
The funding was provided under the defense component of the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, the EU Commission said in a statement.
The money will be used to procure drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition.
"As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
The €90 billion loan package for 2026-2027 includes €60 billion earmarked for defense and €30 billion for budgetary assistance.
The commission said €28.3 billion was planned for disbursement in 2026 to strengthen Ukraine's defense industrial capacity, with further payments under the defense component expected in the coming weeks.
It added that Ukraine still had €29.64 billion in financial support available for the remainder of 2026.
Of that amount, €25.24 billion is available under the Ukraine Support Loan, including €12.54 billion for defense industrial capacity and €12.7 billion in budget support.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion generated from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets, according to the commission.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says US warned it'll cut off intelligence sharing if strikes on Russian oil facilities continue: Report
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Washington warned Kyiv it would cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine if long-range strikes on Russian oil facilities continued, Ukraine's president said Wednesday, according to a media report.
In an interview released late Tuesday by public broadcaster NPR, Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued that the Donald Trump administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel would not bring down fuel prices, and refuted assertions that his country is to blame for the rise in diesel fuel prices.
“Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy also said he found out about Trump's assertion of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine "through social (media),” referring to the US president’s announcement over the weekend.
He reiterated that Ukraine is striking Russian energy and logistics sites to weaken Moscow’s ability to wage a war, adding that while Kyiv seeks to end the ongoing conflict, it will not halt such strikes unless Russia halts attacks on Ukrainian energy sites.
Zelenskyy also said that Russian President Vladimir Putin only “understands force,” arguing that Trump's decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel would not influence domestic prices because of a lack of volume.
On Sunday, Trump announced on his Truth Social media platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy told Axios earlier Sunday that Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, stressing that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by guarantees.
Meanwhile, Peskov said Monday that the Kremlin had no immediate comment on the proposed halt, though contacts with the US concerning the topic were ongoing.

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Russia hits Ukraine's communication, energy infrastructure in massive strike
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Overnight, Russian forces launched a massive strike hitting communication and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev and the Kiev and Kharkov Regions that support Ukraine's military-industrial complex, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has compiled the key details on the targets hit.
Ministry’s statement
- Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces launched a massive strike using ground-based precision weapons and long-range attack drones against targets in Ukraine, the Defense Ministry reported.
- According to the ministry, the strike hit communication and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev and the Kiev and Kharkov Regions used to support the military-industrial complex and the armed forces of Ukraine.
Targets hit
- The ministry later specified that the ATM Ukrsibbank data center in Kiev was hit. The facility handled Internet traffic exchange for gathering intelligence about the Russian Armed Forces.
- Russian forces also struck the Darnitskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-4), powering military-industrial complex facilities in Kiev.
- In addition, the Kievskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-5) was hit; it supplies electricity to military facilities and military-industrial enterprises in Kiev and the Kiev Region.
- The Russian Armed Forces also struck the Kiev CHP-6 plant, powering military logistics facilities and storage sites for weaponry and military hardware in the northeastern part of the Kiev Region.
- In addition, the Tripolskaya thermal power plant, powering military-industrial facilities in Kiev and it's environs, was struck.
- Russian forces also struck the Kievskaya electrical substation, providing for the transmission and distribution of electricity from western Ukrainian regions to Ukraine’s military facilities in the Kiev Region.
- Furthermore, the Kharkov CHP-5 combined heat and power plant, powering military-industrial facilities in Kharkov and the western part of the Kharkov Region, was struck.
- The Russian Armed Forces also struck the Zmiyevskaya thermal power plant, supplying electricity to Ukrainian military facilities in the southeastern part of the Kharkov Region.
Situation in Ukraine
- Energy facilities in Kiev sustained damage following explosions, city mayor Vitali Klitschko reported.
- Strikes were recorded on "several energy facilities in the capital" of Ukraine, he wrote on his Telegram channel.
- He provided no further details.
- Public electric transport services were suspended in two districts of Kiev, the municipal enterprise Kievpastrans reported.
- Power outages began in Kiev due to widespread damage to energy facilities, Klitschko later announced.
- Specifically, he described the strikes on the city's energy infrastructure as massive.
- Emergency power outages began in five of Kiev's ten districts following the explosions and damage to energy facilities, the Ukrainian energy holding company DTEK reported.
- It specified that the Darnitsky, Dneprovsky, Pechersky, and Solomensky districts, as well as part of the Goloseyevsky district, were affected.
- All of Kiev's combined heat and power (CHP) plants, as well as the Kiev Region’s largest energy facility--the Tripolskaya Thermal Power Plant--sustained damage from explosions, the Strana news outlet reported.
- According to the report, strikes on all of the Ukrainian capital's CHP plants were recorded overnight and on Wednesday morning.
- In the region, the Tripolskaya Thermal Power Plant was damaged, along with the Kievskaya and Novokievskaya substations, which have capacities of 750 kilovolts (kV) and 330 kV, respectively.
- The outlet accompanied its report with photos showing massive fires at the sites of the explosions.
- The Epicentr company's last remaining logistics center was destroyed by the explosions, the Ukrainian outlet Insider reported.
- According to the report, the facility was located in the city of Khmelnitsky in western Ukraine.
- The report includes photos and video of the fire at the logistics facility.
- Water supply issues may arise in Kiev's Pechersky district due to a power outage at the city's water pumping station, the utility company Kievvodokanal reported.
- Ukrainian energy facilities sustained significant damage from the explosions, leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity, Vladimir Zelensky stated.

articles.title: The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has analysed how much Russia is spending on the war against Ukraine this year
articles.body:
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine has analysed how much Russia is spending on the war against Ukraine this year
Kyiv • UNN
According to the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, Russia’s military spending in 2026 will reach $177.4 billion. This is more than three times the funding for education and healthcare.
In 2026, Russia allocated 12.1 trillion rubles ($144.4 billion) for so-called "national defense," more than three times the combined spending on education and healthcare. Taking into account other expenses related to the war against Ukraine, Russia’s military budget amounts to nearly $177.4 billion. This was reported by the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (HUR), UNN writes.
In 2026, the budget item of the aggressor state Russia for "national defense" amounts to 12.121 trillion rubles (approximately $144.4 billion), while taking into account the broader range of expenditures related to waging the criminal war against Ukraine, the figure is 14.886 trillion rubles ($177.4 billion). The classified portion of Russia’s so-called "defense" budget is estimated at 9.187 trillion rubles (approximately $109.5 billion)
Moscow has allocated a total of 15.929 billion rubles ($189.8 million) to stimulate the development of the military-industrial complex, military-technical cooperation, and the implementation of research and production programs: 6.167 billion rubles ($73.5 million), 6.310 billion ($75.2 million), and 3.452 billion ($41.1 million), respectively, for each of the three expenditure items.
In addition, additional budget funds have been allocated separately to support Russian defense-industry enterprises: 2.054 billion rubles ($24.5 million) to compensate expenses, 463 million rubles ($5.5 million) to prevent bankruptcies, 500 million rubles ($6 million) to compensate interest on loans, and 1.5 billion rubles ($17.9 million) for compensation payments to employees.
Another 1.25 billion rubles ($14.9 million) has been allocated for high-performance computing needed to develop weapons systems. Such computations are performed in data centers, including on the supercomputers of Yandex and the computing facilities of Sberbank. Thus, the infrastructure of these companies is being used in the armed aggression against Ukraine.
Moscow has allocated 26.178 billion rubles (approximately $312 million) for applied defense research.
Russia has earmarked 10.233 billion rubles ($121.9 million) for the development and production of various types of drones. This amount does not reflect the actual financial volume of the market — it is considerably larger when so-called private investments and procurement are taken into account.
For example, the aggressor state has allocated 687.6 billion rubles (approximately $8.19 billion) to purchase UAVs for the Russian National Guard. The purchased drones are planned to be used not only on the front line of the criminal war against Ukraine, but also inside Russia — to protect critical infrastructure, patrol cities, monitor Russians, and suppress potential protests. Thus, Moscow is strengthening the security forces in order to keep the Russian population under strict control
Overall, Russia’s official expenditures on the genocidal war against Ukraine in 2026 ($144.4 billion) are more than three times greater than the combined funding for education ($21 billion) and healthcare ($22.5 billion).
$144.4 billion is an enormous sum, comparable to the cost of creating the International Space Station (approximately $150 billion) or building more than 150 modern oncology centers in Russia

articles.title: Iran shifts to step up attacks on shipping before US vote
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote
Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.
Iran using spotters
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.
Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy.
The war—and its $3 billion monthly price tag—has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.
The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.
In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.
There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organisation.
"There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said.
Attacks over an expanded area
As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.
Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.
The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.
"Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. "Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz."
The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said.
In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe", the second-highest level.
"IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said.

articles.title: Syria accuses Israel of arming Druze militias in Suweida
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria says Israel funding Druze militias to fuel chaos
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has accused Israel of supplying weapons and financial support to armed militias in the southern province of Suweida, alleging that Israel is seeking to destabilise Syria and undermine its sovereignty.
Speaking at a press conference in Damascus on Tuesday, al-Shaibani said Israel was supporting armed groups operating outside the authority of the Syrian state, amid continuing tensions over the future of the predominantly Druze province.
"Israel supports armed militias operating outside the law in the city of Sweida, providing them with weapons and funding to pursue an agenda of chaos in the region," he said, according to Syria's official SANA news agency.
The accusations come amid mounting concerns over Israel's involvement in southern Syria, where Israeli forces have expanded their military presence since the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Al-Shaibani accused Israel of pursuing a wider campaign to destabilise the country through attacks on infrastructure, the occupation of additional Syrian territory and the displacement and detention of Syrian civilians.
He said the fate of dozens of Syrians detained by Israeli forces remained unknown, calling on the international community to intervene and prevent further escalation.
Suweida has remained largely outside central government control following deadly clashes in July 2025 involving Druze armed factions, Bedouin groups and Syrian government forces.
The violence, which included abuses against Druze civilians by government-linked fighters, deepened mistrust between Damascus and sections of the Druze community.
Israel subsequently launched airstrikes against Syrian government positions, including targets in Damascus, claiming that its intervention was necessary to protect Syria's Druze minority.
However, Israeli involvement has also raised concerns about efforts to encourage the fragmentation of Syria by supporting armed groups opposed to the central government.
Much of Suweida is now controlled by factions associated with Druze religious leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, who has openly advocated separating the province from Damascus and establishing an independent Druze entity under Israeli protection.
In January, al-Hijri told Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth that his movement considered itself closely aligned with Israel and viewed the country as a guarantor of its political future.
"We see ourselves as an inseparable part of the existence of the State of Israel. This relationship is international and of critical importance," he said.
He also called for Syria's partition, arguing that independent or autonomous territories represented a possible future for the country.
In August, al-Hijri went further, declaring during a gathering in Suwayda that his supporters were an "integral part of the State of Israel" and shared its ideology.
His position has nevertheless faced opposition from other Druze religious figures, activists and armed factions who reject Israeli intervention and support maintaining Suwayda within a unified Syrian state.
The New Arab has previously reported on allegations that Israel has provided financial and military assistance to Druze militias operating in Suweida, including the Military Council, an armed faction associated with al-Hijri.
According to a Washington Post investigation published in December 2025, Israeli officials acknowledged providing support to Druze armed groups through the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The report detailed financial transfers, weapons supplies and military assistance, including an alleged payment of $24,000 to help establish the Military Council.
It also described cooperation involving military training and the provision of weapons, including anti-tank missiles, to strengthen Druze factions opposed to Damascus.
The allegations have added to concerns that Israel is seeking to cultivate armed allies in southern Syria as part of a broader effort to prevent the re-establishment of strong central government authority.
Israel has repeatedly demanded the demilitarisation of southern Syria and opposed the deployment of Syrian government forces near its borders, while continuing military operations inside Syrian territory.
Following Assad's overthrow, Israeli forces seized the UN-monitored buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement and expanded their presence beyond positions occupied before December 2024.
Israel has occupied most of Syria's Golan Heights since 1967, an occupation not recognised by the international community.
Despite the tensions, Damascus and Israel have engaged in several rounds of US-mediated negotiations aimed at establishing new security arrangements along their shared frontier.
In August, Syrian and Israeli delegations met in Jordan under American mediation to discuss Israeli military operations, the detention of Syrian civilians and the possibility of withdrawing Israeli forces to positions held before Assad's overthrow.
Al-Shaibani called for Israel to return to the 1974 disengagement agreement and allow the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force to carry out its responsibilities.
He also urged Israel to engage seriously in the US-sponsored negotiations, reiterating Damascus's commitment to reaching an agreement that respects Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The Syrian foreign minister's latest accusations come as the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa continues efforts to consolidate its authority across the country, with Suwayda remaining one of the principal areas outside Damascus's control.

articles.title: Nearly 200 Ukrainian drones flew toward Moscow, while a Sberbank data center came under attack in Russia’s Saratov region
articles.body:
Nearly 200 Ukrainian drones flew toward Moscow, while a Sberbank data center came under attack in Russia’s Saratov region
A total of 493 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Moscow region from the evening of October 13 through the morning of October 14, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
Air defense forces intercepted most of the drones at distant approaches, Sobyanin said, and destroyed 180 more as they neared Moscow. No damage or casualties were reported.
Ukrainian Telegram channels have published footage purportedly filmed in the Moscow region showing a “Pantsir” air defense system firing at targets directly from a highway.
Drones also struck the Saratov region. Saratov Governor Roman Busargin said several residential buildings in Balakovo were damaged and that, according to preliminary information, one person was killed. He later clarified that “all infrastructure facilities in Balakovo are operating normally.”
Monitoring Telegram channels claim the strikes in the Saratov region hit the MegaCOD data center belonging to Sberbank. Construction of the data center in Balakovo began in 2021, and Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko promised it would become the largest in Russia.
The independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo examined photos from the Telegram channels and confirmed they show a damaged Sberbank data center. Fire Point, a Ukrainian manufacturer of drones and missiles, also reported the strike on the Sberbank data center.
The Telegram channel Exilenova+ also confirmed a strike on the industrial zone of the “MZ Balakovo” metallurgical plant, which produces steel and rolled metal products.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Russia-linked bot networks kept their weekly rhythm after drone strikes on three Yandex data centers—disinformation monitor LetsData
articles.body:
The claim that strikes on Russian tech giant Yandex thinned out social media bots finds no support in the networks tracked by Ukrainian disinformation-monitoring company LetsData, co-founder Ksenia Iliuk told Euromaidan Press on 13 October. She cautioned that the strikes may still have affected networks outside the company’s view.
At the Warsaw Security Forum, Lithuania’s prime minister suggested allies should ask Ukraine to strike more Russian data centers because that might help protect European elections from foreign interference. Bot networks are one tool of that interference, so whether the strikes mute them carries weight well beyond Ukraine.
No drop in the networks LetsData tracks
Drones hit Yandex data centers in Sasovo and Vladimir between 8 and 11 October. Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said its FP-1 drones struck Yandex’s Kaluga site in between. On 12 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum that once Ukraine’s response reached Yandex, social media had fewer bots.
More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit
LetsData checked X and Facebook, where bot networks usually stand out clearly, Iliuk said. Its analysts looked at networks attributed to Russia’s influence ecosystem. Among them are groups of X accounts spreading domains from what she called a new wave of Doppelgänger, a Russian campaign that clones real news sites.
Those networks look unaffected, Iliuk said. None of them has stopped posting or broken its usual rhythm, she added. Some are slightly less active, but LetsData’s analysts say that is typical for them. The networks run on a weekly cycle, and the check fell in the part of the week when they post less.
A network that jumped from Germany to Ukraine
LetsData worked with two samples. One covers accounts that systematically target Ukraine, Moldova, and Armenia. The other covers bot networks the company has followed for some time that keep changing their target audience, so they have no fixed country.
Ukrainian drones hit three of Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers in four days. Ukraine’s president says the bots thinned out too
About two weeks ago, one network from that second sample wrote about elections in Germany and spread fake Die Welt sites, she said. It now posts about mobilization in Ukraine and shares a fake site of Ukrinform, Ukraine’s state news agency.
What the check can’t see
The company can compare only within networks whose usual behavior it knows, Iliuk said. Checking the whole internet is impossible because the scale is colossal, she said. A Cloudflare chart that circulated as evidence counted automated web requests from Yandex’s network, including its search crawlers, not social media posts, Cybernews reported.
So the networks LetsData follows show no impact, Iliuk said. That does not mean the strikes had no effect at all, she noted. They may have shown up in networks the company isn’t tracking now. LetsData will keep watching and report other signals if they appear.
Read also
- Russia faked broadcasts from Sweden’s national TV to smear its PM—the same network already hit Germany and France this month
- Russian propagandists fake Polish newspaper claiming Ukraine faces famine
- Russia is stepping up fake Ukrainian government pages as bait for recruiting agents, Ukraine’s security service says

articles.title: EU disburses close to 3 billion euros of defense money to Ukraine ahead of leaders summit
articles.body:
EU disburses close to 3 billion euros of defense money to Ukraine ahead of leaders summit
The EU disbursed 2.86 billion euros ($3.2 billion) in military support to Ukraine on Oct. 14 as part of the bloc's 90 billion-euro ($100 billion) support loan for Kyiv.
"With today's 2.86 billion euro disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The funding will go towards drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition, reads a European Commission press statement.
"As Russia stalls on the front lines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks — cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies," von der Leyen said.
The disbursement lands one day before EU leaders are set to meet for a two-day summit, which President Volodymyr Zelensky is also expected to attend.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," von der Leyen said after an Oct. 11 call with Zelensky.
The latest disbursement was also previewed as a result of that call, with Zelensky thanking von der Leyen for the payment in a Telegram post.
"These funds will strengthen us," Zelensky said.
The latest announcement follows a previous disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) in defense support on Oct. 7, and further disbursements from the EU are expected until the end of the year.
Within the EU's 90 billion euro loan, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) were earmarked for Ukraine's defense needs in 2026, of which 18.26 billion euros ($20.44 billion) have now been disbursed.
Ukraine's plans for how to spend the remaining 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) have already been approved by the EU; all that is required is for Kyiv to send the receipts for sign-off by Brussels.

articles.title: Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs.
“The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation.
In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year.
Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8
— Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026
Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks.
While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast.
Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028.
Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.
Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia.
The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus.
Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe.
The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026
Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.
In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.
Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology.
On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

Leo Greenberg is an assistant editor at Notes from Poland. Based in Kyiv, he writes about global politics, Europe and America, and the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: EU transfers nearly €3bn to Ukraine for drones and urgent military needs
articles.body:
EU transfers nearly €3bn to Ukraine for drones and urgent military needs
The European Commission has transferred €2.86 billion to Ukraine for drones, missiles and urgent battlefield needs.
Source: a press release from the European Commission, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The European Commission disbursed the €2.86 billion as part of the defence component of a €90 billion loan. The funds will be used to purchase drones, air defence equipment, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems and ammunition.
"As Russia stalls on the front lines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks – cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The Commission noted that as Ukraine prepares for its fourth winter since Russia's full-scale invasion, the urgent delivery of defence equipment will ensure that Ukraine's Armed Forces can protect civilians and cities from Russian attacks.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided Ukraine with a total of €231.5 billion in support, including €3.8 billion from proceeds generated by frozen Russian assets.
Background:
- On 11 October, following a phone call with von der Leyen, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the EU will provide Ukraine with approximately €3 billion in military support this week.
- On 18 September, the EU transferred a €3.3 billion tranche to Ukraine under the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan.
