articles.title: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is facing growing backlash over his plan to import diesel from Russia, with some Republican and Democratic lawmakers insisting that the controversial deal “violates” the law.
Congress four years ago passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, which prohibits U.S. imports of Russian-origin energy products covered by Chapter 27 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, including diesel. Democratic Rep. Lloyd Doggett of Texas, the bill's chief sponsor, argued Monday that Trump is “directly violating that law” by “lifting sanctions to permit the first Russian diesel imports into the United States since the law took effect, without satisfying the specific legal conditions it requires.”
He suggested the lack of congressional oversight on Trump’s deal with Putin renders it unlawful, and noted how the plan showcases a sharp turn from Washington, as it comes just weeks after Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine. The sanctions bill was named after Lindsey Graham, the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure.
“Russia can [now] export fossil fuel to the U.S. after Trump violated the specific provisions of a federal statute,” Doggett said on Tuesday in a statement to TIME. “While offering little benefit for Americans, this unlawful action will provide substantial new funding for Putin‘s war machine to continue murdering Ukrainian civilians.”
Doggett’s concerns match those of Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who told NBC’s Meet the Press over the weekend that he believes “there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law.”
Tillis was one of seven Senators who publicly urged the Administration on Sunday to “immediately reverse course” on the agreement announced Friday, arguing that it goes against the 2022 law.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” read the statement co-signed by Republican Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute,” they said.
In a letter sent to Trump on Tuesday, Tillis, Collins, and Murkowski, were joined by fellow Republican Senators Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, John Cornyn of Texas, and Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma alongside six Democratic Senators as they told the President the deal “is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies [and] should be rescinded.” The letter came a day after Trump publicly dismissed the criticism stemming from within his own party.
"Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he told reporters at the White House. “Anything that could help our farmers, our ranchers, I like.”
Trump’s deal to "immediately" supply 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets comes as he faces growing political pressure ahead of the November midterms. Spiraling energy costs have become a key concern for voters, threatening to undermine Republican efforts to maintain their majorities in Congress. The financial upheaval has meant that Trump risks losing his hold on farm country. However, experts are skeptical that an influx of Russian fuel will bring relief to struggling Americans, given how short the supply is due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
While some lawmakers also predict the impact on American consumers will be slight, the key sticking point for many centers on whether Trump’s diesel deal with Putin violates the 2022 law, with some Republicans and Democrats insisting that Trump is pushing the limits of presidential authority. Here’s what to know about the debate—and where legal experts stand on the matter.
According to the 2022 law, what must happen for the import ban on Russian diesel to be lifted?
While Presidents typically have broad authority to waive sanctions, Congress placed specific limits on that power in the April 2022 legislation, says Kristen Eichensehr, a professor of law at Harvard Law School.
“In many sanctions authorities, the President has broad authority to waive imposition of the sanctions or to issue licenses that basically provide an exception to the sanctions,” she tells TIME. “The [2022 act] is an unusual law, given how careful and specific Congress was in providing that the President lacks that flexibility.”
Under Section 3 of the legislation, the President must first consult with the House Ways and Means and Foreign Affairs Committees, along with the Senate Finance and Foreign Relations Committees, and submit a report at least 45 days before providing the required certification.
Lawmakers have argued that the Administration has failed to follow this process.
“The President has to provide a certification to Congress in advance before lifting the prohibition,” says Eichensehr, pointing to the specific criteria set out in the wording of the law.
The law requires a determination by the President to Congress that the Russian Federation has withdrawn and ceased hostilities accepted by Ukraine; poses no immediate threat to any NATO member; and recognizes the right of the Ukrainian people to freely and independently choose their own government.
But Eichensehr insists that these are “not certifications that the President could make at the current moment” because “none of those things have happened, and that's the main restriction in the law.”
Even if all these conditions were met, the legislation would still require the President to wait an additional 90 days before the termination of the import ban could take effect, during which, Congress could enact a joint resolution of disapproval.
“On the substance, the President cannot, as a factual matter, make the certifications because Russia is still attacking Ukraine,” says Eichensehr. “As a procedural matter, [because he reportedly has not consulted Congress], he hasn't followed the process that the law sets out.”
Edward Swaine, a research professor at George Washington University Law School, suggests these restrictions were put in place to ensure that “when the President and the Treasury Secretary decide that circumstances have changed, they go back and explain this to Congress, and give it notice so that it can disagree.”
“The President is supposed to make this determination that Russia has withdrawn its forces and doesn't pose any further threat of aggression. These are fairly high standards,” he tells TIME, noting that the statue provides “Congress with adequate notice to allow it to generate a joint resolution of disapproval.”
“They don't want the President to be able to change this regime on a whim, and so I imagine Congress looking at this action and justifiably thinking that this is inconsistent,” he adds.
Treasury says the diesel deal is being carried out within the legal authorities
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has defended the legality of the agreement, insisting that the Trump Administration is acting within its existing legal authority to help bring energy prices down.
“We’re doing it with all the legal authorities we have, so anyone in Congress who says that—whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill—prohibits us from doing it, is wrong,” he told Fox News on Sunday, without elaborating on which legal authorities he was referring to.
On Friday, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including its importation, until April 7, 2027.
Swaine says that the Administration could argue that “the general license isn't [a] termination of the statutory prohibition; it's a suspension.”
“The [Treasury] Secretary could say this isn't the same thing as ending the prohibition on imports, it's just suspending it until April,” says Swaine. “The second thing [the Administration] could say is that it doesn't apply to all affected products, just a subcategory concerning diesel fuel, so there's [potentially] a difference between the actions that are required for the President to terminate the entire program and the actions that the Secretary is taking here.”
Responding to claims on social media that Bessent and the White House had broken the law, the Office of the Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, part of the Treasury, insisted that the Administration had followed established procedures.
“The granting of this general license is consistent with similar actions previously taken by OFAC and is in compliance with all applicable laws,” the office said over the weekend.
The OFAC permitted transactions involving Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded on vessels, including from vessels previously under U.S. sanctions, to Indian ports in March; the office had also allowed the entry of specified diamonds in August that had been outside Russia before set cutoff dates under a previous Executive Order.
TIME has reached out to the White House and Treasury Department for comment.
How Congress could challenge Trump's diesel deal
Lawmakers could pursue congressional oversight and other political measures to challenge the Administration’s decision.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania has already announced plans to introduce “bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil” under the proposed “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.” Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Republican who has clashed with Trump on other high-profile issues, said he has agreed to co-sponsor the bill, because “Congress must make a stand.”
However, experts tell TIME what Congress is able to do may be limited to more of a symbolic display rather than anything that can move the needle.
“There's limited ability of Congress to do much besides pass legislation and politically enforce that,” says Swaine, suggesting that methods such as “withholding money, appropriations, and hearings” could be used if the situation escalated to that point.

articles.title: Houthis warn of fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia after Sanaa strike
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis warn of fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia after Sanaa strike
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi Arabia struck an oil facility in Sanaa on Tuesday, after the Riyadh-led coalition told civilians to leave the surrounding area in its first evacuation order for the Yemeni capital since the war flared up again.
After a series of strikes on the kingdom's airports and energy sites, the coalition's spokesman said people should leave an oil facility belonging to the Yemen Petroleum Company on the western outskirts of Sanaa before it was attacked.
An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported hearing an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression targets the oil company in Al-Sabaha, west of Sanaa".
The Saudi-led coalition is yet to confirm the reported strike.
Swiftly responding to the earlier coalition warning, the Houthis had issued a threat to target Riyadh's international airport, a refinery, and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces urge all citizens to immediately evacuate and move away from targets that our forces will strike should the Saudi enemy target," military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X, identifying the three targets.
An attack at Riyadh's airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended, rocking the world's top crude oil exporter and deepening the war in Yemen, where the kingdom backs the internationally recognised government.
An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa fearing shortages rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.
The Yemen Petroleum Company sought to reassure the public, saying it had taken all necessary precautions in the event of an emergency to "meet people's needs".
Petroleum stocks were "available in safe facilities and locations, and in sufficient quantities" to meet demand for long periods, it said.
Saudi Arabia was still weathering fresh attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of the kingdom's capital Riyadh.
Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday.
The Saudi coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a humanitarian crisis.
Economic woes
Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.
Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on the Hormuz strait, vital for oil and gas trade, since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.
But the restart in July of Yemen's frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.
Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea - Saudi Arabia's alternative export route.
In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.
Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.
Houthi warning
Blasts were heard over the Saudi capital again late Monday, with the Saudi coalition saying it intercepted a Houthi missile and the group announcing it had again targeted the airport.
On Monday evening, Human Resources Minister Ahmad bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi remained defiant.
"We're not going out," he told the crowd at the Riyadh Economic Forum. "We are safe. With God's will. May God turn their plots back against them."
The Riyadh airport attack prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, after having reportedly rebuffed previous Saudi requests.
The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.
Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

articles.title: Burnham says UK to increase supply of anti-drone missiles to Ukraine, ahead of PMQs and Zelenskyy meeting – UK politics live
articles.body:
Tories blame 'source error' for Badenoch's Right Way policy document overstating cost of net zero by almost £500bn
Peter Walker
Peter Walker is a senior Guardian correspondent.
Kemi Badenoch’s flagship Conservative party conference policy document overstated the estimated cost of net zero by nearly £500bn because of a “source error”, her spokesperson has said, seemingly meaning it was copied from elsewhere and not checked.
A chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a policy document produced for the Tory conference in Birmingham, said the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated in 2020 that reaching net zero by 2050 would cost £957bn.
This baffled experts, and the CCC said it did not recognise the figure. The claimed total was double the £478bn cited in the 2020 document, seemingly because someone tallied a row showing totals for each individual column, along with the figures which made up the totals, thus doubling them.
Badenoch’s spokesperson said:
That was a source error, and it has been corrected online.
The incorrect total was previously published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator, from which it was seemingly copied.
Badenoch’s spokesperson defended the error, saying:
Quite frankly, the people who want to get upset about this should be upset more about the fact that net zero is costing us £500bn.
This is also incorrect. The 2020 estimate from the CCC was £478bn, but its most recent estimate puts the total at £110bn.
At least we learned one thing from PMQs – the Conservative party still has not settled on a reliable line of attack against Andy Burnham (and the one deployed by Kemi Badenoch today was possibly its worst yet.)
Various themes have been deployed: that Burnham is continuity Starmer; that he’s leftwing; that he’s just “eyelashes and a black T-shirt”; that he’s an unprincipled opportunist; and that he is a people pleaser who can’t say no or take tough decisions. There is a bit of truth in most of these assertions (and quite a lot in the final one, which in time may turn out to be the line most useful to the Tories), but none of them has stuck yet, and so today Badenoch tried another.
Badenoch sought to depict Burnham as a serial gaffe-merchant and she set this up with her opening question:
The prime minister has had a busy few weeks tying himself in knots, explaining why national security shouldn’t come at the expense of social security, bumbling into a row still ongoing about Manchester City.
He spent the last 48 hours trying to unsay that Russia influenced the 2016 referendum, when we all heard him say it. Does he ever get tired of putting his foot in his mouth?
What’s true about this is that, unlike his predecessor, whose instinctive response to a question was to recall the No 10 line-to-take and stick to it rigidly, Burnham is someone more inclined to answer questions and to say what he thinks. This has sometimes led to him having to take back something he said (as he did over Manchester City), or reframe an argument in different language (as he did after the PMQs national security/social security answer). But these are not grotesque errors, and any downside is probably more than compensated for by the appeal of a PM who can actually talk a human being.
Badenoch then proceeded to develop this argument by claiming that Burnham received a slap-down from the head of MI5 yesterday. (See 12.16pm.) Given that Ken McCallum told reporters yesterday “I strongly agree with what the prime minister said”, to get from there to Badenoch saying it “the first time I have ever heard the head of MI5 slap down a prime minister for doing Russia’s dirty work for them” required some extraordinarily ingenious spin. It was arguably clever – but also nonsense.
The detail is tedious, but it has to be explained. Essentially, it rests on two acts of misrepresentation. Burnham told the Rest is Politics that there was Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit referendum (which is true), but the Tories have suggested or said outright that Burnham was saying the Russians altered the outcome and that the result was illegitimate. Burnham has never said either of these things.
The second dodgy assertion came yesterday when CCHQ issued a press release saying McCallum had delivered “an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister”. This was in a response to McCallum saying Burnham was right about Russian interference in 2016. McCallum did also say that the impact of Russian interference was limited, and that it would be a mistake to go on about it too much because that would “play into our adversaries’ hands”. But, if that is the problem, you have to ask, who has been banging on it for the past three days? And who raised it at PMQs yesterday?
Burnham saw off the Badenoch attack quite easily. (Badenoch will probably get written up as having scored a great victory in the papers that have swallowed this hogwash, but if the Tories end up believing their own spin, they are in more trouble than they realise.)
One of Burnham’s strengths is that he does not seem to get rattled by this sort of rubbish. His decision to use his final response to Badenoch to praise what she said about race and Englishness at PMQs was a good one, and he even managed to adopt a cordial tone towards Nigel Farage. Being nice and personable does not guarantee success in politics, but it is a start and it helps to explain why Burnham is currently the most admired of the party leaders.
Burnham urges Nigel Farage to accept small boat crossings coming down
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, said every week unidentified males from Iran are arriving in the UK on small boats. He asked Burnham to accept this was a national security emergency.
Burnham began his reply recognising that the person accused of killing Ann Widdecombe has been charged with planning an attack against Farage. He went on:
Can I start by recognising it’s been a hard time for him and his family. There’s a lot we disagree on, but I defend his right to say it, and I will work hard to secure his safety.
On Iran, he said:
We’ve seen the issues at RAF Fairford recently, and they have been dealt with in the right way with the utmost seriousness by the police and security services.
And the key point is, of course, we do need to get, boat crossings down. I hope he would recognise that they are coming down. Removals are up. There is much more to be done, but there is clearly progress in the right direction.
Burnham declines invitation from Ed Davey to agree Trump has committed 'shameful betrayal of Ukrainian people'
Davey asked Burnham to accept that President Trump’s decision to buy diesel from Russia is “yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security”.
Burnham said he called President Zelenskyy on Saturday “because I recognised it was another very dark and difficult moment for him”.
But he said that his role was to “try and repair bridges so that the support comes back”. He wanted to bring people together.
Burnham says further cross-party talks on social care reform to take place soon, 'hopefully within next month'
Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, got a huge cheer when he spoke – a reference to his success in seeing off a supposed threat to his leadership. (See 10.55am.)
He asked when Burnham would hold another round of cross-party talks on social care reform.
Burnham welcomed Davey’s commitment to this issue, and said he was determined to change the system.
He said he would organise more cross-party talks, “certainly before the end of the year, but hopefully within the next month”.
Burnham praises Badenoch for her Tory conference speech attack on Reform UK's ethnonationalism
Badenoch said she met a beauty salon owner yesterday struggling with taxes. She went on:
That is the brutal reality for tens of thousands of small business owners.
She said Burnham promised the biggest change for 40 years when he became PM. But now he is promising a no change budget, she said.
Burnham said he used his conference speech to address difficult decisions.
But he ended praising Badenoch for what she said in her conference speech criticising ethnonationalism.
I’m going to commend her for drawing a line on a decade of division where she drew a line with the party over [Reform UK] there for suggesting that her children weren’t British. That is wrong in every single respect.
She was brave and she was right to call it out. That is what I want to see more of in the next decade as we go forward.
Badenoch said she met Milburn and he told her the report would be published before the budget. Now it is coming after the budget, she said. She said the PM should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.
Burnham said the government would honour its commitments on defence spending.
He went on to taunt Badenoch over her party conference “Iron Dome” interviews.
I recall an interview recently about the Conservatives’ plans for an Iron Dome. And then she said it isn’t our plan. And then it emerged that it was briefed by her team, which doesn’t sound like she’s in control of her own policy on defence.
And then under questioning on LBC for [Nick] Ferrari, she said you’ve got to speak to a defence expert about exactly how it will work. Well, obviously we worked out in that interview she wasn’t a defence expert.
Badenoch moved on to the Jackdow and Rosebank gas and oilfield applications. She said:
The fact is this prime minister will say anything instead of dealing with the tough decisions that only he can take, like on Britain’s energy security.
In July, he said he would approve the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields in the North Sea. What’s he waiting for?
If he’d approved them back then, we would have British gas warming British homes this winter.
Burnham said the government has had to take time making a decision because the decisions taken by the last Tory government were overtuned in court. They messed it up, he said.
Burnham dismisses Badenoch's claim he was criticised by MI5 chief in speech yesterday
Badenoch claims that yesterday the head of MI5 had to slap down Burnham over his Russia comment. She claims she has never heard that before.
This is the first time I have ever heard the head of MI5 slap down a prime minister for doing Russia’s dirty work for them.
Either the prime minister knew what he was doing on that podcast, trying to undermine the 2016 referendum, or he opened his mouth on a matter of national security and said the first thing that came into his head.
So does the prime minister agree with the director-general of MI5 that talking up Russian interference was a mistake?
I think it’s important that we are clear-eyed about what happened in the past. There is, incontrovertible evidence that outside actors, enemies to this country, have interfered in our democratic processes, and it is inconceivable that that was not taking place across the whole of the last decade.
Badenoch was referring to McCallum saying it was important not to overstate the impact of Russian interference in the Brexit referendum.
Burnham defends comment saying Russia interfered in Brexit referendum
Kemi Badenoch says she thinks Burnham’s “carefully worded” answer on Manchester won’t suffice.
She also refers to Burnham’s comments about defence and welfare, and about Russia and the Brexit referendum, and she asks if he ever gets tired of putting his foot in his mouth.
Burnham says he is glad Badenoch has raised Russia again. He says:
It gives me an opportunity to say to the whole house how I intend to lead this country. We have lived through a decade of division, and we know that hostile actors have been seeking to interfere in our democratic process. That is a matter of fact.
He says that, when Badenoch was a minister and in charge of the elections bill, she said she had not even read the Russia report.
He goes on:
I will draw a line. I will defend our democracy, and I will lead this country forward with positivity, unity and hope in the next decade.
Burnham says no one from Manchester City raised with him charges it was facing from Premier League
Jerome Mayhew (Con) asks if anyone from Manchester City raised with him, or anyone from his team, the charges the club was facing from the Premier League.
Burnham says the club did not raise that issue with him.
He says he has released information about his contacts with the club.
Andy Burnham starts by saying he worked with David Amess on the Commons health committee when he was a new MP. He says he was “very fond” of Amess, and he says there is more work to be done on protecting MPs.
He says he is meeting President Zelenskyy later.
And he pays tribute to a Manchester councillor who is retiring.

articles.title: Ukrainian Defence Forces strike Russian drone storage and launch site near Donetsk
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defence Forces strike Russian drone storage and launch site near Donetsk
Ukrinform reports this, citing the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Telegram post.
On October 13 and during the night of October 14, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck several Russian military targets.
In the Donetsk area, they hit a site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones.
Systematic strikes against such facilities are intended to reduce Russia's ability to attack civilian infrastructure across Ukraine.
In addition, Russian military logistics depots were struck near Popova Balka and Hirnyk in the Donetsk region.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck a maintenance base in Russia's Kursk region for self-propelled launchers and transport-loading vehicles belonging to the Iskander-M tactical ballistic missile system.
Photo: ArmyInform

articles.title: Bulgaria summons Russian ambassador after fourth attack on merchant ships in the country’s waters
articles.body:
Two merchant ships were attacked off Bulgaria’s coast overnight into Oct. 13, according to a report by local news agency BGNES, which cited information discussed at an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council that was held on Oct. 13. Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgarian authorities had no evidence linking the strikes to any particular country; however, he added that Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova would be summoned for an explanation. A week earlier, two other merchant ships were attacked in Bulgarian waters, with authorities in Sofia saying then that they also could not determine which country was responsible.
The cargo ship Chelsea 3, sailing under the Maltese flag and registered in Odesa, was attacked by three drones while it was located approximately 18 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian town of Byala. A distress signal was received at around 1:30 a.m. All 15 crew members — seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis — were evacuated and taken to Varna. Five sailors suffered minor injuries.
During the Security Council meeting, officials also disclosed that another merchant ship had been attacked about 17 nautical miles east of the coastal village of Krapets; that ship later sank. Preliminary information indicated that one crew member was rescued.
Radev said “another attack on merchant vessels in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable,” but added that Sofia had no evidence establishing the origin of the drones and therefore could not assign responsibility to a specific country. He said Bulgaria would nevertheless seek an explanation from Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova. Radev explained:
“The logic of what is happening indicates that the outcome of these attacks benefits the Russian Federation.”
A week earlier, on Oct. 6, two civilian merchant ships were attacked by drones in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone: the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able. The crew of the Able was evacuated, while search and rescue operations Alfa Watan produced no results. On Oct. 7, Bulgarian authorities called off the efforts.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at the time that Russia was behind the attack. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, however, said Sofia could not confirm whether the drones were Russian or Ukrainian. He also described Bulgaria as being caught up in the hybrid war between Russia and Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia built new Millerovo drone base for Geran-5 UAVs in one month – satellite images
articles.body:
Russia built new Millerovo drone base for Geran-5 UAVs in one month – satellite images
In just one month, Russia has built a new Millerovo drone launch site for launching Geran-5 attack drones.
Source: Absolutely Reliable Source, a Ukrainian OSINT community
Quote: "On 1 September, there was nothing there but an empty field. Now, the first section of the facility is nearing completion..."
Details: Absolutely Reliable Source said the site has eight designated launcher positions and 32 areas for preparing UAVs for launch. Satellite images taken on 12 October also show drones being unloaded in Zone 3.
The community said construction has been accelerated to expand Russia's attack capabilities following the September strikes on Kyiv. The construction style closely resembles that of the Tsimbulova drone base.
"There will be no conclusions. Conventional kamikaze drones cannot effectively destroy facilities like this. So I very much hope that the ballistic missiles we have been promised will finally start flying for real, rather than just appearing in social media posts," the OSINT community added.
Absolutely Reliable Source also provided the coordinates of the drone launch site: 48.995968, 40.286255.
Background:
- Absolutely Reliable Source previously released satellite images showing damage to Russia's Tsimbulova drone base following an attack on the night of 30 September-1 October. Located near the village of Bolkhov, the base is used, among other things, to launch Geran attack drones.
- Ukrainska Pravda and the Cyberboroshno GEOINT community have investigated Russian drone bases and attacks against them.
Read more: "Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Missile alert interrupts Saudi minister mid-speech (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Missile alert interrupts Saudi minister mid-speech (VIDEO)
A missile alert interrupted a speech by a Saudi minister, Ahmed bin Sulaiman Al Rajhi, while he was addressing an economic forum in Riyadh on Monday, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
The incident occurred at the Riyadh International Convention and Exhibition Centre, when warning notifications sounded simultaneously on the minister’s phone and those of audience members.
Al Rajhi, the human resources and social development minister, briefly acknowledged the alerts before calmly continuing his speech.
“We are under the protection of the Lord of the Worlds. God willing, may God turn their plot back upon them,” he told the audience.
The interruption came after two consecutive Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the weekend, which killed more than a dozen people, including several foreign nationals.
Residents reported hearing several powerful explosions in the Saudi capital on Monday night, according to Al Jazeera. The Saudi military said its air defenses had intercepted at least one Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh, along with two additional projectiles launched toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
Saudi Arabia’s aviation authority announced on Monday that Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport would remain closed until October 17 following the deadly strikes.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack. In an exclusive interview with RT, Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a spokesperson for the group, described the strike as retaliation for years of Saudi bombardment of Yemen’s civilian infrastructure.
He warned that the Houthis would continue targeting Saudi military facilities and critical infrastructure until Riyadh ended its involvement in Yemen, lifted its blockade and agreed to a “comprehensive and permanent peace.”
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015, leading a military coalition supporting the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but flared up again in July after Saudi-backed Yemeni forces struck the Houthi-held Sanaa Airport.
Last month, the Houthis seized large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and territory around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, including the port of Mocha.
Saudi-backed government forces have since launched a counteroffensive, claiming to have recaptured key positions near the vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Riyadh has stepped up its air support for the offensive, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory in recent days. According to the group, Saudi bombardments have killed nearly 400 people since early September, many of them civilians.

articles.title: Gazan families fight to protect slain journalists' legacies
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Killed twice': Gaza families fight to clear the names of journalists branded militants by Israel
"Publishing my son’s name on that list is a second assassination," begins 70-year-old Bakr al-Louh. "The first time, they killed his body. Now they are killing his legacy and his career as a journalist. They are killing him in his grave."
His son, Ahmed al-Louh, was a photojournalist working for Al Jazeera. He was 39 when an Israeli strike hit a civil defence post in Nuseirat refugee camp, in central Gaza, on 15 December 2024. He had returned there shortly before, after filming ambulances carrying the bodies of people killed in an earlier Israeli strike nearby.
On 1 October, the family found Ahmed’s name and photograph in The Press Files, an online database published by the Israeli occupation. It names 170 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed in Gaza and claims they were members or fighters of armed factions.
"This news destroyed us," his father says. He says the allegations against Ahmed are "lies, with no basis in truth."
Ahmed’s page on the site lists him as a military operative in Hamas’s armed wing. When The New Arab viewed it on 11 October, it contained no supporting evidence. Its only image linked to an internal address and did not load.
The Israeli army claims the database is the product of an in-depth investigation, drawing on open-source information, documents seized in Gaza, interrogations of alleged militants and intelligence gathered during military operations.
But the evidence it presents varies widely, from cropped documents to old photographs.
In 49 cases, the main evidence is an obituary published by an armed group. An analysis by +972 Magazine found that 59 of the pages contain no evidence at all, only a line saying the claim is based on intelligence sources.
For Bakr al-Louh, the list is an extension of the war on Gaza’s journalists. Targeting them, he says, is "an attempt to silence the free word and the truth, because the occupation doesn’t want any voice or image to come out of Gaza that exposes its massacres."
The fear does not stop with the dead. "We have a real fear that these accusations will reach the rest of the family," he tells The New Arab. If any of them needs urgent medical treatment outside Gaza, he worries Israel could reject them on security grounds.
‘He moved in the open’
Ahmed Khaireddine, 30, was a cameraman for Al-Quds Al-Youm. He was killed on 27 December 2023, when an Israeli strike hit his home in Beit Lahia, in northern Gaza. His uncle Mohammed Khaireddine, a journalist with Al-Aqsa TV, died with him, along with 23 other members of the family.
The Press Files describes Ahmed as an Islamic Jihad commander and lists his employer as Al-Aqsa TV, the channel his uncle worked for. His brother Basel, 36, a journalist himself, says the photograph on the page is fabricated. He says he had never seen it in his life. He believes the way his brother died is the clearest proof the allegations are false.
"Before he was killed, Ahmed spent more than 80 days moving around with his camera and his blue vest, covering al-Shifa and the Indonesian hospitals," he tells The New Arab.
"If he had really been a military target, they would have picked him off in the streets and public squares, where he moved openly. But he was killed with his family, in a massacre that destroyed three adjoining houses at once and killed more than 30 civilians."
Many of the names on the list, he says, belong to colleagues he saw every day. "We saw them all the time where journalists gathered at hospitals and out in the field, and we never once saw them among gunmen or fighters. They were doing their work in the open, and the drones above them knew very well they were civilians doing their jobs," Basel says.
He says Israel is deliberately confusing political affiliation with combat. "A Palestinian is born with a political affiliation. That is nothing shameful, and it does not take a journalist out of the civilian work protected under international law."
'A ready-made warrant'
Photojournalist Bilal Abu Samak says the database’s real purpose is to justify the killing of journalists who covered the war. He and Mohammed both describe the accusations as a ready-made warrant, one that could be used against journalists who are still alive and still reporting.
Gaza’s journalists, Abu Samak says, are civilians who wear protective vests and carry no weapons.
"Through this list, they are trying to terrify us and force us to abandon journalism, especially as they keep barring international journalists from entering Gaza to document their violations," he says.
"We demand real protection for press crews, and that the professional legacy of our colleagues who were killed be preserved."
Israel has barred foreign reporters from Gaza since the start of the war, apart from brief visits escorted by the army, and denies deliberately targeting journalists.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) told The New Arab it was still reviewing all the claims in the database. When new information emerges about the killing of a journalist anywhere in the world, it said, it reviews each case independently and updates its records.
CPJ published the database a week after completing its own review.
On 24 September, the New York-based group removed 22 people from its list of journalists killed in Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory. It found that 19 of them had been militants or had taken part in combat, and that three could not be confirmed as journalists.
CPJ now counts 191 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed by Israeli forces. It said Israeli forces remain responsible for the large majority of journalist killings worldwide since 2023, and that each case in its review required interviews with at least two independent, credible sources as well as desk research.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate puts the toll higher, at more than 260. Its secretary-general, Ahed Farawneh, says the timing of the Israeli database is no accident.
"The occupation is trying to get around the huge numbers of journalists killed by levelling these false accusations of links to armed groups," he says, "to justify targeting them after a global outcry and strong condemnation from journalists’ unions and international organisations."
When the syndicate looks at the lives of those killed, he says, it finds that "they were working under the sun," in plain sight and far from any armed faction.
The syndicate says it applies criteria matching those of the International Federation of Journalists before recognising anyone as a journalist killed in the line of duty.
It is also building a case file of killings, injuries, arrests, destroyed offices and homes, and families wiped out and documenting the ban on foreign press and on bringing cameras and equipment into Gaza.
"We have obtained power of attorney from the families of those killed, and from injured journalists and former detainees, to file cases at the International Criminal Court," Ahed says.
"Unfortunately, the court is still stalling on opening this file. But together with the International Federation of Journalists, we insist on it, and on the families’ right to take the occupation to court."
He points to earlier legal efforts over the killings of journalists Shireen Abu Akleh, Ahmed Abu Hussein and Yaser Murtaja. The syndicate is also working with rights groups and legal experts to bring cases in countries whose laws allow prosecution of war crimes committed abroad.
'In case of doubt'
Hussein Hammad, a specialist in media and human rights, says the database deliberately blurs the line between political or institutional affiliation and taking a direct part in hostilities.
Working for a media outlet linked to a political faction, or sympathising with one, does not strip a journalist of civilian protection, he says.
International humanitarian law is clear on this. Article 79 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions states that journalists on dangerous professional missions in armed conflict are civilians and must be protected as such.
Under Article 51, civilians lose that protection only "for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities." Article 50 adds that "in case of doubt whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian."
Accusing journalists after they have been killed, with no chance to answer the charges, has no legal value, Hammad says, and amounts to a cover for extrajudicial killing.
International justice, he adds, does not accept military verdicts based on evidence the victim or their lawyer can never see or challenge. He says the response must be to document every violation, gather physical evidence and build cases for court.
For Bakr al-Louh, the fight is also about memory. His son’s last assignment was to document the dead of Nuseirat being carried to hospital. Shortly afterwards, he was among them.
Ismail Nofal is a Gaza-based journalist specialising in human interest stories
This article was published in collaboration with Egab

articles.title: North Korea building military deployment, logistics capabilities through Ukraine war: US general
articles.body:
North Korea is gaining valuable experience in long-distance troop deployments and military logistics through its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, the commander of US Forces Korea said on Tuesday.
Gen. Xavier Brunson told a discussion hosted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington that Pyongyang's support for Moscow had strengthened its operational capabilities, according to Yonhap News Agency.
"They've learned how to go from North Korea to find themselves in Russia to move men, weapons and equipment there," Brunson said.
He said North Korean forces had gained experience in establishing supply chains, moving troops and equipment over long distances and mobilising military resources, extending their capabilities beyond battlefield tactics.
Brunson warned that Pyongyang's ability to incorporate wartime experience into its military operations could complicate deterrence efforts by Washington and Seoul.
He also said Russia had provided North Korea with military equipment, including electronic warfare jammers, in exchange for its support.
Turning to the proposed transfer of wartime operational control from the US to South Korea, Brunson reiterated his support for a conditions-based transition, cautioning against proceeding before critical military requirements were met.
He also proposed expanding cooperation with South Korea's defence industry to establish regional maintenance and repair capabilities for US military equipment.
In July, South Korea was monitoring reports of additional North Korean troop deployments to Russia, while Japan condemned growing military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang.
The two countries strengthened their military partnership after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a mutual defence treaty in June 2024.

articles.title: Russia arrests Japanese Hokkaido Shimbun journalist on suspicion of spying
articles.body:
Moscow's FSB security service said a Japanese national was arrested on the Far East island of Sakhalin, near a disputed cluster of islands, but did not name the individual.
Tokyo summoned the Russian ambassador on Wednesday to lodge a protest over Moscow's arrest of a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, with the foreign ministry urging "fair and impartial treatment."
Russia has arrested several citizens of what it calls "unfriendly" countries in recent years, accusing them of working for Western intelligence services.
Russia's foreign ministry identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper on Tuesday, with a spokesperson saying he was accused of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory."
Moscow's FSB security service said a Japanese national was arrested on the Far East island of Sakhalin, near a disputed cluster of islands, but did not name the individual.
It said the person had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia's defences.
On Wednesday, the Japanese foreign ministry said European Affairs Bureau official Kimitake Nakamura summoned the Russian ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev.
Nakamura "lodged a strong protest with the Russian side over the detention of a Japanese national and the issuance of unilateral statements regarding the case", the ministry said in a statement.
It added that Tokyo had not received any explanation concerning the case.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitri Peskov meanwhile said in a briefing that the security service "is doing its job."
"If there are spies, they get caught," he said.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Japan has not been able to contact the individual and did not know about the arrest until the official announcement from Moscow.
Japanese diplomats in Russia have requested "the prompt provision of information" and "humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment," Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the Russian announcement but was "still confirming the details."
"Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority and we are responding accordingly," the newspaper said.
Territorial dispute
The FSB said it had "opened a criminal case against the Japanese national" and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, TASS and RIA Novosti news agencies reported, citing the security service.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
"Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia...to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
This was "not an isolated case," she added.
The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Media rights group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called for the journalist's "rights to be respected and for his release," saying in a statement on X that the gathering of information is part of journalism.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him.
He was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention.
It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred.

articles.title: Uvision shows remote kamikaze drone launcher at AUSA
articles.body:
- Uvision is showing an eight-canister HERO 120 launcher at AUSA 2026, designed for remote operation in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations.
- The HERO 120 is already on contract with the U.S. Army under a Lethal Unmanned Systems deal worth up to $982 million.
Israeli loitering munition maker Uvision is showing an eight-canister launcher for its HERO 120 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, pitching the remotely operated system as a way to spread strike capacity across land and maritime platforms and tie it to the company’s AI-enabled CORTEX mission management software.
The Multi-Canister Launcher holds up to eight HERO 120 loitering munitions and is designed for remote operation, according to the company’s Oct. 13 announcement. Uvision says it can be fielded in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations, and that CORTEX, which the company describes as an AI-enabled battle intelligence and mission management system, links the launcher with sensors and decision-makers in what it calls a sensor-to-effect network.
Loitering munitions, often called kamikaze drones, can circle over an area while an operator searches for a target and then dive onto it with a warhead. The HERO 120 is a mid-range design aimed at armored vehicles and other high-value targets, combining reconnaissance and strike in one airframe with a built-in camera that lets the operator abort an attack and re-engage.
Uvision singled out border defense as one use for the multi-canister setup, with launch nodes spread across long stretches of border in mobile and fixed positions and connected through CORTEX to surveillance assets, so that a threat spotted in one sector can be answered from the nearest launcher. The company did not name any customer that has ordered the launcher or say whether it is being offered to the U.S. Army.
At the same show, Uvision is demonstrating Wayland Autonomy’s IRIS airborne surveillance payload running with Tactical CORTEX, a version of the software for forward units. The company says the pairing adds wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in areas where GPS signals are jammed or unavailable.
“It’s not just about having more effects in the field. It’s about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of Uvision.
The HERO 120 already has a foothold in the U.S. Army, and in October 2025 the service awarded Mistral Inc. and Uvision a multi-year contract worth up to $982 million under the Lethal Unmanned Systems program to buy, field, train on and sustain the weapon, with Mistral as prime contractor and Uvision as design authority. Production systems passed their first lot acceptance tests in August 2026, and the companies then received an additional order worth more than $50 million to increase the number of HERO 120 systems and support equipment going to soldiers.
The smaller HERO 90 supports the U.S. Army’s Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort, known as LASSO, which tests soldier-portable, tube-launched loitering munitions for infantry units. The U.S. Marine Corps fitted HERO 120 munitions on one of its Long-Range Unmanned Surface Vessels in 2023, an early example of the maritime launch role Uvision now advertises for the multi-canister launcher.
Beyond the HERO line, Uvision markets the VIPER encapsulated multi-mission systems and the PEREGRINE tactical kinetic systems, and says CORTEX is meant to manage effectors across all three families.
